Service · Geotechnical
# Landslide and slope stability investigation and protection design
For hill roads, railways and project sites, DATA PKT finds which slopes are likely to fail, why, and what will hold them: drone LiDAR and 3D models, seismic refraction, geological mapping, stability analysis and the design of slope protection.
What we investigate
Road and rail cut slopes, embankments, hill sites and rockfall zones
Methods
Drone LiDAR and 3D models, seismic refraction tomography, geological mapping, DGPS
What you get
Factor of safety per section, hazard map, priority list, protection design
Recent project
~66 km road corridor in Assam
In short: DATA PKT is a landslide and slope stability investigation company. We combine three independent data sets in one ground model: drone LiDAR for the shape of the slope, seismic refraction tomography for what lies below the surface, and geological mapping for how the soil and rock behave. A stability analysis turns that model into a factor of safety for every critical section, and we design the protection each stretch needs.
## Why slopes fail, and why one method is not enough
Most slope failures along Indian hill roads and railways come from a few mechanisms: shallow slides in soil and weathered rock after heavy rain, erosion and scour at the toe, and rock blocks sliding or toppling along joints. Each needs different information; no single method supplies it all, so we combine methods and check them against each other.
A terrain model shows the geometry but not what is underneath; a borehole shows one point; a geologist sees the rock face but not its depth. That is why we combine the methods below.
Desk study · alignment data · drone permission · DGPS control network DRONE LiDAR the surface SEISMIC REFRACTION what lies below GEOLOGICAL MAPPING how the material behaves DTM, contours, sections slope angle, scarps, 3D P-wave velocity sections soil thickness, rock depth RMR, GSI, SMR, joints strength c' and φ' Integrated ground model geometry + layering + strength Slope stability analysis factor of safety: dry, saturated, earthquake Hazard zonation · priority list · protection design inputs
How the three investigation streams combine into one ground model, a stability analysis and a hazard map.
## What we do
### 1. Drone LiDAR survey and 3D models
RTK/PPK drone LiDAR tied to DGPS ground control captures the slope and the road edge, even under vegetation. Multiple laser returns let the point cloud be classified into ground and vegetation, so we deliver a bare-earth digital terrain model (DTM), a surface model (DSM), contours, an orthophoto, slope-angle and aspect maps, longitudinal and cross-sections, and 3D models of critical stretches. See LiDAR survey .
### 2. Seismic refraction tomography (SRT)
A line of geophones (typically 24 channels) is laid on the slope or road edge and a hammer source is struck at several shot points along it. First-arrival times are picked and inverted into a P-wave velocity section that shows the thickness of loose cover, the depth to weathered and fresh rock, and low-velocity zones that are weak or saturated. Every profile is positioned by DGPS so it plots directly on the LiDAR cross-sections. See seismic refraction survey .
### 3. Engineering geological mapping
Geologists map lithology and structure at the critical locations, measure joints by scanline and window surveys, test strength in the field with a Schmidt hammer and point-load tester, and classify the rock mass with RMR , GSI and SMR . Stereonets and kinematic analysis show which failure modes are possible: planar sliding, wedge sliding or toppling.
### 4. Strength parameters
Shear strength (cohesion c′ and friction angle φ′) is derived from GSI and field strength through the generalised Hoek–Brown criterion, with Barton–Bandis for joints, cross-checked against the SRT velocities. Laboratory tests on borehole samples are recommended for the most critical sections.
### 5. Slope stability analysis
Limit-equilibrium analysis (Bishop, Spencer and Morgenstern–Price methods) gives a factor of safety for each critical section in three cases: dry, saturated (monsoon) and earthquake (pseudo-static, with the seismic coefficient for the site's IS 1893 zone). Rock slopes are also checked for planar and wedge failure.
Road Ground surface drone LiDAR Soil / loose cover SRT: low velocity Weathered rock SRT: medium velocity Joints geological mapping Fresh rock SRT: high velocity Possible slip surface
What each method shows on one road cut slope: the surface from LiDAR, the layering from seismic refraction, the joints from geological mapping, and the slip surface the analysis checks.
### 6. Hazard zonation and protection design
Every stretch is ranked Low, Medium, High or Critical, so the owner knows where to act first. For each stretch we recommend and design protection matched to its failure mechanism:
Problem found | Typical protection we design | Key inputs from the investigation
Water in the slope, saturated soil | Surface and sub-surface drainage, weep holes, catch-water drains | Seepage points, saturated case factor of safety, LiDAR drainage paths
Shallow slides in soil and weathered rock | Soil nails with flexible high-tensile mesh, re-grading, vegetation and erosion-control mats | Thickness of loose cover from SRT, c′ and φ′, slope geometry
Rock blocks on joints | Rock anchors and bolts, cable nets, rockfall drapes | Joint sets and kinematics, block size, depth to competent rock
Rockfall from higher slopes | Rockfall barriers and catch fences located on trajectory analysis | Source zones from mapping, fall-line profiles from LiDAR
Toe erosion and scour beside rivers | Toe walls, gabions, river-training measures | Toe profile, scour-prone sections, flood levels
## What you receive
- Classified point cloud, DTM and DSM, contours, orthophoto, slope-angle maps, cross-sections and 3D models (LAS/LAZ, GeoTIFF, DWG/DXF, SHP, OBJ, KMZ)
- SEG-2 field data, velocity tomograms with interpretation and depth to competent strata for every SRT profile
- Geological plans and sections, discontinuity database, stereonets, RMR/GSI/SMR sheets and strength parameters
- Stability analysis for each critical section, hazard zonation map and priority list
- Protection design: concept and design drawings, design parameters and quantities for each stretch
- An integrated report with all data on a drive, in your coordinate system
## Standards and practice
DGPS control tied to Survey of India or CORS; LiDAR accuracy reported against independent check points (ASPRS); discontinuity surveys to IS 11315; point-load testing to IS 8764; RMR to IS 13365; seismic zones and coefficients to IS 1893; roadside work-zone safety to IRC:SP:55; drone operations under the Drone Rules, 2021 with Digital Sky permissions.
## Where this matters
Hill roads and railways in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Sikkim, the Himalayan states, the Western Ghats and the Nilgiris; tunnel portals and cuttings; hydropower, transmission and pipeline corridors through hills. See our work in Northeast India .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What does a slope stability investigation include?
Three independent data sets combined in one ground model: drone LiDAR for the shape of the slope, seismic refraction tomography for what lies below the surface, and geological mapping for how the soil and rock behave. A stability analysis then gives a factor of safety for each critical section, and the slopes are ranked by hazard with remedial measures.
Q: What is seismic refraction tomography (SRT) used for on slopes?
On slopes, SRT shows the thickness of loose soil, the depth to weathered and fresh rock, and weak or saturated zones, which sets the length of soil nails and anchors and the depth of possible slip surfaces. It reads these from the speed of sound waves sent into the ground from a hammer source and recorded on a line of geophones.
Q: Why use drone LiDAR instead of a photo survey for slopes?
Slopes beside hill roads are usually under trees and shrubs. LiDAR records several returns from each laser pulse, so the ground under the vegetation can be classified and a bare-earth terrain model produced. That gives true slope angles, heights, scarps and cross-sections where a photo survey would only see the canopy.
Q: What are RMR, GSI and SMR?
They are rock mass classification systems. RMR (Rock Mass Rating) and GSI (Geological Strength Index) describe rock quality from strength, joints and groundwater; SMR (Slope Mass Rating) adjusts RMR for how the joints sit relative to the slope face. Together with field strength tests they give the strength parameters used in the stability analysis.
Q: Does DATA PKT design slope protection?
Yes. From the investigation we prepare the design inputs and the design of protection measures such as drainage, soil nails and anchors, flexible high-tensile mesh, rockfall drapes and barriers, and erosion control, matched to each stretch's failure mechanism and hazard level. We survey, investigate and design; we do not install.
Q: Which areas of India need this most?
Hill roads and railways in the Himalaya, the Northeast, the Western Ghats and the Nilgiris, where heavy monsoon rain, weak weathered rock and seismic activity combine. Much of the Northeast lies in seismic Zone V under IS 1893, the highest zone.

Service · Geophysical
# Seismic refraction survey and tomography (SRT)
See below the surface without digging: DATA PKT runs seismic refraction surveys to find soil thickness, depth to rock and weak zones for slopes, roads, tunnels, dams and foundations, positioned by DGPS and read together with drone LiDAR and geology.
Finds
Soil thickness, depth to weathered and fresh rock, weak or saturated zones
Typical depth
About 20–30 m with a 24-channel spread
Used for
Landslides and slopes, roads, tunnels, dams, bridges, foundations
Recent project
66 profiles along a road corridor in Assam
In short: seismic refraction measures how fast sound travels through the ground. Sound moves faster in harder material, so the arrival times recorded by a line of geophones show where loose soil ends, where rock begins and where the ground is weak. Tomographic inversion turns those times into a velocity section along each profile, which engineers use to set the depth of slip surfaces, soil nails, anchors and foundations.
## How a seismic refraction survey works
A line of 24 geophones is laid along the profile, typically 3–5 m apart. A sledgehammer is struck on a steel plate at several shot points along and beyond the line, and the seismograph records the waves at every geophone. The pattern of first-arrival times reveals each layer's depth and velocity.
Each shot is repeated and stacked to lift the signal above traffic and wind noise. Waves that refract along faster layers reach distant geophones first.
Hammer 24 geophones, 3–5 m apart, cable to the seismograph Soil / loose cover · slow Weathered rock · faster Fresh rock · fastest Waves bend along each faster layer and return to the surface; their arrival times give each layer's depth and velocity.
A seismic refraction spread: hammer source, geophone line and the refracted wave paths that reveal each layer.
## What the velocities tell you
P-wave velocity rises as the ground gets harder and less fractured. Velocities below about 800 m/s usually mean dry soil, fill or loose colluvium; 800–1,500 m/s compact or saturated soil or highly weathered rock; 1,500–2,500 m/s weathered or fractured rock; and above about 2,500 m/s fresh, competent rock.
The ranges below are typical guides only; every site is calibrated against geology and, where available, boreholes.
Seismic refraction in a two-layer model. Beyond the crossover distance, the wave refracted along the faster layer arrives first. The slopes of the travel-time plot give V₁ and V₂, and the intercept gives the depth to the interface. The method needs velocity to increase with depth.
Typical P-wave velocity | What it usually means | Why it matters
Below about 800 m/s | Dry soil, fill, loose colluvium | Material most likely to slide; thickness sets nail length and excavation
About 800–1,500 m/s | Compact or saturated soil, highly weathered rock | Often the zone of shallow slides after rain; water table indicator
About 1,500–2,500 m/s | Weathered or fractured rock | Possible slip zones; rock that can often be ripped
Above about 2,500 m/s | Fresh, competent rock | Anchor bond zone, foundation level, tunnel rock
## Where we use it
- Landslides and slopes: thickness of unstable cover and depth of possible slip surfaces. See landslide and slope stability .
- Roads and railways in hills: cut-slope design, depth to rock along the alignment, rippability for excavation.
- Tunnels and portals: rock quality and weak zones at portals and shallow sections.
- Dams, weirs and barrages: depth to bedrock along the axis and at abutments.
- Bridges, substations and buildings: foundation level between boreholes.
## Why combine it with drone LiDAR
Every geophone and shot point is surveyed by DGPS, and the ground elevations along the profile come from our drone LiDAR terrain model. The tomogram therefore sits exactly on the true ground surface and plots directly on the LiDAR cross-sections, so surface shape and subsurface layers are read together in one ground model. That is how we work on LiDAR and slope projects.
## Specifications we work to
Item | Typical specification
Seismograph | 24-channel engineering seismograph, SEG-2 output
Geophones | Vertical, 10–14 Hz, at 3–5 m spacing
Source | 8 kg sledgehammer on a steel plate, stacked shots
Shots | About 9 per spread: off-ends, ends and interior
Positioning | DGPS for every geophone and shot; elevations from LiDAR
Processing | First-break picking, delay-time starting model, tomographic inversion; RMS misfit target under 5%
Quality checks | Daily line and geophone tests, reciprocal-time check, repeat of noisy shots, second-person review of picks
Guidance | IS 15681 and ASTM D5777
## What you receive
- Field data (SEG-2) and observer logs
- Profile location map (KMZ, DWG) in your coordinate system
- First-break picks and time–distance plots
- Velocity tomogram for each profile, with ray coverage and RMS error
- Interpreted section: soil, weathered and fresh rock, weak or saturated zones
- Depth to competent strata along each profile, and a short report

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is a seismic refraction survey?
A geophysical survey that measures how fast sound waves travel through the ground. A hammer or other source sends waves into the ground and a line of geophones records them. Waves travel faster in harder material, so the arrival times show the thickness of soil, the depth to weathered and fresh rock, and weak zones, without digging.
Q: What is the difference between seismic refraction and seismic refraction tomography (SRT)?
Classic refraction interpretation assumes a few flat layers, while tomography divides the ground into many small cells and solves for the velocity of each, so it shows gradual changes, dipping layers and local weak zones. That makes it better suited to slopes and variable ground.
Q: How deep can seismic refraction see?
Roughly one-third to one-fifth of the spread length. A 24-channel spread with geophones 3 to 5 m apart typically investigates about 20 to 30 m, which covers most slope, road and foundation problems. Longer spreads or stronger sources reach deeper.
Q: Does seismic refraction replace boreholes?
No. It covers the ground between and beyond boreholes, at far lower cost per metre, and shows where boreholes are most needed. Boreholes then give samples, laboratory strength and a check on the velocity model. The two work best together.
Q: When does seismic refraction not work well?
Where a hard layer lies above a softer one (a velocity inversion), the softer layer can be missed. Heavy traffic or machinery adds noise. We plan spreads, shot timing and stacking around these limits, and check results against geology and boreholes.
Q: What do you deliver?
SEG-2 field data, first-break picks, a velocity tomogram for each profile with ray coverage and RMS error, an interpreted section showing soil, weathered and fresh rock and weak zones, depth to competent strata, and a location map in your coordinate system.

## What to plan for in Delhi NCR
In Delhi NCR, plan for airspace permission around Indira Gandhi International Airport, where yellow zones need air traffic control permission and red zones Central Government permission; the monsoon from around 27 June to 25 September; dense winter fog; and Stage III air quality curbs, under which railway, metro and highway projects may continue.
Airspace. Under the Drone Rules, 2021, the ground up from 5 to 8 km of an operational airport perimeter, and the airspace above 200 feet from 8 to 12 km, is a yellow zone needing air traffic control permission; red zones need Central Government permission ( PIB, 2021 ). This applies around Indira Gandhi International Airport, and the 2018 drone regulations named Vijay Chowk in central Delhi as a no-drone zone ( PIB, 2018 ).
Monsoon and fog. On India Meteorological Department normals the monsoon reaches New Delhi around 27 June and withdraws around 25 September ( IMD ). A study in IMD’s journal MAUSAM describes IGI airport as highly susceptible to dense fog in winter, focusing on December and January ( MAUSAM ).
Air quality curbs. Under Stage III of the Commission for Air Quality Management’s (CAQM) Graded Response Action Plan, dust-generating construction such as earthwork and piling is restricted across NCR, though railway, metro and highway projects may continue ( PIB, 2024 ).
Common projects. The 1,380 km Delhi–Mumbai Expressway begins with its Delhi–Faridabad–Sohna section ( PIB ); the 19 km Haryana section of the Dwarka Expressway opened in 2024 ( PM India ); and the 82 km Delhi–Ghaziabad–Meerut Namo Bharat corridor has been fully operational since February 2026 ( NCRTC ).

Flood plains and river crossings are easier to survey in the dry months, November to May. At substation sites, high flood level (HFL) data goes into the recommended finished ground level.
Common projects. UPEIDA gives the lengths of the Agra–Lucknow (302 km), Purvanchal (341 km) and Bundelkhand (296 km) expressways and the Meerut–Prayagraj Ganga Expressway (594 km) ( UPEIDA ). In 2023, eight solar projects totalling 4,995 MW were approved for the Bundelkhand region ( PV Tech ); once running, plants like these are inspected with drone thermography . Transmission lines, railway yards, and rivers and canals ( water resources , bathymetry ) are also common survey sites.
Drone permissions. Under the Drone Rules, 2021, the Ministry of Civil Aviation’s airspace map, published on DGCA’s Digital Sky platform, divides India into green, yellow and red zones. Green zones need no flight permission. Yellow zones, which include the ground up from 5 to 8 km of an operational airport perimeter and the airspace above 200 feet from 8 to 12 km, need air traffic control permission. Red zones need Central Government permission ( PIB ). We check each site on the map, and on long corridors each stretch in a yellow or red zone is cleared before the flight date.
General guidance by project type:
Project type | What to plan for | Typical deliverables
Transmission line route | Alternate routes, land and right of way, crossings | Route comparison on drone and khasra maps, profiles, tower schedules
Substation site | HFL, soil and earthing design | Contour survey, geotechnical and soil resistivity inputs
Expressway or highway | Long corridors, airspace along the route, monthly cycles | Orthomosaics, comparative monthly video, DPR survey drawings
Solar park | Large flat blocks; thermal flights in clear, steady sun | Topographic survey before build, thermography report in operation
Flood plain or river crossing | Flood season from June to October; dry-season access | DTM, cross-sections, bathymetry

Between November and May where possible. ## What to plan for in Maharashtra

Monsoon. On India Meteorological Department normals the monsoon reaches Mumbai around 11 June and withdraws around 8 October; for Pune the dates are around 10 June and 11 October, and for Nagpur around 15 June and 6 October ( IMD ). ## What to plan for in Northeast India
In Northeast India, plan around an early, long monsoon that arrives around 4 or 5 June and withdraws around mid-October, so field work mostly fits late October to May. An early, long monsoon. On India Meteorological Department normals the monsoon reaches Guwahati, Dimapur and Agartala around 4 June and Shillong, Imphal, Aizawl and Itanagar around 5 June, and withdraws from them around 14 or 15 October ( IMD ). Most field work fits between late October and May.
Landslides. The Geological Survey of India has mapped landslide susceptibility at 1:50,000 scale across about 4.3 lakh sq km of landslide-prone hills in parts of 19 states and union territories, including the Tertiary belt of North-eastern India ( Ministry of Earth Sciences, 2025 ).
Forest cover. In the Forest Survey of India’s 2019 assessment, about 1.71 lakh sq km of the eight north-eastern states’ 2.62 lakh sq km was forest ( Lok Sabha answer, 2020 ). Photographs see the canopy; LiDAR ground classification separates terrain from trees.
Agency and permissions. NHIDCL, a public sector undertaking under the road transport ministry, is the nodal highway agency in the North Eastern region ( NHIDCL ). Red zones under the Drone Rules, 2021 need Central Government permission ( PIB, 2021 ), and the 2018 regulations named areas near the international border as no-drone zones ( PIB, 2018 ), so border sites are checked early.

# Highway drone monitoring: more than 3 lakh km of data for authorities and contractors
For highway authorities, highway contractors and private developers, DATA PKT sets DGPS control, flies drone photogrammetry and aerial videography every month, and turns the data into analytics that show progress and problems on the road.
Published 26 October 2026 · Updated 25 November 2026
Clients
Highway authorities, highway contractors and private developers
Services used
Drone photogrammetry , aerial videography , DGPS control and analytics
Highway data captured
More than 3 lakh km in six years, imagery and videography
Empanelment
Three NHAI zones
In short: every month our pilots fly each highway package along the same path, tied to DGPS ground control. The imagery becomes georeferenced maps (photogrammetry), the video becomes the comparative monthly record, and both feed analytics that measure the rate of completion and flag anomalies on completed highways.
## Scale and speed
3 lakh+ km
Highway data captured in the last six years, for authorities and private contractors
70,000+ km
Captured so far in FY 2026-27, and counting
20+ pilots
A team of about 22 drone pilots
About 35 km a day
Highway imagery for photogrammetry, per team
About 50 km a day
Highway aerial videography, per team
## What a drone service provider does
Highway drone programmes separate two roles. The drone service provider (DSP) works in the field and on the data: it flies the highway, captures it and turns it into information. The technology service provider (TSP) runs the technology platform the data goes into. As a DSP, DATA PKT delivers:
- DGPS ground control , so every map is tied to real coordinates
- Drone photogrammetry : georeferenced orthomosaics and measurements of each package
- Aerial videography : the comparative monthly video
- Analytics on that data, including AI analytics, described below
## What the analytics find
Finding | Why it matters to the highway owner
Rate of completion on projects under construction | Progress measured month on month, not estimated
Encroachments and broken boundaries along the right of way | Land and ROW protection; evidence for action
Unauthorised U-turns and paths cut by the public where traffic rules are not followed | Points to close, regularise or redesign
Potholes and surface damage | Maintenance targeted where it is needed
Black spots and accident-prone stretches | Corrections planned and amendments checked in later flights
Visual condition of the corridor | What an inspector would note on a site walk, captured for every kilometre and tracked over time
## Why drones are faster
A ground survey with DGPS and total station measures one point at a time, so a long corridor takes weeks. A DATA PKT drone team captures around 5 sq km of survey data in a day , which is then mapped and analysed in the office.
On a linear corridor such as a highway, one team captures about 35 km of drone imagery for photogrammetry, or about 50 km of aerial video, in a day , and DATA PKT has more than 20 drone pilots (a team of about 22) to put in the field. Ground instruments are still used, but only where they matter most: for the control points that fix the map to real coordinates, for checkpoints that prove the accuracy, and for detail the drone cannot see.
## Why highways need a monthly drone record
In 2021 NHAI made drone video recording mandatory for national highway projects, every month, at every stage: development, construction, and operation and maintenance ( Mobility Outlook, June 2021 ). Videos compare the current month with the previous one and can be used as evidence in disputes (see NHAI's monthly drone video rule for what each video must show). Contractors and private developers use the same record for their own progress reports and billing.
From a DATA PKT comparative drone video of a highway improvement project in Uttar Pradesh: the same chainage recorded six months apart.
## How a monthly cycle runs
- Package plan: chainages, flight path and camera settings are fixed once, so every month is flown the same way.
- Control and permissions: DGPS ground control is set, and stretches in yellow or red airspace zones are cleared before the flight date.
- Flight: DATA PKT pilots fly the full length of the package.
- Processing and analytics: orthomosaics, the comparative video and the analytics are prepared in the office.
- Hand-over: files go to the client's monthly progress report and data portal.
Development phase: right of way and centre line marked on the drone frame.
Construction phase: progress recorded at each chainage.
## How a highway survey like this is done
The monthly cycle above rests on survey engineering that is planned once for each package and then repeated, so that month-on-month comparisons show change on the road rather than change in the survey.
### Flight planning
- Ground sample distance (GSD) first, height second. The GSD is fixed from what the deliverables have to measure, and the flight height follows from the camera: GSD = (sensor width × flight height) ÷ (focal length × image width in pixels). Our GSD calculator does the arithmetic.
- Corridor flight lines. A highway is a strip, not a block. A single strip of photos is weak geometry; two or more overlapping parallel strips along the alignment, covering the carriageway, shoulders, service roads and right of way, with short cross-strips where needed, hold the block together.
- Terrain following. On grades, embankments and hill sections the ground rises and falls under a fixed-altitude flight, so the GSD changes along the package. Terrain-following flight keeps the height above ground, and therefore the GSD, close to the target.
- Separate video runs. The comparative video is flown on its own saved route with fixed height, speed and camera pitch, so that the same chainage appears at the same point in every month's video.
- Airspace. Flights are planned on the DigitalSky platform under the Drone Rules, 2021 , and flown by DGCA Remote Pilot Certificate holders on drones with a Unique Identification Number. Stretches in yellow or red zones are cleared before the flight date.
### Ground control design for a corridor
- GCP pairs on alternate sides. Ground control points (GCPs) are laid out along both sides of the alignment, with extra points at the package ends, at major bends, at flyovers and interchanges, and where the grade changes sharply. GCPs in a single line down the centre of a corridor leave the model free to tilt sideways; pairs across the corridor stop that.
- Permanent marks. On a monthly programme, permanent marks (pillars, or painted marks on kerbs and structures) are re-used every cycle, so that each month is in exactly the same frame.
- Checkpoints held out. Checkpoints are measured exactly like GCPs but kept out of the adjustment and used only to test the result.
- Datum and heights. GNSS gives ellipsoidal heights, while design levels on highway drawings are orthometric (mean sea level). Heights are converted with a geoid model and checked on a benchmark. In India the difference between the two can be tens of metres, so a missed geoid step is not a small error.
Ground control for a linear corridor. GCPs alternate on both sides of the alignment and are paired at the ends. Checkpoints are held out of the adjustment so that accuracy can be checked independently. Spacing and offset follow from the GSD and the accuracy target.
### Processing chain
- Field data check: image count, blur, exposure and GNSS logs are checked before the team leaves the stretch.
- Image positions: RTK or PPK processing of the drone's GNSS log against a base station or CORS gives the position of each image.
- Aerial triangulation (bundle adjustment): tie points are matched between overlapping images, the camera is self-calibrated, and the GCPs fix the block to the ground.
- Dense matching: a dense point cloud is built from the oriented images.
- DSM and DTM: the digital surface model (DSM) keeps vehicles, trees and structures; the digital terrain model (DTM) is filtered to ground. Earthwork and pavement levels come from the DTM, edited where filtering has left vehicles or plant on the surface.
- Orthomosaic and chainage referencing: the orthomosaic is tiled by chainage, and the design centre line is loaded so that every output can be read by chainage and offset.
The photogrammetry chain. Each output is built from the one before it, and the checkpoint QA at the end tests the whole chain against points the adjustment never saw.
### What a controlled monthly survey can show
- Layer-wise progress by chainage: each layer of the pavement crust (embankment, subgrade, granular sub-base, wet mix macadam, dense bituminous macadam, bituminous concrete, as specified in the MoRTH Specifications for Road and Bridge Works) and each structure marked complete, in progress or not started.
- Cross-sections and longitudinal sections compared with the design sections, to show where formation or finished levels are high or low.
- Volumes: cut and fill between this month's surface and the previous month's, or the design surface, for earthwork and stockpiles.
- Analytics layers: encroachments, unauthorised openings, potholes and black-spot observations as GIS features that carry their chainage.
### How accuracy is reported
Accuracy is reported as root mean square error (RMSE) at independent checkpoints, following the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data, Edition 2 (2023): horizontal accuracy as RMSE H , and vertical accuracy on open, hard ground as non-vegetated vertical accuracy (NVA). Edition 2 reports RMSE alone, without the confidence-level figures of Edition 1, asks for at least 30 checkpoints for a product accuracy assessment, and includes the error of the checkpoint survey itself in the reported figure.
Absolute accuracy is how close the map is to true coordinates. Relative accuracy is how consistent it is within itself and, on a monthly programme, from one month to the next. Progress and volume figures depend mostly on relative accuracy between months, which is why the same permanent control is reused every cycle.
### Common failure modes and how they are prevented
Failure | What it looks like | How it is prevented
Doming or bowing of a long corridor block | Levels drift up or down away from control, worst in the middle of the package | GCP pairs along the full length, more than one strip, good camera calibration, RTK or PPK image positions
Ellipsoidal heights left uncorrected | All levels wrong by a large, nearly constant offset | Geoid applied and checked on a benchmark for every package
Mixed coordinate frames | Old control and new CORS-based control disagree by centimetres to decimetres | One frame and epoch for the project; old control transformed and checked, not mixed in raw
Vehicles and plant in the surface | False bumps in sections and volumes | Ground filtering, manual edits, and the DTM rather than the DSM for levels
A different route each month | Videos and maps that do not line up | Saved flight plans, with the same heights and camera settings every cycle
Shadow and glare on new bitumen | Poor image matching on dark, uniform pavement | Flight time chosen for the light, exposure adjusted, overlap kept at the planned values
## Getting the best results
- Fix the package plan once (chainages, flight lines, heights, camera settings) and change it only when the road changes.
- Put permanent control in at the start of the contract; re-measuring temporary targets every month adds error and cost.
- Give the survey team the design alignment and design sections in CAD at the start, so outputs come out by chainage and can be compared with design.
- Agree with the client which surface is used for each measurement: the DTM for earthwork and pavement levels, the DSM for structures and stockpile tops.
- Keep vertical bias small for volumes: a constant 2 cm error over one hectare changes a volume by 200 m³, whatever the GSD.
- Record each month's flight conditions (date, time, wind, light) with the data, so differences between months can be explained.
- Fly the video and the mapping as separate missions; settings that suit one rarely suit the other.
## How it started
Our first highway drone work, in October 2020, was aerial imagery, videography and survey for highway projects in Nagaland and Manipur. It grew into NHAI empanelment in three zones and a client base that mixes highway authorities, highway contractors and private developers.
Monthly flights record structures, earthwork and pavement at every stage.
Send us the site KML or chainage and the outputs you need. We reply with a scope and quote.
Send an enquiry WhatsApp +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: How many kilometres of highway has DATA PKT flown?
More than 3 lakh km of highway data in the last six years, drone imagery and aerial videography combined, for highway authorities and private contractors. In this financial year (2026-27) we have already captured more than 70,000 km, and the count is still rising.
Q: How fast can a drone team cover a highway?
One DATA PKT drone team captures about 35 km of highway imagery for photogrammetry, or about 50 km of aerial video, in a day. We have more than 20 drone pilots, a team of about 22.
Q: What is a DSP in a highway drone programme?
A drone service provider (DSP) flies the highways, sets DGPS ground control, captures imagery and video, and processes the data. A technology service provider (TSP) runs the technology platform the data feeds into. DATA PKT works as a DSP.
Q: What can the analytics find on a highway?
The rate of completion on projects under construction, and on completed highways: encroachments and broken boundaries, unauthorised U-turns and paths cut by the public, potholes, black spots and accident-prone stretches.
Q: Are monthly drone surveys mandatory on national highway projects?
Yes. Since 2021 NHAI has required monthly drone video recording of national highway projects across development, construction, operation and maintenance, uploaded to its Data Lake portal.
Q: Is DATA PKT empanelled with NHAI?
Yes. DATA PKT is empanelled with NHAI in three zones for monthly drone survey work, and has flown highway drone surveys since October 2020.
Q: Why are checkpoints kept out of the processing?
A point used to fix the map cannot also prove it is right. Checkpoints are measured in the same way as ground control points but left out of the adjustment, and the difference between their surveyed and mapped coordinates is the honest accuracy of the survey.
Q: Can monthly drone data be used for earthwork quantities?
Yes, when the survey is controlled for it: the same ground control every month, a ground-filtered terrain model rather than the raw surface, and checked vertical accuracy. Volumes are only as good as the vertical accuracy, so the accuracy report should go with the quantities.

# Yard plans and drainage plans for two railway divisions
For two railway divisions, DATA PKT surveyed station yards with drones and DGPS and turned the data into yard plans and drainage designs: 61 plans submitted in eastern India, and drainage design for 32 yards in Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.
Published 26 October 2026 · Updated 25 November 2026
Eastern India
30 yard plans and 31 drainage plans, all submitted
Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh
Drainage planning and design for 32 yards
Method
Drone survey with DGPS control, CAD drafting, field checks
Contract periods
Six months each
In short: railways need accurate plans of each yard before remodelling or drainage works. Measuring yards on foot beside running lines is slow and risky. DATA PKT flies each yard, builds an orthomosaic and terrain model, and drafts the yard plan or drainage design from it, with critical details checked on the ground.
## Eastern India: 30 yard plans and 31 drainage plans
Under two contracts, each with a six-month completion period, DATA PKT prepared 60+ yard plans (ESPs) and drainage plans in total (30 yard plans and 31 drainage plans), from suburban yards to junctions on the main line, and all of them have been submitted.
A station yard captured as one orthomosaic: the base on which tracks, platforms and structures are drawn.
## Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh: drainage design for 32 yards
A further contract, with a six-month completion period, covers planning and design of drainage in 32 existing yards, from small wayside stations to junctions. The railway asked for LiDAR or an equivalent advanced survey method. DATA PKT has completed the ground survey of all 32 yards, and drainage plans are being prepared and submitted for approval.
For each yard the work covers:
- A survey report with site conditions and levels
- An estimate of waste water generated in the yard
- Drainage slopes and the disposal location
- Manholes and septic tanks with dispersal trenches, sized for the yard, with a cleaning arrangement
- Layout plans for the railway's approval
## How the work runs
- Control: surveyors fix DGPS ground control points around the yard.
- Flight: the drone captures the whole yard in one short window, with little time spent beside running lines.
- Processing: an orthomosaic and terrain model are built and checked against independent checkpoints.
- Drafting: tracks, turnouts, platforms, structures, drains and levels are drawn into the yard plan or drainage design.
- Field check and approval: critical details are verified on the ground, and plans are revised until approved.
## How a yard survey like this is done
Each of the five steps above is planned around two facts: the yard is beside running lines, and the plan has to show rails, turnouts, drains and small structures in their true positions and at the right levels.
### Flight planning
- GSD from the drawing scale. The ground sample distance (GSD) is set from the plotting scale and the smallest feature to be drawn, and the flight height follows from the camera (GSD = (sensor width × flight height) ÷ (focal length × image width in pixels); see our GSD calculator ).
- Block or corridor. Large junction yards are flown as a block of parallel lines; long, narrow wayside yards are flown as a corridor of lines along the track. Overlap is raised where long rows of wagons, sheds or platform canopies make image matching harder.
- Short windows beside running lines. Flights are timed with the division, the drone stays well clear of the 25 kV overhead equipment (OHE) and its masts, and take-off points are off the track.
- Permissions. Flights are planned on the DigitalSky platform under the Drone Rules, 2021, with yellow- or red-zone stretches cleared before the flight date, plus the railway's own written permission for the yard. Pilots hold DGCA Remote Pilot Certificates and drones carry a Unique Identification Number.
### Ground control design for a yard
- Layout. GCPs are placed around the outside of the yard and through its length, off the track and outside the danger zone. For a long, narrow yard they go in pairs on both sides of the station lines, so the model cannot tilt across the yard.
- Checkpoints. Checkpoints are measured the same way and held out of the adjustment. Some are best placed on rail heads and platform edges, because those are the levels the railway checks.
- Datum, chainage and levels. Heights are converted from ellipsoidal to orthometric with a geoid model and tied to the railway's benchmark, so that rail levels and drain inverts match the railway's own level datum. Kilometrage is tied to the railway's kilometre posts or chainage reference.
### What the air sees, and what the ground must measure
- Camera: a full-colour, scale-true orthomosaic and terrain model, the base for drafting tracks, turnouts and structures.
- LiDAR, where specified: laser returns reach the ground through vegetation along overgrown drains and yard edges, where photogrammetry only sees the canopy.
- Ground instruments: thin, shiny rail heads and the inside of drains and culverts are poorly reconstructed from the air, so rail levels, drain inverts, culvert openings and outfall levels are measured on the ground with a total station, level or GNSS, on the same control.
### Processing chain
- Aerial triangulation (bundle adjustment) with self-calibration of the camera, and the GCPs fixing the block.
- Dense point cloud, DSM and DTM. The digital surface model (DSM) keeps wagons, sheds and trees; the DTM is filtered to ground. LiDAR data, where flown, is classified into ground, vegetation, buildings and noise using the ASPRS LAS 1.4 classes .
- Orthomosaic, with the lean of tall structures and canopies checked where it hides track.
- Contours and a spot-level grid for the drainage design.
### Yard plan (ESP) layers
The yard plan is drafted to the division's layering and title-block standard: running lines, loops and sidings with track centres; turnouts with the position of each switch; platforms, foot over bridges, buildings and goods sheds; bridges, culverts and level crossings; the railway boundary; and chainages. Turnout positions and kilometrage are confirmed on the ground before submission.
A yard ESP built as layers on one control network. Tracks, points, structures, drainage and the land boundary are kept as separate layers, so each can be checked, issued and updated on its own.
### Drainage design on the survey
- Catchments and flow paths from the DTM: where water falls, where it collects (often between tracks and at platform ends), and where it can leave the yard.
- Storm-water flow by the rational method, Q = C·i·A / 360 (Q in m³/s, C the runoff coefficient, i the rainfall intensity in mm/h for the time of concentration, A in hectares).
- Drain sizing by Manning's equation, with longitudinal slopes chosen from the surveyed levels so that drains stay self-cleansing at design flow and fall towards the disposal point.
- Waste water estimated from the yard's users and facilities, commonly with per-capita rates such as those in the CPHEEO Manual on Sewerage and Sewage Treatment Systems (2013).
- Septic tanks and dispersion trenches sized to IS 2470 (Code of practice for installation of septic tanks), Part 1 for design and construction and Part 2 for secondary treatment and disposal of the effluent, with manholes at changes of direction and gradient and a cleaning arrangement.
- Drawings: layout plan, longitudinal sections of each drain with invert levels, typical cross-sections, manhole and septic tank details, and the disposal arrangement, for the railway's approval.
### How accuracy is reported
Accuracy is reported as root mean square error (RMSE) at independent checkpoints, following the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data, Edition 2 (2023): horizontal accuracy as RMSE H , and vertical accuracy on open, hard ground as non-vegetated vertical accuracy (NVA). Edition 2 reports RMSE alone, without the confidence-level figures of Edition 1, asks for at least 30 checkpoints for a product accuracy assessment, and includes the error of the checkpoint survey itself in the reported figure. A single yard rarely has that many checkpoints, so results are usually given as per-yard checks plus a combined figure across yards.
For drainage, relative accuracy matters most. A drain works if its levels are right relative to each other and to the outfall, so level differences between surveyed points along each drain line are checked, not only absolute accuracy, before slopes are fixed.
How accuracy is proved. Each checkpoint's residual is the map value minus the ground value. RMSE is the square root of the mean of the squared residuals, calculated separately for X, Y and Z, and the checkpoints must be independent of the GCPs.
### Common failure modes and how they are prevented
Failure | Effect on the plan | Prevention
Rail levels taken from photogrammetry alone | Rail and formation levels off by more than drainage design can tolerate | Rail levels measured on the ground
Wagons left in the terrain model | False high ground that diverts the designed flow | Ground filtering plus manual edits; flights timed for empty lines where possible
Vegetation over drains | Drain beds mapped at the top of the grass or shrubs | LiDAR where flown, and invert levels taken on the ground
Wrong height datum | Drain falls to an outfall that is actually higher | Geoid applied, and levels tied to the railway's benchmark
Turnout drawn from the image only | Switch in the wrong place on the ESP | Every turnout confirmed on site
Shadow under canopies and foot over bridges | Gaps in the orthomosaic | Flight time chosen for sun angle; ground survey fills the gaps
## Getting the best results
- Get the division's drawing standard (layers, symbols, title block, chainage convention) before drafting starts; redrawing to a new standard is slow.
- Ask for the railway's benchmark and kilometrage reference at the start and tie everything to it.
- Measure on the ground what the air cannot see well: rail levels, drain inverts, culvert openings and outfall levels.
- Map existing drains and their condition (silted, broken, missing) on the orthomosaic before designing new ones.
- Check the disposal point first: a design that cannot discharge by gravity changes everything upstream.
- Keep the orthomosaic and terrain model with the drawings; they answer later queries without another site visit.
- For drainage design, survey a little beyond the railway boundary to see where water enters and leaves the yard.
## Why drones are faster
A ground survey with DGPS and total station measures one point at a time, so a long corridor takes weeks. A DATA PKT drone team captures around 5 sq km of survey data in a day , which is then mapped and analysed in the office.
On a linear corridor such as a highway, one team captures about 35 km of drone imagery for photogrammetry, or about 50 km of aerial video, in a day , and DATA PKT has more than 20 drone pilots (a team of about 22) to put in the field. Ground instruments are still used, but only where they matter most: for the control points that fix the map to real coordinates, for checkpoints that prove the accuracy, and for detail the drone cannot see.
## Other railway work
DATA PKT has also carried out level-crossing surveys in two divisions (18 and more than 15 level crossings), railway bridge inspections , and location plans for traction substations and sectioning posts, described in our 220/132 kV substation and transmission line case study .
Read more: Engineering Scale Plans and DPR surveys and what an ESP is .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: How many railway yard plans has DATA PKT prepared?
For one railway division in eastern India we submitted 30 yard plans and 31 drainage plans. For a second division, in Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, we have surveyed all 32 yards in the contract and are preparing their drainage designs.
Q: What does a railway yard drainage plan include?
Ground levels and slopes, the estimated waste water from the yard, the disposal location, and the design of drains, manholes and septic tanks with dispersal trenches, with a cleaning arrangement.
Q: Why survey railway yards with drones?
A drone captures a whole yard in one short window, so staff spend far less time on or beside running lines, and the orthomosaic and terrain model stay on file for later questions.
Q: Can rail levels be measured from a drone survey?
Rail heads are narrow and reflective, so photogrammetry reconstructs them poorly. A drone survey gives the yard layout and the ground surface; rail levels and other critical levels, such as drain inverts and outfalls, should be measured on the ground and tied to the same control.
Q: Which height datum should a yard drainage design use?
The same one as the railway's existing drawings and benchmarks. GNSS gives heights above the ellipsoid, which must be converted to orthometric heights with a geoid model and checked on a known benchmark before any drain slope is designed.

Case study · Power transmission
# 220/132 kV substation and transmission lines in Uttar Pradesh
For a railway traction power project in Uttar Pradesh, DATA PKT is carrying out the survey and design of a new 220/132 kV grid substation, the 220 kV and 132 kV lines that feed it, and location plans for 19 sites along the railway.
Published 26 October 2026 · Updated 25 November 2026
Location
Uttar Pradesh
Substation
220/132 kV grid substation (GSS)
Lines
220 kV D/C (32 m ROW) and 132 kV D/C (25 m ROW)
Status
In progress; six-month programme
In short: the project needs power for 2x25 kV railway traction. DATA PKT finds three alternate routes for each new line, compares them on maps made from current drone data laid over khasra maps, surveys the approved route in detail, investigates and designs the substation, and prepares location plans for traction substations and sectioning posts.
## Scope
Part | What DATA PKT delivers
220 kV D/C line, state grid substation to the new GSS | Three alternate routes, comparative feasibility report, then detailed survey of the approved route
132 kV D/C line, new GSS to an existing 132 kV line | Three alternate routes with the LILO (loop-in loop-out) point on the existing line, then detailed survey
220/132 kV GSS | Contour survey, geotechnical investigation, soil resistivity, HFL and finished ground level
Location plans | 19 sites: the GSS, 4 traction substations (TSS) and 14 sectioning posts (SP) and sub-sectioning posts (SSP) in two sections
Design | Power-supply diagram, GSS switchyard GAD, GSS building GAD, LT wiring plan and LT single line diagram, vetted by IIT, NIT or CPRI
## Three alternate routes, compared on current drone maps
For each line the client asked for three alternate routes and a comparative feasibility report with a techno-economic recommendation. The usual starting point is Survey of India toposheets, satellite imagery and revenue maps, but these are often years out of date. DATA PKT flies each corridor with drone photogrammetry, so every route is compared on how the ground looks today.
- Route length, angle points and deviation angles
- Crossings: rivers and canals, national and state highways, railways, power lines from LT to 765 kV, telecom and optical fibre
- Forest, settlements and obligatory points
- Right-of-way sensitivity for each alternative
Alternate routes and angle points marked on a terrain base before the comparison (illustrative).
A khasra (revenue) map in GIS: each plot boundary and number, ready to be overlaid on drone maps.
## Drone maps on khasra maps: land acquisition made clear
The drone orthomosaic of each corridor is superimposed on the khasra (revenue) maps. The khasra gives the plot numbers; the drone data shows what is on each plot today. Together they show, for every alternative:
- Which plots the line and each tower would fall on
- Whether the land is residential, commercial, agricultural or forest
- Where a small shift in an angle point avoids houses, shops or sensitive land
- The land acquisition and right-of-way picture before the route is approved
That turns route approval from a debate over old maps into a comparison of facts, and makes the land acquisition (LA) work that follows far easier.
## How a line survey like this is done
### Two survey stages, two accuracy levels
- Route alternatives (reconnaissance mapping). Each alternate corridor is flown wide enough either side of the trial alignment for angle points to move without a second flight. The aim is a current, georeferenced picture for the route comparison and land planning.
- Approved route (detailed survey). The approved route is surveyed in detail with DGPS, total station and levelling for the profile, tower spotting and schedules, with the drone data as the base for plan features and crossings.
### Flight planning
- Height from GSD. Flight height is set from the target ground sample distance and the camera (GSD = (sensor width × flight height) ÷ (focal length × image width in pixels); see our GSD calculator ).
- Corridor lines. Parallel flight lines run along each corridor, and the corridor is broken into segments at each angle point so that the lines stay parallel to the alignment.
- Terrain following where the ground height changes along the route, so the GSD stays near the target.
- Existing lines. Corridors cross existing power lines from LT to EHV. The drone keeps well clear of energised conductors, and crossing spans are flown higher or measured from the ground.
- Airspace. Flights are planned on the DigitalSky platform under the Drone Rules, 2021, and flown by DGCA Remote Pilot Certificate holders on drones with a Unique Identification Number. Stretches in yellow or red zones are cleared before the flight date.
### Ground control design for a line corridor
- GCP layout. GCP pairs on alternate sides of the corridor, with extra points at angle points, at the substation ends and at major crossings, where the profile matters most.
- Checkpoints measured like GCPs and held out of the adjustment.
- Control network. Static GNSS control pillars form the backbone, and the angle points and reference points are coordinated (X, Y, Z) from this network.
- One height system. Heights are orthometric, converted from ellipsoidal heights with a geoid model and tied to a benchmark, and the HFL and rail levels used for the substation's finished ground level are in the same height system.
Ground control for a linear corridor. GCPs alternate on both sides of the alignment and are paired at the ends. Checkpoints are held out of the adjustment so that accuracy can be checked independently. Spacing and offset follow from the GSD and the accuracy target.
### What each sensor is for
Task | Sensor | Why
Corridor orthomosaic and terrain | Drone camera (photogrammetry) | Current, scale-true base for the route comparison and the khasra overlay
Terrain under trees, existing conductor heights at crossings | Drone LiDAR, where used | LiDAR returns from thin wires and from ground under vegetation; photogrammetry reconstructs neither reliably
Profile levels, angle points, crossing clearances | Total station, GNSS and level | Detailed survey to the accuracy the profile and tower schedule need
### Processing chain
- Aerial triangulation (bundle adjustment), with GCPs fixing each corridor block.
- Dense matching, DSM, ground-filtered DTM and orthomosaic.
- Where LiDAR is flown: trajectory processing, strip adjustment and classification to the ASPRS LAS 1.4 classes, including ground (class 2), vegetation (3 to 5), buildings (6) and, for existing lines, wire guard or shield wire (13), wire conductor (14) and transmission tower (15).
- Khasra maps georeferenced to the orthomosaic using boundary points that can be identified on both, with the residuals recorded. Where a revenue map does not fit the ground, the misfit is reported rather than the orthomosaic being stretched to match it.
### Line design on the profile
- Longitudinal profile of the approved route, with ground levels, crossings and obstacles along the centre line, and at the outer conductor offsets where side slopes are steep.
- Tower spotting with a sag template. Towers are placed on the profile with a sag template cut for the ruling span and conductor: the hot curve (maximum sag at maximum conductor temperature, still air); the ground clearance curve (the hot curve dropped by the minimum ground clearance); the tower footing curve (the hot curve dropped by the conductor attachment height of the standard tower); and the cold curve (minimum temperature, to check uplift on towers in low ground).
- Clearances. Ground clearance at maximum sag is checked against the minimum clearances in the Central Electricity Authority (Measures relating to Safety and Electric Supply) Regulations, 2023. Crossings over railways, highways and other power lines are checked against the requirements of the owner of each crossing, and against any higher values in the project's design basis.
- Schedules and plans: the tower schedule, the crossing schedule, the route alignment plan on the orthomosaic, and tree and crop enumeration within the right of way.
Clearances on an overhead line. Sag, ground clearance and vegetation clearance are measured along the span. Right-of-way width and horizontal clearance are measured across it. A LiDAR or photogrammetric model measures all of them from one survey.
### Quality checks
- Drone maps: Accuracy is reported as root mean square error (RMSE) at independent checkpoints, following the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data, Edition 2 (2023): horizontal accuracy as RMSE H , and vertical accuracy on open, hard ground as non-vegetated vertical accuracy (NVA). Edition 2 reports RMSE alone, without the confidence-level figures of Edition 1, asks for at least 30 checkpoints for a product accuracy assessment, and includes the error of the checkpoint survey itself in the reported figure.
- Control network: loop closures and a network adjustment report.
- Profile levels: levelling loops closed within the specified tolerance.
- Absolute and relative accuracy. Tower coordinates need absolute accuracy so towers can be set out on the ground. The profile needs relative vertical accuracy along each span, because clearance is the difference between conductor and ground levels.
### Common failure modes and how they are prevented
Failure | Consequence | Prevention
Ground under crops or scrub taken from the photogrammetric surface | Profile too high, clearance overstated | Ground-filtered DTM, LiDAR where flown, ground levels on the profile
Side slope ignored on hill or river-bank spans | Outer conductor clearance missed | Side-slope levels at the outer conductor offset
Existing line heights estimated | Crossing clearance wrong | Conductor heights at crossings measured by total station or LiDAR, with the temperature noted
Revenue maps stretched to fit | Wrong plots listed for towers and right of way | Khasra georeferenced to the orthomosaic, with residuals reported
Mixed height systems | HFL, rail level and survey levels not comparable | One orthometric height system and benchmark for all
## Getting the best results
- Fly the alternatives early: a current map of each corridor settles many route questions before detailed survey starts.
- Keep the reconnaissance corridor wide enough for angle points to move without a second flight.
- Get the revenue maps for every village on the corridors before the comparison, and check their fit against the orthomosaic.
- Measure existing line heights at every crossing and record the conductor temperature or time of day.
- Take side-slope levels wherever the ground falls across the line, not only along the centre line.
- Confirm the design basis (conductor, ruling span, maximum temperature, clearances) with the client before tower spotting.
- Put HFL, rail levels and survey levels in one height system before fixing the substation's finished ground level.
## Detailed survey of the approved route
- DGPS and total station survey with levelling, and coordinates (X, Y, Z) of every angle and reference point
- Longitudinal profiles (horizontal 1 cm = 20 m, vertical 1 cm = 2 m) with tower spotting and optimisation to IS 5613 and IS 802
- Tower schedules (type, extension, span, deviation angle, chainage, ground level) and the route alignment plan
- Crossing schedules with chainage, crossing angle and clearance
- Tree and crop enumeration along the corridor
## Substation investigations and design
At the GSS site DATA PKT carries out a contour survey, boreholes with standard penetration tests and laboratory testing for the geotechnical report, and Wenner four-electrode soil resistivity tests to IS 3043 for earthing design. HFL data and rail levels set the recommended finished ground level.
The design work covers the general arrangement drawing (GAD) of the 220/132 kV switchyard (bus-bars, transformers, breakers, isolators, CTs, CVTs, lightning arresters, gantries, roads, drains and fire fighting), the GAD of the GSS building, the general power-supply diagram of the 220 kV, 132 kV and 2x25 kV network, and the LT wiring plan, LT single line diagram and distribution board schedules. The final GAD is vetted by an IIT, NIT or CPRI.
## Location plans for 19 sites
Along the railway, DATA PKT surveys the GSS plot and each proposed traction substation, sectioning post and sub-sectioning post and prepares its location plan with boundary, area, levels, utilities and railway chainage. The 19 sites are the new GSS, 4 traction substations and 14 sectioning and sub-sectioning posts across two sections.
Survey and design decide where each tower stands and how the line crosses every obstacle.
## Why drones are faster
A ground survey with DGPS and total station measures one point at a time, so a long corridor takes weeks. A DATA PKT drone team captures around 5 sq km of survey data in a day , which is then mapped and analysed in the office.
On a linear corridor such as a highway, one team captures about 35 km of drone imagery for photogrammetry, or about 50 km of aerial video, in a day , and DATA PKT has more than 20 drone pilots (a team of about 22) to put in the field. Ground instruments are still used, but only where they matter most: for the control points that fix the map to real coordinates, for checkpoints that prove the accuracy, and for detail the drone cannot see.

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What does this project cover?
Survey and design of a new 220/132 kV grid substation (GSS) in Uttar Pradesh, a 220 kV double-circuit line from the state grid to the GSS, a 132 kV double-circuit line from the GSS to an existing line, and location plans for 19 sites: the substation, 4 traction substations and 14 sectioning and sub-sectioning posts.
Q: How do drones help choose a transmission line route?
Drone photogrammetry maps each alternate corridor as it is today. Laid over khasra (revenue) maps, it shows which plots each route crosses and what is on them: farmland, houses, shops or forest. That makes the route comparison and land acquisition planning far easier.
Q: Does DATA PKT design substations?
Yes. The scope includes the general arrangement drawing (GAD) of the 220/132 kV switchyard, the GAD of the substation building, the power-supply diagram, the LT single line diagram and LT wiring plan, vetted by an IIT, NIT or CPRI.
Q: Is the project complete?
No. It is in progress, with field survey under way in October 2026 and a six-month programme from award.
Q: What is a sag template and why is it used?
A sag template is a curve of the conductor's shape at a chosen temperature, cut to the profile's scales. Laid on the ground profile, it shows where towers can stand so that the conductor keeps the required clearance at maximum sag, and, with the cold curve, whether any tower in low ground would be pulled upward.
Q: Can a drone survey replace the detailed survey of a transmission line?
Not entirely. Drone mapping gives a current base for comparing routes, land planning, crossings and plan features. The tower schedule and profile still rely on control, levelling and total station work on the approved route, tied to the same coordinates.

Home / Case studies / Water and irrigation
Case study · Water and irrigation
# Groundwater recharge system for Mahendragarh: survey and design of two canal-fed lines
In Mahendragarh district, in southern Haryana, DATA PKT is surveying and designing a groundwater recharge system. Two lines, of about 45 km and 15 km, take water from an existing canal or river and carry it to structures that return it to the aquifer.
Published 26 October 2026 · Updated 25 November 2026
Location
Mahendragarh (Mahindergarh) district, Haryana
Purpose
Recharge groundwater with surplus canal or river water
Network
Two lines, about 45 km and 15 km long
Our scope
Drone and DGPS survey, planning and design of the recharge system
In short: water that a canal or river carries in surplus is drawn off, carried along two lines and put back into the ground through recharge structures. DATA PKT surveys the corridors with drones and DGPS and designs the system on that survey: the off-take, the alignment and levels of each line, the crossings and the recharge structures.
## The need
Mahendragarh is a semi-arid district in southern Haryana. Farms and villages draw most of their water from the ground, rainfall is short and seasonal, and groundwater levels have been falling for years. Canals and rivers carry more water at some times of the year than is used. A recharge system stores that surplus underground, where it does not evaporate and can be pumped back by wells across the area.
## How the recharge system works
The system is designed as a chain, from the source to the aquifer. Each link is sized from the survey levels and the water that can be drawn:
- Off-take at the canal or river: an intake with a regulator or gate, so water is drawn only when it is available and in the quantity allowed.
- Silt control: a desilting or sedimentation chamber and filter, because silt that reaches a recharge well clogs it.
- Conveyance lines: the two lines, about 45 km and 15 km, laid to an alignment and gradient that move water by gravity wherever the ground allows.
- Crossings: structures where the lines cross roads, railways, other canals, drains and utilities.
- Recharge structures: recharge wells and shafts, percolation pits and recharge ponds, and existing village ponds revived to hold and soak water, placed where the ground can take it.
- Escapes and monitoring: outlets for excess water, and points to watch water levels so the effect can be measured.
An off-take regulator: the gate decides when, and how much, water leaves the canal for the recharge lines.
## How drones make the design possible
A recharge network is a long, linear project across farmland and villages. Designing it needs the levels and features of every kilometre, and a conventional ground survey of 60 km would take weeks. A drone survey tied to DGPS ground control captures the corridors in days and gives the designers the whole picture at once.
Survey output | What the designer uses it for
Orthomosaic of each corridor | Choosing an alignment that avoids houses, wells, trees and difficult land, and keeps crossings to a minimum
Terrain model and contours | Checking that water can flow by gravity, fixing gradients and finding where pumping or drops are needed
Longitudinal and cross-sections | Depth of the line, trench and earthwork quantities, and levels at every structure
Overlay on khasra (revenue) maps | The land each kilometre passes through, so land and right-of-way needs are known early
Inventory of crossings and utilities | Every road, railway, canal, drain and service line the network must cross, with its position and level
Low ground, depressions and village ponds | Candidate recharge sites, where water collects naturally and can be held to soak in
Canal or river section at the off-take | Bed and water levels for the intake design, with bathymetry where the water is deep
Wet and dry ground mapped from the air: one input for picking where water will soak in.
## How a recharge-line survey like this is done
A gravity line across nearly flat farmland can have a fall of only a few metres over many kilometres, so a survey for a recharge network is planned around vertical accuracy, not picture detail.
### Flight planning
- GSD from the design need. The ground sample distance is chosen for the vertical accuracy the levels need, and the flight height follows from the camera (GSD = (sensor width × flight height) ÷ (focal length × image width in pixels); see our GSD calculator ).
- Corridors, not a block. The 45 km and 15 km lines are flown as corridors wide enough to shift the alignment around houses, wells and trees without another flight.
- Wider blocks at key sites. The off-take, major crossings and candidate recharge sites (low ground and village ponds) are flown as small blocks around the corridor, so the structures can be laid out on them.
- Season and crops. Standing crops hide the ground from photogrammetry. Flights are best timed after harvest, and areas still under crop or trees are covered by ground levels or LiDAR.
- Airspace. Flights are planned on the DigitalSky platform under the Drone Rules, 2021, and flown by DGCA Remote Pilot Certificate holders on drones with a Unique Identification Number. Stretches in yellow or red zones are cleared before the flight date.
### Ground control and levels
- Control along both corridors. Static GNSS control pillars form the backbone, with GCP pairs on alternate sides of each corridor.
- Checkpoints are held out of the adjustment and placed on open, hard ground (roads, canal bunds, pads), so that they test vertical accuracy fairly.
- Benchmarks for levels. Temporary benchmarks along the lines are tied by levelling to a Survey of India or irrigation department benchmark, so the levels at the off-take, at each crossing and at each recharge structure are in one system.
- Orthometric heights. GNSS ellipsoidal heights are converted with a geoid model and checked on the benchmarks, so canal bed and water levels from the irrigation department's records can be compared directly with the survey.
### What each sensor is for
Task | Sensor | Why
Corridor orthomosaic and terrain | Drone camera (photogrammetry) | Current base for alignment, crossings and land
Ground under trees and crops | Drone LiDAR, where used | Laser returns reach the ground through gaps in vegetation
Canal or river section at the off-take | Bathymetry or ground sections | Bed levels under water, which neither a camera nor topographic LiDAR can see
Levels at structures, crossings and benchmarks | Total station and level | Design levels where the hydraulics are most sensitive
### Processing chain
- Aerial triangulation (bundle adjustment), with GCPs fixing each corridor block.
- Dense point cloud and DSM; ground filtering to a DTM, edited by hand where crops, hedges or houses remain. LiDAR, if flown, is classified to the ASPRS LAS 1.4 classes (ground, vegetation, buildings, water, noise).
- Orthomosaic and contours.
- Alignment trials, each with a longitudinal section and cross-sections at regular intervals.
- Khasra (revenue) maps georeferenced to the orthomosaic, for the land each kilometre crosses.
The photogrammetry chain. Each output is built from the one before it, and the checkpoint QA at the end tests the whole chain against points the adjustment never saw.
### Hydraulic design on the survey
- Water available at the source. The design flow is set from the surplus the canal or river can release and for how long, usually from the irrigation department's discharge records.
- Head available. The surveyed level at the off-take minus the level at each recharge site gives the head that can move water by gravity.
- Line sizing. Open channels are sized by Manning's equation; pipelines by Darcy–Weisbach or Hazen–Williams head-loss calculations. Where the surveyed head is not enough, the longitudinal section shows where pumping or a change of route is needed.
- Crossings are drawn on the cross-sections at each road, railway, canal, drain and service line, with the levels and clearances the crossing owner needs.
### Choosing recharge sites
Recharge structures only work where water can move from the surface into the aquifer. Sites are usually chosen in two passes:
- GIS screening. Layers for slope (from the DTM), low ground and ponds (from the DTM and orthomosaic), land use, soil, geology and geomorphology, drainage, and depth to water level are combined in a weighted overlay to rank candidate sites. This follows the approach of the Central Ground Water Board's Manual on Artificial Recharge of Ground Water (2007) and its Master Plan for Artificial Recharge to Groundwater in India (2020).
- Field confirmation. Shortlisted sites are confirmed on the ground, typically with double-ring infiltration tests (ASTM D3385), electrical resistivity soundings for the thickness of the unsaturated zone and the aquifer, and a check of existing wells.
- Structure type follows the ground: recharge shafts or wells where a clay layer near the surface would stop water soaking in; percolation pits and recharge ponds where permeable soil is near the surface; existing village ponds revived where they already collect water.
- Silt and water quality: desilting chambers and filters are sized for the expected silt load, because recharge must not carry silt or contaminants into the aquifer.
### How accuracy is reported
Accuracy is reported as root mean square error (RMSE) at independent checkpoints, following the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data, Edition 2 (2023): horizontal accuracy as RMSE H , and vertical accuracy on open, hard ground as non-vegetated vertical accuracy (NVA). Edition 2 reports RMSE alone, without the confidence-level figures of Edition 1, asks for at least 30 checkpoints for a product accuracy assessment, and includes the error of the checkpoint survey itself in the reported figure. For cropped and scrub areas, vegetated vertical accuracy (VVA) is reported as well; under Edition 2 it is reported without a pass or fail threshold.
What decides gravity flow is relative accuracy: whether the level at one end of a line is right relative to the level at the other. Levelling along the benchmarks, closed within tolerance, checks the drone terrain model along the full length.
How accuracy is proved. Each checkpoint's residual is the map value minus the ground value. RMSE is the square root of the mean of the squared residuals, calculated separately for X, Y and Z, and the checkpoints must be independent of the GCPs.
### Common failure modes and how they are prevented
Failure | Consequence | Prevention
Crops, hedges and trees left in the terrain model | Ground mapped too high; gradients and earthwork wrong | Survey after harvest where possible; ground filtering and manual edits; ground levels or LiDAR under cover
Slow vertical drift over a long corridor | A line that falls on the drawing but not on the ground | Benchmarks and levelling along the full length; GCP pairs throughout
Canal levels from records in a different datum | Off-take head over- or under-estimated | Canal bed and water levels surveyed and tied to the same benchmark
Water and wet ground in photogrammetry | Holes or noise in the surface | Sections and bathymetry for water; ground levels at ponds
Recharge sited on the map alone | A structure on ground that does not take water | Field checks at shortlisted sites before design
## Getting the best results
- Survey the off-take first; its levels decide whether the rest of the line can work by gravity.
- Fly after harvest where the season allows; it is cheaper than editing crops out of the terrain model.
- Tie the survey to the irrigation department's benchmark so its canal records can be used directly.
- Keep the corridor wide enough to move the alignment around houses, wells and trees without re-flying.
- Map existing ponds, wells and drains on the orthomosaic before choosing new recharge sites.
- Treat desilting as part of the design, not an add-on: a recharge well clogged with silt stops working.
- Plan monitoring points with the design, so the effect on groundwater levels can be measured afterwards.
## Why drones are faster
A ground survey with DGPS and total station measures one point at a time, so a long corridor takes weeks. A DATA PKT drone team captures around 5 sq km of survey data in a day , which is then mapped and analysed in the office.
On a linear corridor such as a highway, one team captures about 35 km of drone imagery for photogrammetry, or about 50 km of aerial video, in a day , and DATA PKT has more than 20 drone pilots (a team of about 22) to put in the field. Ground instruments are still used, but only where they matter most: for the control points that fix the map to real coordinates, for checkpoints that prove the accuracy, and for detail the drone cannot see.
## How we run the survey and design
- Desk study: canal and river records, existing maps and groundwater information for the area.
- Reconnaissance: the off-take point, the possible routes and the recharge sites are walked and photographed.
- DGPS control: ground control points and benchmarks are set along both corridors, so every map and level is tied to real coordinates.
- Drone mapping: the 45 km and 15 km corridors are flown and processed into orthomosaics, terrain models and contours.
- Ground survey: levels at the canal or river, at crossings and at structure sites are checked with DGPS and total station.
- Design: alignment, longitudinal sections, hydraulic sizing of the lines, and drawings of the off-take, silt chambers, crossings and recharge structures.
- Hand-over: drawings, sections, quantities and the survey data, in CAD and GIS formats.
## Other irrigation, canal and river surveys
The same methods serve irrigation and water departments on other work: longitudinal and cross-sections of canals, distributaries and drains; bathymetry of rivers, reservoirs and canal beds; mapping of regulators, falls, bridges and outfalls; encroachments and lining condition along canal banks; flood-plain and river-course mapping; and command-area maps for irrigation planning.
