## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is a groundwater recharge system?
A network that takes surplus water from a canal or river when it is available and lets it soak back into the aquifer through recharge structures such as recharge wells and shafts, percolation pits and ponds, instead of letting it run off or evaporate.
Q: What is DATA PKT doing in Mahendragarh?
We are carrying out the survey and design of a groundwater recharge system for the Mahendragarh area in Haryana. Two lines, of about 45 km and 15 km, take water from an existing canal or river and carry it to the recharge structures.
Q: How do drones help design a recharge system?
A drone survey tied to DGPS control maps the whole corridor as an orthomosaic and terrain model in days. Designers use it to choose the alignment, check that water can flow by gravity, draw longitudinal and cross-sections, find crossings and pick recharge sites such as low ground and village ponds.
Q: How long does it take to survey a 45 km line?
One DATA PKT drone team captures about 35 km of linear corridor imagery in a day, so the flying for both lines takes a few days. DGPS control, ground checks and processing come on top.
Q: Does DATA PKT survey canals and rivers for irrigation departments?
Yes. We survey canals, distributaries, minors, drains and rivers: longitudinal and cross-sections, bathymetry of the water channel, structures such as regulators, falls and bridges, encroachments, lining condition and command areas.
Q: Why does a recharge line survey need such accurate levels?
An open gravity channel flows only if its bed falls continuously; a gravity pipeline flows only if the head at the off-take is more than the level at the outlet plus the friction losses along the way. Either way the design rests on level differences. On flat farmland the total fall over many kilometres can be small, so a vertical error that would not matter on a map can decide whether the line flows, needs pumping or has to be rerouted.
Q: Can a drone survey see the ground under crops?
A photo survey cannot: photogrammetry maps the top of whatever covers the ground, so standing crops and trees raise the surface. Surveys are best timed after harvest, and remaining areas are covered by ground levels or LiDAR, whose laser returns can reach the ground through gaps in vegetation.

Home / Case studies / Slope stability, Assam
Case study · Landslide and slope stability
# Slope stability investigation of a 66 km road corridor in Assam
For a private client, DATA PKT investigated the road-side slopes of a ~66 km hill road corridor in Assam with drone LiDAR, seismic refraction tomography and geological mapping, and delivered a stability report that ranked every stretch and gave the inputs to design its protection.
Published 2 November 2026 · Updated 25 November 2026
Location
Road corridor in Assam, Northeast India
Length
About 66 km of road-side cut and fill slopes
Client
Private client (name withheld)
Duration
About 9 weeks, with about 3 weeks in the field
In short: we flew drone LiDAR along the full ~66 km corridor, shot 66 seismic refraction profiles (about one per kilometre), mapped the geology in detail at 7 critical locations (2.12 km) , and combined all three in one ground model. The stability analysis gave a factor of safety for each critical section in dry, monsoon-saturated and earthquake conditions, and every stretch was ranked by hazard with remedial measures and protection design inputs.
## The challenge
The client needed to know which slopes along the corridor were most likely to fail, how, and what it would take to hold them, so that slope stabilisation and rockfall protection could be selected and dimensioned for the critical stretches. The corridor is a hard place to answer that question:
- Very heavy monsoon rain , of the order of 2,500–3,500 mm a year, which saturates the slopes
- Seismic Zone V under IS 1893, the highest seismic zone in India
- Dense vegetation covering the slopes, hiding the ground from photographs
- Soft alluvial soils and weathered sedimentary rock in the cut sections
- Failures mainly through rain-induced shallow slides , erosion and toe scour , and structurally controlled rock failures
- A narrow, live road: every field crew had to work around traffic
## Scope of work
Item | Quantity | What it involved
Mobilisation | Team of 8 with all equipment | Gurugram to Assam and back
Seismic refraction tomography (SRT) | 66 profiles (~1 per km) | 24-channel profiles, 3–5 m geophone spacing, 9 shots per spread, tomographic inversion and interpretation
Drone LiDAR survey | ~66 km, ~100 m wide corridor | RTK/PPK drone LiDAR with DGPS control; classified point cloud, DTM/DSM, contours, orthophoto, cross-sections
Geological mapping | 7 locations, 2.12 km | Engineering geological mapping, discontinuity survey, field strength tests, RMR, GSI, SMR, Hoek–Brown strength
Analysis and report | Corridor-wide | Integrated interpretation, slope stability analysis, hazard ranking, remedial measures, draft and final report
0 km 10 km 20 km 30 km 40 km 50 km 60 km G1 G2 G3 G4 G5 G6 G7 Drone LiDAR corridor (~100 m wide, full length) SRT profile (~1 per km, 66) Geological mapping (7 sites)
How the investigation covered the corridor: LiDAR along the full length, a seismic profile about every kilometre, and detailed geology at the seven most critical stretches (G1–G7). Distances are relative.
## Our approach: three data sets, one ground model
No single method can characterise a slope. We planned three independent investigations, each answering its own question, and brought them together for the analysis:
- Drone LiDAR showed what the ground surface looks like: slope height and angle, benches, cracks, scarps, drainage paths and changes at the road edge, under the vegetation.
- Seismic refraction showed what lies below: the thickness of loose cover, the depth to weathered and fresh rock, and low-velocity zones that are weak or saturated.
- Geological mapping showed how the material behaves: rock mass quality, joint orientations, possible failure mechanisms and shear strength.
- The stability analysis put the three together: geometry from LiDAR, layering from SRT and strength from geology gave a factor of safety for each critical section.
Desk study · alignment data · drone permission · DGPS control network DRONE LiDAR the surface SEISMIC REFRACTION what lies below GEOLOGICAL MAPPING how the material behaves DTM, contours, sections slope angle, scarps, 3D P-wave velocity sections soil thickness, rock depth RMR, GSI, SMR, joints strength c' and φ' Integrated ground model geometry + layering + strength Slope stability analysis factor of safety: dry, saturated, earthquake Hazard zonation · priority list · protection design inputs
The integrated workflow, from mobilisation and DGPS control to the hazard map and protection design inputs.
Seismic profiles were placed where they gave the most information: high cuts and embankments, visible distress, scour-prone sections beside water, and the seven geology locations. Their exact positions were fixed after reconnaissance and a quick-look LiDAR model, and every profile was surveyed by DGPS so the tomograms plot directly on the LiDAR cross-sections.
Road Ground surface drone LiDAR Soil / loose cover SRT: low velocity Weathered rock SRT: medium velocity Joints geological mapping Fresh rock SRT: high velocity Possible slip surface
On each critical section, the LiDAR surface, the SRT layering and the mapped joints define the slip surfaces checked in the stability analysis.
## How a corridor investigation like this is planned
### LiDAR flight design
- Point density is set by the flight. For one strip, point density is roughly the sensor's pulse rate divided by (ground speed × swath width), and swath width is 2 × height × tan(half the scan angle). Flying lower or slower, or adding strips, raises density. Height, line count and density in a specification such as the one below are traded off against each other in this way.
- Ground-point density decides the bare-earth model. Under dense canopy only a fraction of pulses reach the ground, so what matters for the DTM is the density of ground points after classification, not total density.
- Scan angle and multiple returns. A narrower usable scan angle gives more near-vertical pulses that pass through gaps in the canopy, and recording multiple returns per pulse lets the last returns reach the ground.
- Terrain following keeps the height above ground near constant on a road that climbs and falls through hill sections.
- IMU and trajectory. Flights begin and end with an alignment manoeuvre (such as a figure-of-eight) to settle the inertial solution, and the base station logs for the whole flight for the PPK trajectory.
- Boresight calibration fixes the small angles between the laser scanner and the IMU, so that overlapping strips agree.
### Control design for a hill corridor
- Two layers of control. Static GNSS pillars, tied to Survey of India or CORS, form the backbone; ground control points and check points are measured from them.
- Where LiDAR GCPs go. On LiDAR, GCPs are used mainly to remove vertical bias between strips and flights and to check the boresight, so they belong on flat, open, hard surfaces (road pavement, culvert tops, clearings) rather than on slopes, where a small horizontal error turns into a large vertical one.
- Check points held out. Check points are kept out of every adjustment and spread along the full length, with a separate set under vegetation for the vegetated vertical accuracy (VVA) test.
- One frame for every discipline. Geophones, shot points and geology stations are positioned from the same network as the LiDAR, so tomograms and mapped joints plot directly on the LiDAR sections, as they did on this corridor.
## Methods and specifications
Component | Method and key specifications
DGPS control | Static control pillars about every 7–8 km tied to Survey of India / CORS; WGS 84 / UTM; about 70 ground control points and at least 30 independent check points for the LiDAR
Drone LiDAR | RTK/PPK survey-grade drone LiDAR; 60–80 m above ground; 3 flight lines over the ~100 m corridor; at least 100 points per m²; vertical accuracy target of 5 cm RMSE (ASPRS 2023); multiple returns for a bare-earth DTM under vegetation
Seismic refraction | 24-channel seismograph; 10–14 Hz geophones at 3–5 m; 9 shots per spread with a stacked 8 kg hammer source; about 20–30 m investigation depth; tomographic inversion with RMS misfit under 5%
Geological mapping | Mapping at 1:500 to 1:1,000; scanline and window discontinuity surveys (IS 11315); Schmidt hammer and point-load tests (IS 8764); RMR (IS 13365), SMR (Romana), GSI (Hoek–Marinos); kinematic analysis on stereonets
Strength parameters | Generalised Hoek–Brown (2002) with equivalent Mohr–Coulomb c′ and φ′ over the slope stress range; Barton–Bandis for joints
Stability analysis | Limit equilibrium (Bishop, Spencer, Morgenstern–Price) for soil and rock-mass slopes; planar and wedge checks for rock; static, saturated and pseudo-static seismic cases (IS 1893 Zone V)
## How each stream was processed
- LiDAR: raw scans and GNSS/IMU data → PPK trajectory from the base station → point cloud and strip adjustment → check against ground control and classification → DTM, DSM and contours → sections, slope maps, 3D models and KMZ.
- Seismic refraction: SEG-2 shot records → geometry and elevations from LiDAR → first-break picking → delay-time starting model → tomographic inversion → velocity section and interpretation.
- Geology: field sheets and photographs → discontinuity database → stereonets and kinematics → RMR, SMR and GSI → Hoek–Brown c′ and φ′ → stability input parameters.
## From point cloud and tomogram to stability model
### LiDAR classification under canopy
- Point clouds are classified to the ASPRS LAS 1.4 classes: ground (2), low, medium and high vegetation (3, 4, 5), buildings (6), low noise (7), water (9) and high noise (18).
- Ground is extracted with an automatic filter (progressive TIN densification and cloth simulation are common choices) and edited by hand on steep cuts, where automatic filters tend to clip the crest and toe of a slope or leave low vegetation in as ground.
- Where canopy leaves too few ground returns for the DTM to be trusted, those areas are flagged, so that stability sections are not drawn through interpolated ground.
The LiDAR chain. A single pulse can return several times as it passes through vegetation. The last returns reach the ground, which is why LiDAR can map terrain under trees.
### Building the stability model
- Sections. Critical sections are cut from the DTM at the spacing given in the deliverables below, each carrying the LiDAR surface, the SRT velocity layers and the mapped discontinuities.
- Layer boundaries from velocity. P-wave velocity ranges are assigned to materials (loose cover, weathered rock, fresher rock) and cross-checked against exposures at the geology locations.
- Strength. Hoek–Brown parameters from GSI and field strength are converted to equivalent Mohr–Coulomb c′ and φ′ over the slope stress range, and joint strength is taken from Barton–Bandis.
- Load cases. Limit equilibrium analyses (Bishop, Spencer, Morgenstern–Price) are run for dry or normal conditions; for monsoon-saturated conditions, with pore pressure set by a raised phreatic surface or a pore-pressure ratio (r u ); and for pseudo-static seismic conditions, with a horizontal seismic coefficient derived from the zone factor for the site under IS 1893 (Part 1).
- Rock slopes. Planar and wedge checks come from kinematic analysis of the mapped joint sets on stereonets.
- Hazard ranking. A Low, Medium, High or Critical ranking typically weighs the factor of safety in the governing case, the failure mechanism, observed distress and the consequence of failure for the road.
## Execution and schedule
The work took about nine weeks from the work order. The field window was about three weeks, with the LiDAR, geology and seismic crews working in parallel in the post-monsoon dry season.
W1 W2 W3 W4 W5 W6 W7 W8 W9 Field window (~3 weeks) Kick-off, data, drone permission Mobilisation, reconnaissance, DGPS control Drone LiDAR, 66 km Geological mapping, 7 sites Seismic refraction, 66 profiles LiDAR processing and deliverables SRT inversion and interpretation RMR / GSI / SMR, c' and φ' Stability analysis, hazard zonation Draft report and presentation Final report and data hand-over
Nine-week schedule: field work in weeks 2–4, processing and analysis in weeks 4–7, draft and final report by week 9.
A typical field day ran from a 06:30 toolbox talk (safety, traffic, weather and equipment check), through field work by three crews from 07:00 to 16:30 (the LiDAR crew flew in the calm morning air; the seismic crew shot in gaps in the traffic), to data download, dual backup and quality checks in the evening. The client received a daily progress report: chainage covered, profiles done, issues and the next day's plan.

## Quality assurance
Activity | Checks
DGPS | Closure of the static network; repeat observations on 10% of control points; RMS under 2 cm; checks against known benchmarks
LiDAR | Boresight calibration; strip-overlap difference under 3 cm; independent check points (ASPRS); visual QC of classification
Seismic refraction | Daily line and geophone tests; reciprocal-time check within ±1 ms; repeat of noisy shots; RMS misfit under 5%; second-person review of picks
Geology | Compass declination correction; at least 10 point-load tests per unit; RMR/GSI/SMR assessed independently by two geologists
Analysis and report | Model checked by hand calculation on one section; internal peer review by a senior engineer; document control and revision log
Data | Chainage-based file naming; dual backup (SSD and cloud) every day; master data register
## How accuracy is reported, and the limits of each method
LiDAR accuracy is reported to the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data, Edition 2 (2023), the standard named in the specification above. Edition 2 reports RMSE only, without confidence-level figures, needs at least 30 checkpoints for a product assessment, and includes the checkpoint survey's own error in the reported figure. Non-vegetated vertical accuracy (NVA) is the pass or fail measure; vegetated vertical accuracy (VVA) is reported without a pass or fail threshold.
Slope geometry (height, angle, bench widths) depends on relative accuracy within each section. Plotting tomograms, joints and LiDAR together depends on all three being in the same absolute frame. Both need checking.
### What each method cannot do, and how that is handled
- LiDAR ground under dense canopy. Few pulses reach the ground, so ground-point density is checked, low-confidence areas are flagged and VVA is reported separately from open ground.
- Filters clipping crests and toes. Automatic ground filters treat sharp breaks in slope as objects, so ground on cut slopes is edited by hand.
- Velocity inversion and hidden layers. Seismic refraction needs velocity to increase with depth and layers thick enough to return first arrivals (see ASTM D5777, Standard Guide for Using the Seismic Refraction Method for Subsurface Investigation). A slower layer beneath a faster one, or a thin layer, can be missed, so interpretation is cross-checked with geology and exposures, and weak zones are read as low-velocity anomalies in the tomogram rather than as layers.
- Resolution falls with depth. Fewer rays reach the deeper parts of a section, which is why ray coverage is delivered with each tomogram and interpretation is limited to covered zones.
- Traffic noise on a live road. Shots are taken in traffic gaps, stacked, and repeated when noisy.
- Rock-mass strength from surface mapping. Joints at depth may differ from those on the face, which is why strength is best carried into the analysis as a range rather than a single value.
Seismic refraction in a two-layer model. Beyond the crossover distance, the wave refracted along the faster layer arrives first. The slopes of the travel-time plot give V₁ and V₂, and the intercept gives the depth to the interface. The method needs velocity to increase with depth.
## Safety and environment
- Roadside work-zone traffic management to IRC:SP:55: cones, signboards, flagmen and reflective jackets at every seismic spread and drone take-off point
- Drone operations under the Drone Rules, 2021 with Digital Sky permissions; no flying in rain, wind over 10 m/s, poor visibility or over crowds
- Rock-face mapping only after a check for loose blocks; helmets at all times; an observer watching for rockfall; no climbing without rope access
- Hammer-source safety: gloves, goggles, ear protection and a clearance zone
- No tree felling; vegetation cleared by hand only along seismic lines; all waste taken back

Component | Deliverables | Formats

## How the results feed slope protection design
The investigation was scoped so that its outputs could be used directly to select and dimension flexible high-tensile steel protection systems:
Design need | Why it matters | Where it came from
Slope geometry: inclination, height, length, surface irregularity | Mesh and anchor layout, system choice, quantities | LiDAR DTM, 0.5 m contours, slope-angle map, sections, 3D models
Thickness of the unstable layer and depth to competent strata | Soil nail and anchor length, bond zone | SRT velocity tomograms, cross-checked with geology
Shear strength (c′, φ′) and unit weight | Dimensioning and stability checks | Hoek–Brown from GSI and field strength; SRT correlations
Rock mass structure, joint sets, block size, failure mechanism | Mesh, cable net or barrier; anchor pattern | Discontinuity survey, stereonets, kinematics, RMR / SMR / GSI
Rockfall source zones and fall-line profiles | Rockfall trajectory, barrier location and energy class | Geological mapping of sources; LiDAR profiles; orthophoto
Groundwater and seepage | Drainage alongside the protection system | Seepage mapping; saturated stability case
Where to act first | Prioritising protection works over 66 km | Stretch-wise hazard ranking, factor of safety and priority list
## Why it worked
- One team, three disciplines: survey, geophysics and geology planned together and positioned on the same DGPS control, so every data set lines up.
- LiDAR first, then the ground: a quick-look LiDAR model guided where the seismic lines went, putting effort where the risk was.
- Built for the design that follows: every deliverable was chosen for the protection design it feeds, not for its own sake.
- Corridor scale, short field window: parallel crews kept about 66 km of field work to about three weeks.
## Getting the best results
- Plan LiDAR for ground-point density under the canopy, not total point density.
- Put LiDAR check points on open, flat, hard ground for NVA, and a separate set under vegetation for VVA.
- Fly the LiDAR first and use a quick-look DTM to place the seismic lines.
- Survey every geophone and shot point on the same control as the LiDAR, so geophysics and geometry line up without manual shifting.
- Read seismic velocities with the geology alongside; refraction alone can miss a weak layer beneath a stronger one.
- Carry strength as a range and test the sensitivity of the factor of safety to it, rather than relying on one "best estimate".
- Run the saturated case for every critical section in a heavy-monsoon region; it is often the case that governs.
- Deliver ray coverage and misfit with every tomogram, so the designer knows how far to trust each part of it.

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What did DATA PKT do on the Assam corridor?
We investigated the road-side cut and fill slopes along about 66 km of road in Assam: a drone LiDAR survey of the full corridor, 66 seismic refraction tomography profiles (about one per kilometre), detailed geological mapping at 7 critical locations totalling 2.12 km, and a slope stability analysis with stretch-wise hazard ranking and remedial recommendations.
Q: Why were three methods combined?
Each answers a different question. LiDAR shows the shape of the slope, seismic refraction shows what lies below the surface, and geological mapping shows how the material behaves. Combined in one ground model, they give a factor of safety for each critical section that none of them could give alone.
Q: How long did the investigation take?
About nine weeks from the work order to the final report, with about three weeks in the field. The LiDAR, seismic and geology crews worked in parallel to keep the field window short.
Q: Why is this corridor difficult?
The region gets very heavy monsoon rain, lies in seismic Zone V under IS 1893, and has dense vegetation, soft alluvial soils and weathered sedimentary rock in the cuts. Slopes fail mainly through rain-induced shallow slides, erosion and toe scour, and failures controlled by rock joints.
Q: How were the results used?
The report gave the slope geometry, the thickness of unstable layers, shear strength parameters and failure mechanisms needed to select and dimension flexible high-tensile steel protection systems such as soil-nailed mesh, rockfall drapes and barriers, together with a priority list of where to act first.
Q: Can drone LiDAR map the ground under dense forest?
Partly. Some laser pulses pass through gaps in the canopy and return from the ground, and multiple-return sensors record them. How well the ground is mapped depends on how many ground returns remain after classification, so a good survey reports ground-point density and vegetated vertical accuracy separately from results on open ground.
Q: What can seismic refraction not tell you about a slope?
Refraction relies on velocity increasing with depth, so it can miss a slower, weaker layer lying beneath a faster one, or a layer too thin to show in the first arrivals, and its resolution falls with depth. It is strongest when read together with geological mapping and, where available, boreholes.

Home / Insights / Drone survey accuracy
Survey accuracy
# How accurate is a drone survey? GSD, GCPs and RTK explained
Drone surveys can reach survey-grade accuracy, but only when the flight, the ground control and the processing are planned for it. Here is what decides the number, and how to check it.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 26 October 2026 · Updated 24 November 2026
Short answer: a well-planned drone survey with RTK or PPK positioning and ground control points typically achieves accuracy of a few centimetres. The real figure for your project depends on the ground sample distance (GSD), the ground control, the terrain and the processing, and it should always be proved with independent checkpoints in an accuracy report.
## 1. Ground sample distance (GSD): the level of detail
GSD is the size of one image pixel on the ground. A GSD of 2.5 cm means each pixel covers 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm. It depends on the camera sensor, the lens and the flying height: fly lower or use a higher-resolution camera, and the GSD gets smaller.
GSD sets the limit on what you can see and measure. You cannot reliably map a feature smaller than a few pixels. A common rule of thumb is that horizontal accuracy with good ground control is around one to two times the GSD, and vertical accuracy around one and a half to three times the GSD.
For reference, a typical 20-megapixel survey drone camera flown at about 100 m above ground gives a GSD of roughly 2.5–3 cm.
## 2. Ground control points (GCPs): tying the map to the real world
A GCP is a clearly marked target on the ground whose coordinates are measured with DGPS. During processing, GCPs anchor the drone map to the project coordinate system and correct errors in the drone's own position data.
- Spread GCPs around the edges of the site and through the middle, not in one cluster.
- On long corridors such as highways and railways, place them along the full length, alternating sides of the alignment.
- Measure them in the same coordinate system and height datum the design team will use.
Ground control for a linear corridor. GCPs alternate on both sides of the alignment and are paired at the ends. Checkpoints are held out of the adjustment so that accuracy can be checked independently. Spacing and offset follow from the GSD and the accuracy target.
## 3. Checkpoints: proving the accuracy
Checkpoints are measured exactly like GCPs but are not used in processing. After the map is built, the coordinates read from the map are compared with the surveyed coordinates. The difference, usually reported as RMSE (root mean square error) in X, Y and Z, is the honest accuracy of the survey. A survey without independent checkpoints has an unproven accuracy. To work out the figures from your own checkpoints, use our free checkpoint RMSE calculator .
How accuracy is proved. Each checkpoint's residual is the map value minus the ground value. RMSE is the square root of the mean of the squared residuals, calculated separately for X, Y and Z, and the checkpoints must be independent of the GCPs.
## 4. RTK and PPK: better positions for every photo
RTK (real-time kinematic) corrects the drone's GNSS position during the flight using a base station or correction network. PPK (post-processed kinematic) applies the same corrections after the flight. Both give each photo a position accurate to a few centimetres, which reduces the number of GCPs needed and makes results more consistent. They do not remove the need for checkpoints.
## 5. What limits accuracy in the field
Condition | Effect | What helps
Dense vegetation | Photogrammetry maps the top of the canopy, not the ground | LiDAR, or ground survey under trees
Water and shiny surfaces | Few matching features, so poor reconstruction | Bathymetry for water; extra control nearby
Low image overlap | Gaps and distortion in the model | Plan around 75–80% forward and 65–70% side overlap
Uniform terrain (sand, fresh earthwork) | Hard to match images | Lower flights, more overlap, more control
Wind, haze and harsh shadows | Blurred or inconsistent images | Fly in stable conditions and good light
## Photogrammetry or LiDAR?
For open ground, photogrammetry is usually the most economical choice and also gives a true-colour orthomosaic. Where the ground is under vegetation, or where you need wires and fine 3D detail, LiDAR is the better tool. Many corridor projects combine LiDAR and photogrammetry . See our photogrammetry page for typical deliverables.
## What to ask your survey provider
- What GSD will the survey be flown at?
- How many GCPs and how many independent checkpoints, and where?
- Which coordinate system and height datum will be used?
- Will you supply an accuracy report with RMSE in X, Y and Z?
- How will vegetated areas, water and structures be handled?
See our drone survey glossary for the terms used in accuracy reports.
Planning a survey? Tell us the site and the outputs you need.
Send an enquiry Call +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: How accurate is a drone survey?
A well-planned drone survey with RTK or PPK positioning and ground control points typically achieves accuracy of a few centimetres. The real figure depends on the GSD, the ground control, the terrain and the processing, and it should always be proved with independent checkpoints reported as RMSE in X, Y and Z.
Q: What is GSD in a drone survey?
Ground sample distance is the size of one image pixel on the ground; a 2.5 cm GSD means each pixel covers 2.5 cm by 2.5 cm. It depends on the camera sensor, lens and flying height. As a rule of thumb, horizontal accuracy is around one to two times the GSD and vertical accuracy one and a half to three times.
Q: Does an RTK drone still need ground control points?
Yes, but fewer of them. RTK and PPK give each photo a position accurate to a few centimetres, which reduces the number of GCPs needed and makes results more consistent. They do not remove the need for independent checkpoints, which are the only way to prove the accuracy of the finished survey.
Q: Where should ground control points be placed?
Spread GCPs around the edges of the site and through the middle, not in one cluster. On long corridors such as highways and railways, place them along the full length, alternating sides of the alignment. Measure them with DGPS in the same coordinate system and height datum the design team will use.
Q: How is drone survey accuracy reported?
Checkpoints are measured like GCPs but left out of processing, then compared with the coordinates read from the finished map. The difference is reported as RMSE in X, Y and Z, and in general practice can be stated against a standard such as the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards. A survey without checkpoints has unproven accuracy.

Railways
# What is an Engineering Scale Plan (ESP) in railway projects?
An Engineering Scale Plan is the base drawing for almost any change to a railway yard. Here is what it shows, when it is needed, and how drone and LiDAR surveys make it faster and safer to prepare.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 26 October 2026 · Updated 24 November 2026
Short answer: ESP stands for Engineering Scale Plan. In railway drawings it is a drawing of a station yard or section, made to scale, that shows the tracks, points and crossings, platforms, buildings, bridges, level crossings and chainages in their true positions. Railways use the approved ESP as the base for yard remodelling, new lines and signalling plans.
## What an ESP shows
- All running lines, loops and sidings, with track centres
- Points and crossings (turnouts), with their positions
- Platforms, foot over bridges, station buildings and goods sheds
- Bridges, culverts, level crossings and road over or under bridges
- Railway land boundary and nearby features that affect the work
- Chainages (kilometrage) along the line
A yard ESP built as layers on one control network. Tracks, points, structures, drainage and the land boundary are kept as separate layers, so each can be checked, issued and updated on its own.
## When an ESP is needed
An up-to-date ESP is usually needed whenever the layout of a yard or section is going to change: yard remodelling, new lines, doubling or tripling , new platforms, goods terminals and sidings. Other drawings, such as signal interlocking plans, are typically prepared from the approved ESP, so errors in the ESP flow into everything that follows.
## How an ESP used to be prepared
Traditionally, survey teams measured the yard on foot with total stations and tapes. In busy yards this means long hours working next to live tracks, with the work squeezed into traffic blocks, and it is easy to miss details that are only noticed later.
## How drones and LiDAR change it
- Plan: fix the extent of the yard, the coordinate system, permissions and flight timings with the railway.
- Ground control: surveyors place and measure GCPs with DGPS at safe locations around the yard.
- Capture: the drone flies the yard in a short window, capturing photos and, where needed, LiDAR.
- Process: the team produces an orthomosaic and terrain model accurate to a few centimetres, checked against independent checkpoints.
- Draft: drafters trace every track, turnout and structure from the georeferenced base in CAD.
- Verify: the field team checks critical details such as turnout positions and chainages on the ground.
- Deliver: the ESP in CAD (DWG) and PDF, with the orthomosaic as a reference layer.
## Why it is worth it
- Safety: far less time for staff on or near live tracks.
- Completeness: the orthomosaic records the whole yard, so missed details can be checked without another site visit.
- Reuse: the same survey supports drainage plans, land plans and progress monitoring later.
Learn more about our ESP and DPR surveys and railway survey work .
Planning a survey? Tell us the site and the outputs you need.
Send an enquiry Call +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is the full form of ESP in railway drawings?
ESP stands for Engineering Scale Plan. It is a drawing of a railway station yard or section, made to scale, that shows tracks, points and crossings, platforms, structures and chainages in their true positions.
Q: When is an ESP needed?
Whenever the layout of a yard or section is going to change: yard remodelling, new lines, doubling or tripling, new platforms, goods terminals and sidings.
Q: Which drawings are prepared from the ESP?
Other drawings, such as signal interlocking plans, are typically prepared from the approved ESP, so an error in the ESP flows into everything that follows.
Q: How is an ESP prepared with a drone survey?
Surveyors measure ground control points with DGPS, the drone flies the yard in a short window, and the team builds an orthomosaic and terrain model checked against independent checkpoints. Drafters trace the yard in CAD, the field team verifies turnouts and chainages, and the ESP is delivered in DWG and PDF.

Solar
# Solar plant drone thermography: what the inspection report should include
A thermal drone flight is only as useful as the report that comes out of it. Use this checklist to plan an inspection and judge whether a report is good enough to act on.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 26 October 2026 · Updated 24 November 2026
Short answer: a good solar thermography report lists every defect with its type, exact location (block, string, module), temperature difference and severity, backed by a thermal and a visual image of each one, a plant map, and a record of the conditions during the flight. The widely used standard for aerial thermography of PV plants is IEC TS 62446-3 .
## Flight conditions that matter
Thermal images only show faults clearly when the modules are working hard and conditions are stable. IEC TS 62446-3 sets a minimum irradiance of 600 W/m² in the plane of the modules, with clear sky and stable conditions. In practice this means flying around the middle of the day on clear days with the plant running normally.
- Use a radiometric thermal camera, which records a temperature for every pixel.
- Record irradiance, ambient temperature, wind and cloud cover during the flight.
- Fly at a height and angle that give enough thermal resolution on each module and avoid sun reflections.
## Common defects found
Defect | How it looks in thermal | Typical cause
Single-cell hot spot | One cell much hotter than its neighbours | Cell crack, damage or local shading
Multi-cell or patchwork heating | Several warm cells in a pattern | Cell degradation, potential-induced degradation (PID)
Substring hot | One third of the module uniformly warmer | Bypass diode active or failed
Whole module warm | Entire module warmer than others | Module disconnected or open circuit
String off | A whole row of modules warmer | String fault, fuse or connector failure
Junction box or connector heating | Small, very hot point at the box or cable | Loose or corroded connection
Soiling and shading | Irregular warm areas | Dust, bird droppings, vegetation, structures
## Checklist: what the report should contain
- Plant details, date, time and the weather and irradiance during the flight.
- Equipment used, including the thermal camera and whether it is radiometric.
- A plant map or orthomosaic with every defect marked.
- For each defect: type, location (block, inverter, string, module), temperature difference against normal modules, and severity.
- A thermal image and a matching visual image of each defect.
- A summary table by defect type and severity, with recommended action.
- Data files your O&M team can use, such as a spreadsheet and GIS layers.
## What the report is used for
Owners and O&M teams use the report to prioritise repairs, support warranty claims with module makers, plan cleaning and vegetation control, and compare plant health year on year. A repeat flight after repairs confirms the faults are fixed.
See our solar plant drone thermography and power sector services.
Planning a survey? Tell us the site and the outputs you need.
Send an enquiry Call +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: What should a solar plant drone thermography report include?
It should record plant details, date, time, weather and irradiance; the equipment used and whether the camera is radiometric; a plant map or orthomosaic with every defect marked; each defect's type, location, temperature difference and severity with matching thermal and visual images; a summary table with recommended actions; and spreadsheet and GIS files for the O&M team.
Q: Which standard applies to drone thermography of solar PV plants?
The widely used standard for aerial thermography of PV plants is IEC TS 62446-3. It sets a minimum irradiance of 600 W/m² in the plane of the modules, with clear sky and stable conditions, so that faults show clearly in the thermal images.
Q: What defects can a thermal drone inspection find on a solar plant?
Typical findings are single-cell hot spots, multi-cell or patchwork heating linked to cell degradation or PID, hot substrings from active or failed bypass diodes, whole modules warm from disconnection or open circuit, strings off due to fuse or connector faults, junction box and connector heating, and soiling or shading.
Q: When should a solar thermography drone flight be done?
In general practice, around the middle of the day on clear days with the plant running normally, so the modules are working hard and conditions are stable. A radiometric thermal camera should be used, and irradiance, ambient temperature, wind and cloud cover recorded during the flight.
Q: Who analyses your solar thermography data?
Our thermal team includes a thermographer certified to ISO 9712 Level 2, and our in-house GIS team processes the survey data. ISO 9712 is the international standard for qualifying and certifying non-destructive testing personnel, a scheme that includes infrared thermography.
Before a report is written, the flight data has to pass quality checks. See our solar thermography data QC case study .

Survey methods
# LiDAR vs photogrammetry: which drone survey to choose
Choose LiDAR when trees, crops or scrub hide the ground, or when you need wires, OHE and other thin structures in 3D. Choose photogrammetry for open, bare sites, mines and stockpiles, where it comes close to LiDAR’s height accuracy and gives the sharper map for less money. Most highway and railway projects use both.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 27 October 2026 · Updated 25 November 2026 · 12 min read
Short answer: on open, bare ground the two are close: both reach about 10–15 cm height accuracy with good control, and photogrammetry gives the sharper map for less money. Once vegetation hides the ground, photogrammetry's error tripled to about 36 cm in one study while LiDAR stayed near 11 cm. Choose LiDAR for vegetation, forests, wires and long corridors; photogrammetry for open sites, mines and stockpiles; and both on most highway and railway projects.
11 cm vs 36 cm
height error under vegetation over 60 cm, LiDAR vs photos [1]
≈1,000 vs 18
ground points per hectare under dense tropical forest [4]
32 vs 1
echoes per laser pulse (RIEGL VUX-120-23) vs one surface per photo ray [15]
93 cm → 5.5 cm
corridor height error when GCPs move from one side to a zigzag [8]
## LiDAR vs photogrammetry: the comparison table
Figures come from peer-reviewed field studies, standards and manufacturer specifications (marked as such). Each number links to its source below.
Parameter | Drone LiDAR | Drone photogrammetry | Better choice
Height accuracy, bare ground | ≈10–11 cm RMSE [1] [2] | ≈14–15 cm RMSE with GCPs [1] [2] ; ≈1.5 cm where ground is clearly visible [3] | Close: photogrammetry can match LiDAR on open ground
Height accuracy, vegetation over 60 cm | ≈11 cm, almost unchanged [1] | ≈36 cm, rising with plant height [1] | LiDAR , 3× smaller error
Dense tropical forest terrain | About 3% of points reach the ground [4] | About 0.01% reach the ground; terrain error 2.1 m [4] | LiDAR
Ground coverage, dense leaf-off forest | Nearly 100% [3] | 80.7%: gaps where nothing is seen [3] | LiDAR
Echoes per laser pulse / ray | Up to 5 (L2), 16 (L3), 32 (RIEGL VUX-120-23) [12] [13] [15] | One: the visible surface only | LiDAR
Point density, typical survey | 35–200 points/m² [1] [2] [6] | ≈100 to thousands of points/m², on visible surfaces only [1] | Photogrammetry on open surfaces; LiDAR on hidden ground
Area per flight (maker figures) | 2.5 km² (L2) [12] | 3 km² (P1) [14] | Similar within India's 120 m green-zone ceiling [16]
Ground control, area survey | Few checkpoints, mainly to check strip fit [10] | ≥1, ideally ~4 GCPs per 100 photos [7] | LiDAR needs less control
Ground control, long corridor | Checkpoints along the route | ≥7 GCPs, zigzag both sides (~5 per km) for under 10 cm [8] | LiDAR
Light and surface | Active sensor: works at night; strong sun and dark surfaces cut range (L2: 450 m → 250 m) [12] | Needs daylight, contrast and texture; struggles on snow, water, uniform sand | LiDAR for poor light
Power lines, OHE, thin structures | Wires captured as 3D points; clearance to decimetres [6] | Stereo matching fails along the wire [5] | LiDAR
True-colour map (orthomosaic) | From the built-in camera: 20 MP on L2, 2×100 MP on L3 [12] [13] | 45 MP full-frame mapping camera (P1) [14] | Photogrammetry for the sharpest map
Sensor cost | L2 about USD 13.6–14.7k (2023); high-end sensors far more | Lower | Photogrammetry
Mine and stockpile volumes | Best on dark or uniform material, or in poor light | Meets the IBM drone SOP (orthomosaic ≤5 cm GSD) [11] ; 4–6% volume error at 0.8 cm GSD [17] | Photogrammetry for routine monthly volumes
Fits accuracy standards for vegetated land | Strong: ASPRS Ed. 2 vegetated accuracy reported, USGS QL0 = 5 cm [9] [10] | Often fails under cover | LiDAR
## How each sensor sees the ground
Photogrammetry is passive. The drone takes hundreds of overlapping photos and software finds the same feature in several of them, then works out its 3D position. Every point is something the camera saw : the top of a tree, a roof, a road. If nothing in the photos shows the ground, there is no ground in the model.
LiDAR is active. The scanner fires hundreds of thousands of laser pulses a second and times each echo. A single pulse can return several echoes: the first from leaves, later ones from branches, the last from the ground through a gap. A DJI Zenmuse L2 records up to 5 echoes per pulse, the newer L3 up to 16 and a RIEGL VUX-120-23 up to 32 [12] [13] [15] . Software then keeps the last echoes and builds a bare-earth terrain model.
Photogrammetry LiDAR Sees only the top of the canopy Pulses slip through gaps to the ground first return (leaves) last return (ground)
Figure 1. A camera can only map surfaces it can see. A laser pulse can split: its first echo comes from leaves (white dots), its last from the ground below (red dots).
That one difference, seeing versus measuring through gaps, explains almost every result below.
## Accuracy: on open ground it's a draw
Two independent studies flew drone LiDAR and drone photogrammetry over the same ground and checked both against RTK survey points:
- On short grass (under 20 cm), LiDAR reached 10.9 cm RMSE and photogrammetry at 2 cm GSD 13.9 cm , against 193 checkpoints [1] .
- On the bare crest of a river levee, LiDAR reached 9.7 cm and RTK photogrammetry 14.7 cm [2] .
- Where the camera sees the ground clearly, photogrammetry can even beat LiDAR: about 1.5 cm in one leaf-off forest test [3] .
So for a bare, open site, a well-controlled photogrammetry survey is accurate enough for most engineering work, and cheaper.
## Add vegetation and the gap opens
As plants grow taller, the camera maps their tops and the "ground" rises with them. LiDAR's last echoes keep finding the real surface:
10 cm 20 cm 30 cm 40 cm 11 14 Bare / low cover study A 10 15 Bare ground study B 31 41 Dense shrubs, unfiltered study B 11 36 Vegetation over 60 cm study A Drone LiDAR Drone photogrammetry Vertical error, RMSE (cm) - lower is better
Figure 2. Vertical error (RMSE, cm) from two field studies flown with both sensors. Study A: Salach et al., 2018. Study B: Kang et al., 2026. Under vegetation over 60 cm, photogrammetry error is more than three times LiDAR’s.
- As vegetation grew from about 20 cm to over 60 cm, photogrammetry error rose from 24 → 27 → 36 cm . LiDAR held at about 11 cm [1] .
- Under dense shrubs below 1 m, unfiltered terrain error was 41 cm for photogrammetry and 31 cm for LiDAR. Good ground filtering cut both to about 17–18 cm [2] : processing skill matters as much as the sensor.
## Under forest canopy, it isn't close
Photogrammetry: about 18 LiDAR: about 1,000 Points within 1 m of the ground, per hectare of dense tropical forest (one dot = one point)
Figure 3. Points landing within 1 m of the forest floor, per hectare, in dense tropical forest: about 18 from photogrammetry against about 1,000 from LiDAR (Zhang et al., 2021).
- In dense tropical forest, only 0.01% of photogrammetry points fell within 1 m of the ground, against 3% of LiDAR points. The photogrammetric terrain model was off by 2.1 m RMSE [4] .
- In dense young forest, photogrammetry saw only 80.7% of the ground. LiDAR covered nearly all of it, and 89% of its ground points came from later echoes, not the first [3] .
This is why hill roads, landslide slopes, forest corridors and transmission routes through the Northeast and the Himalayas are LiDAR jobs. A slope stability model built on a canopy surface puts the slip surface in the wrong place.
## Wires, towers and overhead equipment
Photo 1 Photo 2 Photos along the line: wire and search line run parallel The software searches along the dashed line, so every point on the wire looks the same and the match fails. The wire drops out of the model. LiDAR Every pulse that hits the wire is a 3D point: sag and clearance follow
Figure 4. Photogrammetry matches points along a search line between overlapping photos. A wire running along the flight strip lies along that line, so the match fails. LiDAR simply records each pulse that hits the wire.
- Photos taken along a power line cannot match the wire, because the conductor runs parallel to the software's search line. Workarounds need cross-strip photos and manual stereo work, and reach only about ±0.5 m [5] .
- Drone LiDAR at about 35 points/m² measured conductor-to-vegetation clearance on 220 kV lines to decimetre accuracy, automatically [6] .
The same principle applies to railway overhead equipment, catenary and signal posts: if the deliverable includes thin structures in 3D, fly LiDAR.
## Ground control: where photogrammetry projects go wrong
Photogrammetry needs ground control points (GCPs) to fix scale and height. Its height error is typically about 2.5 times its horizontal error [7] , and on long, narrow corridors the layout of GCPs decides the result:
GCPs on one side only height error up to 93 cm Zigzag on both sides, pair at each end (11 GCPs, ~5 per km) height error 5.5 cm Same 2.1 km road, same photos: only the ground control layout changed
Figure 5. The same 2.1 km road, flown once and processed with different ground control. GCPs on one side only: height error up to 93 cm. A zigzag on both sides with a pair at each end (11 GCPs, about 5 per km): 5.5 cm (Ferrer-González et al., 2020).
- Area surveys: below 1 GCP per 100 photos, accuracy falls quickly. About 4 per 100 photos gave the best height accuracy, about 1.5× GSD [7] .
- Corridors: at least 7 GCPs were needed to get under 10 cm on the 2.1 km road [8] .
- LiDAR's position comes from GNSS and an inertial unit on the drone. Checkpoints are still used, mainly to confirm that overlapping strips fit together [10] .
"Survey-grade without GCPs" claims from sensor makers (3 cm horizontal / 5 cm vertical for P1, 4 cm / 5 cm for L2) are measured in ideal conditions [12] [14] . On a real project, plan checkpoints either way.
## Light, surfaces and weather
- Light: photogrammetry needs daylight and shadows that don't hide detail. LiDAR is an active sensor and works at night, but strong sun and dark surfaces shorten its range. The L2 reaches 450 m on a 50%-reflective target in the dark but 250 m on a 10%-reflective target in 100,000-lux sunlight [12] .
- Texture: photogrammetry needs visual texture to match. Snow, ice, still water, uniform sand and fresh black asphalt are classic weak spots. LiDAR doesn't need texture, but neither sensor sees through water.
- Flight height: in India's green zone, drones fly without permission up to 400 ft (about 120 m) [16] . Long-range LiDAR is rated for far higher flights, so in India its range mostly buys wider swaths and better penetration, not altitude.
## Where photogrammetry is the right choice
- The sharpest true-colour map. A 45 MP full-frame mapping camera (P1) beats the smaller cameras built into LiDAR units for orthomosaic detail [12] [14] .
- Mines and stockpiles. The Indian Bureau of Mines drone SOP asks for an orthomosaic at 5 cm GSD or better, at least 5 GCPs per km² and an RMSE report [11] . Photogrammetry meets that naturally. Stockpile volumes came within 4–6% at 0.8 cm GSD in a 2025 study [17] .
- Open, bare sites : graded land, quarries, urban and cadastral mapping, construction progress.
- Budget. A survey LiDAR unit such as the L2 cost about USD 13,600–14,700 at launch, and high-end scanners cost far more. A mapping camera is cheaper, and so is each repeat flight.
## Orthomosaic vs photogrammetry
An orthomosaic is not an alternative to photogrammetry: it is one of its outputs. Photogrammetry is the process, matching overlapping photos to build a 3D model of the visible surface (a point cloud and a digital surface model). The orthomosaic is made by using that surface to correct every photo for camera tilt and terrain relief, then stitching them into one map with a uniform scale, so distances and areas can be measured on it. The same flight usually also gives the point cloud, DSM and contours. A LiDAR unit with a built-in camera can produce an orthomosaic too.
## Which to choose, by project
Is the ground hidden by trees, crops or scrub? yes no LiDAR for the terrain Wires, OHE or thin structures needed? yes no LiDAR (+ camera) Photogrammetry with zigzag GCPs Need a sharp true-colour map too? Fly LiDAR + RGB
Figure 6. A quick way to decide. Most highway and railway corridors end up on the LiDAR + RGB branch.
Project | Usual choice | Why
Highway DPR / topography | Hybrid: LiDAR + RGB | LiDAR for the terrain under trees on verges and medians, the orthomosaic for features. Photogrammetry alone only on bare alignments, with zigzag GCPs.
Railway corridor and yard ESP | LiDAR + RGB on corridors; photogrammetry + ground checks in open yards | Long corridors punish thin ground control; overhead equipment (OHE) needs 3D points. Open yards are clearly visible from above.
Transmission line route | LiDAR | Conductors, sag and vegetation clearance in 3D.
Mine and stockpile volumes | Photogrammetry | Meets the IBM SOP and repeats cheaply every month. Add LiDAR on vegetated benches and dumps.
Hill road and landslide slopes under forest | LiDAR | Under canopy, photogrammetric terrain error reaches metres.
Urban and cadastral mapping | Photogrammetry | Boundaries and features are read from the orthomosaic. Add LiDAR when roofs and facades matter.
Solar plant site | Photogrammetry; LiDAR where scrub hides the ground | Bare, graded land suits photos; grading design on scrubby, undulating land needs LiDAR terrain.
Floodplain and riverbanks | LiDAR for vegetated banks | Neither maps through water: river beds need bathymetric sonar or green LiDAR.
## How the accuracy should be reported
Ask for a checkpoint report whichever sensor you choose. The ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards, Edition 2 (2023), are the current reference [9] :
- At least 30 checkpoints (up to 120 on large projects), surveyed at least twice as accurately as the product.
- One headline number: RMSE . The old "95% confidence" figure is gone.
- Accuracy on open ground ( NVA ) must meet the spec. Accuracy under vegetation ( VVA ) is reported, so you can see how each sensor did where it matters.
The USGS quality levels give a simple density and accuracy yardstick for LiDAR terrain [10] :
Quality level | Point density | Height accuracy, open ground (RMSE)
QL0 | ≥ 8 points/m² | 5 cm
QL1 | ≥ 8 points/m² | 10 cm
QL2 | ≥ 2 points/m² | 10 cm
QL3 | ≥ 0.5 points/m² | 20 cm
These levels were written for aircraft surveys. Drone LiDAR at 35–200 points/m² is far denser.
## What's new in 2025–2026
- DJI Zenmuse L3 (late 2025): a 1535 nm laser with a 0.25 mrad beam, up to 16 echoes per pulse and two 100 MP cameras, rated at 3 cm vertical / 4 cm horizontal accuracy at 120 m [13] . Its cameras narrow the map-quality gap with photogrammetry.
- RIEGL VUX-120-23 : up to 2 million measurements a second, with forward, backward and nadir scanning for steep cuttings, poles and facades [15] .
- Gaussian splatting : a newer way to build 3D models from photos, now in DJI Terra 5.0 (2025). In one 2026 study, point measurements on splat models reached 1–2 cm, and thin structures came out better than on meshes [18] . It is promising for visual models, but it doesn't solve the problem of ground hidden under vegetation.
## How we decide at DATA PKT
We fly both, and on most highway, railway and hill-road projects we combine them: LiDAR for the terrain and anything thin, and a camera for the map. Before quoting, we look at three things: how much of the ground is hidden, whether the deliverable needs wires or vertical faces, and how long and narrow the corridor is. Then we plan ground control to match. Send us the KML and the outputs you need, and we'll tell you which method, or which mix, gives the accuracy you need at the lowest cost.
See LiDAR surveys , photogrammetry , how accurate is a drone survey? and the free GSD calculator .

- Chen et al., UAV LiDAR for transmission line clearance inspection, Remote Sensing 10(4):613, 2018. www.mdpi.com
- Sanz-Ablanedo et al., Accuracy of UAV photogrammetry vs number of GCPs, Remote Sensing 10:1606, 2018. www.mdpi.com
- Ferrer-González et al., GCP layout for UAV photogrammetry on road corridors, Remote Sensing 12:2447, 2020. www.mdpi.com

Figures from single studies apply to the conditions of that study (sensor, flight height, vegetation). Manufacturer figures are measured in ideal conditions.
Send us the site KML or chainage and the outputs you need. We reply with a scope and quote.
Send an enquiry WhatsApp +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: Is LiDAR more accurate than photogrammetry?
On open, bare ground they are close: field studies found about 10–11 cm height error for drone LiDAR and 14–15 cm for photogrammetry with good ground control. Under vegetation over 60 cm, photogrammetry error rose to about 36 cm while LiDAR stayed near 11 cm, and under dense forest photogrammetric terrain was off by about 2 m.
Q: Can photogrammetry see the ground under trees?
Only where the ground is visible between trees. In dense tropical forest only about 0.01% of photogrammetry points fell within 1 m of the ground, against about 3% for LiDAR, because laser pulses return several echoes and the last one often comes from the ground.
Q: Which is cheaper, LiDAR or photogrammetry?
Photogrammetry is usually more economical: the camera costs less and repeat flights are cheap. A survey LiDAR such as the DJI Zenmuse L2 cost about USD 13,600–14,700 at launch. LiDAR earns its cost where the ground is hidden, on long corridors and where wires or thin structures must be mapped.
Q: How many GCPs does a drone photogrammetry survey need?
For area surveys, research found accuracy falls quickly below 1 GCP per 100 photos and was best at about 4 per 100. On a 2.1 km road, at least 7 GCPs in a zigzag on both sides (about 5 per km) were needed to get under 10 cm; GCPs on one side only gave errors up to 93 cm.
Q: Can I get a colour map from LiDAR?
Yes. Most survey LiDAR units carry a camera: 20 MP on the DJI L2 and two 100 MP cameras on the L3, so the point cloud can be coloured and an orthomosaic made from the same flight. A dedicated full-frame mapping camera still gives the sharpest orthomosaic.
Q: Which is better for power lines and railway OHE?
LiDAR. Photogrammetry fails to match wires that run along the flight strip, while LiDAR records each pulse that hits a conductor as a 3D point, so sag and vegetation clearance can be measured to decimetre accuracy. See our guides to inspecting power lines by drone and drone inspection of railway bridges and OHE .

=== https://datapkt.com/insights/drone-survey-vs-dgps-total-station.html ===
Home / Insights / Drone vs DGPS and total station
Survey methods
# Drone survey vs DGPS and total station: which should you use?
When a drone survey beats DGPS and total station, when it does not, and why most infrastructure surveys combine all three. Coverage, accuracy, safety and deliverables compared.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 27 October 2026
Short answer: they do different jobs. DGPS gives a few points of very high accuracy, a total station measures detail where satellites or drones cannot reach, and a drone captures everything across the whole site. Most infrastructure surveys use all three: DGPS for control, a drone for coverage and a total station for hidden detail.
## What each method does best
 | Drone survey | DGPS | Total station
What it captures | Every visible surface across the site | Individual points, very accurately | Individual points, including hidden ones
Coverage per day | Large areas and long corridors | Limited by walking between points | Limited by line of sight and set-ups
Under trees | Photos: no. LiDAR: yes | Weak signal under canopy | Yes
Safety near traffic or tracks | Staff stay off the carriageway or line | Staff walk the site | Staff work on site, often for long periods
Outputs | Orthomosaic, terrain models, contours, 3D | Control points, coordinates | Detailed points, levels, as-built data
On railway sections, the drone keeps staff off the running line for most of the survey.
## The combined workflow we use
- DGPS fixes ground control points and independent checkpoints in the project coordinate system.
- The drone flies the whole site or corridor, with RTK or PPK where available.
- Total station or DGPS picks up what the drone cannot see: ground under dense trees, inside culverts, structure levels.
- Processing merges everything into one terrain model and drawing set, and the checkpoints prove the final accuracy.
## When a ground-only survey still makes sense
- Very small plots, where flight planning and processing outweigh the fieldwork saved
- Sites under continuous dense canopy, if LiDAR is not in budget
- Indoor, underground or under-bridge detail
- Red-zone airspace where flight permission is not available in time
For the accuracy side, read how accurate a drone survey is ; for budgets, see what decides the cost .
Send us the site KML or chainage and the outputs you need. We reply with a scope and quote.
Send an enquiry WhatsApp +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: Does a drone survey replace DGPS?
No. DGPS measures the ground control points and checkpoints that make a drone survey accurate. The drone captures the whole area; DGPS ties it to real coordinates and proves the accuracy.
Q: When is a total station still needed?
Under dense trees, inside structures, for precise levels of bridge bearings , drains and rail tops, and wherever a drone cannot fly or see.
Q: Is a drone survey accepted for DPRs?
Drone surveys tied to DGPS control are widely used for DPR topography in India, with ground survey completing the details a drone cannot capture.

Home / Insights / How to choose a drone survey company
Buying guide
# How to choose a drone survey company in India: a 10-point checklist
A 10-point checklist for hiring a drone survey company in India: DGCA pilots and registered drones, accuracy reports, sample deliverables, references, processing in-house and data ownership.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 27 October 2026
Short answer: look past the drone. The firm should have legally registered drones and certified pilots, prove its accuracy with independent checkpoints, show sample deliverables and references from similar projects, and process the data in-house. Everything else follows from those.
## The checklist
- Registered drones and certified pilots. Under the Drone Rules, 2021 , drones are registered on the Digital Sky platform and pilots hold a DGCA remote pilot certificate from an authorised drone school.
- An accuracy report with checkpoints. Ask for RMSE in X, Y and Z measured on checkpoints that were not used in processing. Without it, the accuracy is unproven.
- The right GSD for the job. The quote should state the ground sample distance. Check it with our GSD calculator .
- DGPS ground control by surveyors. Who measures the GCPs, with what equipment, in which coordinate system and height datum?
- Sample deliverables. Ask for a sample orthomosaic, terrain model and drawing from a past project, in the formats your team uses.
- References from similar projects. A highway DPR, a railway ESP and a solar panel thermography job need different skills. Ask for named clients.
- Processing and drafting in-house. Firms that only fly hand the hard part to someone else. Ask who builds the models and drawings.
- Airspace planning. They should check the Digital Sky zone map for your site and plan any permission before quoting dates. See our guide to drone survey permissions in India .
- Clear scope and data ownership. The contract should list every deliverable and say that the raw and processed data belong to you.
- Method honesty. A good firm will tell you when LiDAR or a ground survey is the better tool. See LiDAR vs photogrammetry .
## Questions to ask in the first call
- What GSD and how many GCPs and checkpoints will you use?
- Will you give an accuracy report with RMSE?
- Which similar projects have you done, and for whom?
- Who processes the data and prepares the drawings?
- What exactly will I receive, in which formats, and when?

We are empanelled with NHAI in three zones, have flown highway surveys since October 2020, and our GIS and drafting teams work in-house in Gurugram. Our clients include NHAI, NHIDCL, Indian Railways, DMRC and more than 80 contractors. See our case studies and company facts .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What licences does a drone survey company need in India?
Under the Drone Rules, 2021, drones are registered on the Digital Sky platform and flown by pilots holding a DGCA remote pilot certificate issued through an authorised drone school. Ask to see both.
Q: What should a drone survey contract include?
The area, GSD and accuracy, the number of control points and checkpoints, the coordinate system, the list of deliverables and formats, the schedule, and who owns the data.
Q: How do I check a drone survey company's experience?
Ask for named references on similar projects, sample deliverables and an accuracy report from a past survey.

Home / Insights / Drone survey deliverables
Deliverables
# Drone survey deliverables explained: orthomosaic, DSM, DTM, contours and point clouds
What you get from a drone survey: orthomosaic, DSM, DTM, contours, point cloud and CAD drawings, what each is used for, and the file formats (GeoTIFF, LAS, DWG, SHP, KMZ).
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 27 October 2026
Short answer: a drone survey normally delivers an orthomosaic (a measurable aerial map), a surface model and a terrain model, contours, and drawings or GIS layers of the features. LiDAR surveys add a classified point cloud. Each comes in standard formats that open in CAD and GIS software.
## The main deliverables
Deliverable | What it is | Used for | Usual formats
Orthomosaic | A single aerial image corrected so that distances can be measured on it | Base map, features, progress, encroachments | GeoTIFF, ECW, KMZ
DSM | Surface model of the top of everything: ground, buildings, trees | Obstacles, heights, line-of-sight | GeoTIFF
DTM | Bare-earth terrain model with buildings and vegetation removed | Design, drainage, earthwork, flood studies | GeoTIFF, LandXML
Contours | Lines of equal height from the DTM | Drawings and layouts | DWG, DXF, SHP
Point cloud | Millions of 3D points, classified as ground, vegetation, buildings, wires | Corridors, power lines, detailed terrain | LAS, LAZ
CAD drawings | Features drawn as lines and blocks: roads, tracks, structures, utilities | DPRs, ESPs, yard plans , as-builts | DWG, DXF, PDF
GIS layers | Features with attributes for analysis | Asset registers, land records, planning | SHP, GeoPackage, KML
Accuracy report | Checkpoint errors (RMSE) in X, Y and Z | Proving the survey is fit for purpose | PDF
A surface model (DSM): heights of everything on the site.
Contours drawn from the terrain model (DTM).
A land use and land cover map: one of the GIS layers produced from drone and satellite imagery.
## DSM or DTM?
The DSM includes trees and buildings; the DTM removes them to show the ground. Designers and quantity surveyors almost always need the DTM. Under dense vegetation a reliable DTM needs LiDAR or ground survey, because photos only see the canopy.
For other survey terms, see our drone survey glossary .
## Agree these before the survey starts
- Coordinate system and height datum (for example a UTM zone and the vertical datum the design uses)
- GSD of the orthomosaic and grid size of the elevation models
- Contour interval and drawing layers
- Point-cloud classes , if LiDAR is flown
- File formats and software versions your team uses
For accuracy, read how accurate a drone survey is .
Send us the site KML or chainage and the outputs you need. We reply with a scope and quote.
Send an enquiry WhatsApp +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is the difference between a DSM and a DTM?
A DSM (digital surface model) is the top surface, including buildings and trees. A DTM (digital terrain model) is the bare ground with those removed, which is what design and earthwork calculations need.
Q: What file format is an orthomosaic delivered in?
Usually a GeoTIFF, which carries its coordinates inside the file, often with a compressed copy such as ECW or a KMZ for quick viewing in Google Earth.
Q: Can drone survey data open in AutoCAD and GIS software?
Yes. Drawings and contours come as DWG or DXF for CAD, layers as shapefiles or GeoPackage for GIS, and point clouds as LAS or LAZ.

=== https://datapkt.com/insights/landslide-survey-india.html ===
Home / Insights / Landslide survey in India
Landslides and slopes
# Landslide survey in India: methods, standards and what it costs
How a landslide survey is done in India: drone LiDAR, seismic refraction, geological mapping, stability analysis, IS codes and what decides the cost.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 2 November 2026
Short answer: a landslide survey finds which slopes may fail, why, and what will hold them. In India it normally combines four things: a drone LiDAR terrain model, seismic refraction and boreholes for the ground below, geological mapping of rock and joints, and a stability analysis in dry, monsoon and earthquake conditions. The result is a hazard map, a priority list and the design inputs for drainage, soil nails, anchors, mesh and rockfall barriers.
## Why landslide surveys matter in India
The Geological Survey of India estimates that about 12.6% of India's land area, outside snow-covered ground, is prone to landslides, across the Himalaya, the Northeast, the Western Ghats and the Nilgiris. Heavy monsoon rain, steep cut slopes beside new roads and railways, weathered rock and earthquakes combine to trigger failures every year. A survey before protection works are chosen puts money where the risk actually is.
## The four parts of a landslide survey
Desk study · alignment data · drone permission · DGPS control network DRONE LiDAR the surface SEISMIC REFRACTION what lies below GEOLOGICAL MAPPING how the material behaves DTM, contours, sections slope angle, scarps, 3D P-wave velocity sections soil thickness, rock depth RMR, GSI, SMR, joints strength c' and φ' Integrated ground model geometry + layering + strength Slope stability analysis factor of safety: dry, saturated, earthquake Hazard zonation · priority list · protection design inputs
How the survey streams combine into one ground model, a stability analysis and a hazard map.
### 1. Terrain: drone LiDAR and 3D models
Slopes beside hill roads are usually under trees. Drone LiDAR records the ground through gaps in the canopy, giving a bare-earth terrain model, contours, slope-angle maps and cross-sections. It also shows cracks, scarps, old slide scars and drainage paths. Repeat flights compare surfaces over time to measure movement. See LiDAR vs photogrammetry .
### 2. Subsurface: seismic refraction and boreholes
Seismic refraction tomography measures how fast sound travels through the ground to show the thickness of loose cover, the depth to weathered and fresh rock, and weak or saturated zones, continuously along each profile. Boreholes give samples and laboratory strength at chosen points. See seismic refraction survey .
### 3. Material: engineering geological mapping
Geologists map rock types and joints, measure joint orientations, test strength in the field and classify the rock mass with RMR, GSI and SMR. Kinematic analysis on stereonets shows whether planar sliding, wedge sliding or toppling is possible.
### 4. Stability analysis and hazard zonation
Geometry from LiDAR, layering from seismic refraction and strength from geology go into a limit-equilibrium analysis that gives a factor of safety for each critical section: dry, saturated (monsoon) and earthquake (pseudo-static, using the IS 1893 seismic zone). Stretches are then ranked Low, Medium, High or Critical.
Road Ground surface drone LiDAR Soil / loose cover SRT: low velocity Weathered rock SRT: medium velocity Joints geological mapping Fresh rock SRT: high velocity Possible slip surface
What each method contributes on one slope, and the slip surface the analysis checks.
## Which method answers which question
Question | Method | Output
How high and steep is the slope? Where are cracks and scarps? | Drone LiDAR, orthophoto | DTM, contours, slope-angle map, sections, 3D model
How thick is the loose material? Where is rock? | Seismic refraction tomography | Velocity section, depth to competent strata
How strong is the soil and rock? | Geological mapping, field tests, boreholes, laboratory | RMR, GSI, SMR, c′ and φ′
How will it fail? | Kinematic analysis | Planar, wedge or toppling; shallow slide; toe scour
How close is it to failure? | Limit-equilibrium analysis | Factor of safety: dry, saturated, earthquake
Is it moving? | Repeat LiDAR, survey prisms, inclinometers | Change maps, displacement over time
Where do we act first? | Hazard zonation | Low / Medium / High / Critical map and priority list
## Indian standards and guidelines
- NDMA guidelines on the management of landslides and snow avalanches: the national framework for hazard assessment and mitigation
- IS 14496 (Part 2) : preparation of landslide hazard zonation maps in mountainous terrain
- IS 1893 : seismic zones and design seismic coefficients
- IS 11315 : quantitative description of rock discontinuities
- IS 13365 : rock mass rating (RMR)
- IS 8764 : point-load strength of rock
- IS 15681 : seismic refraction method
- IRC:SP:55 : traffic management in road work zones; Drone Rules, 2021 for drone operations
## What you should receive
- LiDAR point cloud, DTM, contours, orthophoto, slope maps, cross-sections and 3D models
- Seismic refraction field data, tomograms and interpreted sections
- Geological maps and sections, joint data, stereonets, RMR/GSI/SMR, strength parameters
- Stability analysis for each critical section, hazard zonation map and priority list
- Remedial recommendations and protection design inputs, or the protection design itself
## Common protection measures
Failure type | Typical measures
Water-driven shallow slides | Surface and sub-surface drainage, re-grading, vegetation, erosion-control mats
Slides in soil and weathered rock | Soil nails with flexible high-tensile mesh
Rock blocks on joints | Rock bolts and anchors, cable nets, rockfall drapes
Rockfall from above | Rockfall barriers and catch fences located by trajectory analysis
Toe erosion beside rivers | Toe walls, gabions, river training
## What decides the cost
- Length or area: kilometres of corridor or hectares of slope.
- Access and vegetation: remote hill roads, forest and traffic slow field work.
- Number of seismic profiles and boreholes: often one profile per kilometre plus extra at critical slopes.
- Detailed geology: how many locations need mapping and testing.
- Accuracy and deliverables: point density, section spacing, 3D models.
- Design scope: design inputs only, or full protection design with drawings and quantities.
## An example: 66 km of road-side slopes in Assam
DATA PKT investigated about 66 km of road-side slopes in Assam, in seismic Zone V with heavy monsoon rain: drone LiDAR of the full corridor, 66 seismic refraction profiles, geological mapping at 7 critical locations and a stability report with stretch-wise hazard ranking and protection design inputs, in about nine weeks. Read the case study or see our landslide and slope stability service .
Send us the site KML or chainage and the outputs you need. We reply with a scope and quote.
Send an enquiry WhatsApp +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is a landslide survey?
A study of a slope or corridor to find where it may fail, how, and what will stabilise it. It usually combines a terrain survey (often drone LiDAR), subsurface investigation (seismic refraction and boreholes), geological mapping and a stability analysis, and ends with a hazard map and remedial design.
Q: Which Indian standards apply to landslide and slope investigation?
Common references include IS 14496 (Part 2) for landslide hazard zonation, IS 1893 for seismic zones and coefficients, IS 11315 for rock discontinuity surveys, IS 13365 for rock mass rating, IS 8764 for point-load testing, IS 15681 for seismic refraction, and IRC:SP:55 for road work-zone safety. The NDMA guidelines on landslide management set the national framework.
Q: How long does a landslide survey take?
It depends on length and access. As an example, investigating about 66 km of road-side slopes in Assam took about nine weeks, including about three weeks in the field.
Q: What decides the cost of a landslide survey?
Corridor length or slope area, access and vegetation, the number of seismic profiles and boreholes, how many locations need detailed geology, the accuracy and deliverables required, and whether protection design is included. Send the KML and your objectives for a scoped quote.
Q: Can a drone survey alone assess landslide risk?
No. A drone LiDAR survey shows the shape of the slope, cracks and scarps, and repeat flights show movement, but it cannot see soil thickness or rock strength. Those need seismic refraction, boreholes and geological mapping before a factor of safety can be calculated.

# Drone GSD calculator
Work out the ground sample distance, the image footprint and the flight height you need for a target GSD. Pick a camera or enter your own sensor.
Ground sample distance
-
Image footprint on the ground
-
Flight height for target GSD

## How the calculator works
GSD is the size of one image pixel on the ground. It is set by the camera sensor, the lens and the flying height:
GSD (cm/px) = sensor width (mm) × height (m) × 100 ÷ ( focal length (mm) × image width (px) )
The footprint is the ground area covered by one photo. The flight height for a target GSD reverses the same formula. Camera presets use manufacturers' published sensor sizes; check your own camera's specification before planning a project.
## Using GSD to plan a survey
- Accuracy: with good ground control, horizontal accuracy is typically one to two times the GSD and vertical accuracy one and a half to three times. Read how accurate a drone survey is .
- Next: once the survey is processed, check your accuracy with the RMSE calculator using your independent checkpoints.
- Height limit: in India's green zones, flights up to 400 ft (about 120 m) above ground need no permission. Above that, or in yellow and red zones, permission is needed.
- Overlap: mapping flights usually use about 75 to 80% forward and 65 to 70% side overlap. Lower GSD means more photos and longer processing.
Want us to plan it? Send the site and the accuracy you need and we will set the GSD, control and flight plan. See what decides the cost .
Send us the site KML or chainage and the outputs you need. We reply with a scope and quote.
Send an enquiry WhatsApp +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is ground sample distance (GSD)?
GSD is the size of one image pixel on the ground. A 2 cm GSD means each pixel covers 2 cm by 2 cm. Smaller GSD means more detail.
Q: How is GSD calculated?
GSD (cm/pixel) = sensor width (mm) × flight height (m) × 100 ÷ (focal length (mm) × image width (pixels)).
Q: What GSD do I need for a topographic survey?
It depends on the accuracy required. As a rule of thumb, horizontal accuracy with good ground control is about one to two times the GSD and vertical accuracy about one and a half to three times the GSD.
Q: How high can a survey drone fly in India?
In green zones of the Digital Sky airspace map, drones can fly up to 400 ft (about 120 m) above ground without permission. Higher flights or yellow and red zones need permission.
