=== https://datapkt.com/insights/drone-survey-for-highway-dpr.html ===
Home / Insights / Drone survey for highway DPRs
Highways
# Drone survey for highway DPRs: what consultants need
What a Detailed Project Report survey must deliver under IRC:SP:19, which parts a drone does well, which still need ground instruments, and what to write into the scope so the data passes review.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 27 October 2026
Short answer: a highway DPR needs a strip plan of the whole right of way, contours, cross-sections at set intervals and a levelled benchmark network tied to one datum. A drone survey on DGPS control delivers the strip plan, contours and cross-sections for the whole corridor in one pass. Benchmarks, levelling and hidden detail at culverts and bridges still need DGPS, auto level or total station on the ground.
## What the DPR survey has to deliver
The Indian Roads Congress manual IRC:SP:19-2001, Manual for Survey, Investigation and Preparation of Road Projects sets out what the survey behind a road DPR must contain. It specifies outputs and accuracy, not the instrument. The figures below are from the 2001 edition; the consultancy's terms of reference can ask for more.
Item | IRC:SP:19-2001
Width of survey | Generally the entire right of way, with allowance for shifting the centre line (clause 8.2.5)
Plan scale | 1:1,000 in built-up areas and hilly terrain; 1:2,500 in plain and rolling terrain (8.3.2)
Contours at critical locations | 1–3 m interval, especially in rolling or hilly terrain (8.3.1)
Cross-sections, final location survey | About 50–100 m in plain terrain, 50–75 m in rolling terrain and about 20 m in hilly terrain, plus curve points and critical locations, out to the right-of-way limit (12.4.2)
Benchmarks | Permanent benchmarks every 2 km; temporary benchmarks every 250 m (500 m exceptionally) and at all drainage and underpass structures, on one datum, preferably GTS (12.3.1)
Control and traverse | Control pillars about every 500 m to 2 km; distance accuracy of at least 1 in 10,000; GPS is accepted for control (8.2.2, 8.2.3)
## Which parts a drone does well
A drone survey captures every visible surface along the corridor, not only the points a surveyor chose to walk to. That suits the parts of a DPR survey that are about coverage.
- Strip plan of the right of way. The orthomosaic shows the existing carriageway, shoulders, buildings, boundary walls, trees, poles, wells and junctions along the whole length, ready to digitise at 1:1,000 or 1:2,500.
- Terrain model and contours. A ground-only terrain model (DTM), not the surface model with trees and vehicles on it, gives contours at whatever interval the design needs .
- Cross-sections at any interval. Once the terrain model exists, sections can be cut every 20 m, 50 m or at each curve point without going back to site, and re-cut if the alignment shifts.
- Alignment options. Bypasses and realignments can be compared on one map before the final location survey.
- Safety. Staff stay off a live carriageway for most of the work.
A corridor frame with the right of way and centre line marked: the base the strip plan is drawn on.
## Which parts still need ground instruments
- Control and checkpoints. DGPS fixes the ground control points that tie the drone map to real coordinates, and separate checkpoints that prove its accuracy.
- Benchmarks and levelling. The permanent and temporary benchmark network, connected to GTS, is still built and levelled on the ground. The drone terrain model is then checked against it.
- Hidden detail. Culvert inverts, bridge bearings and soffits , ground under dense trees and detail inside built-up stretches need a total station, or LiDAR where the canopy is heavy.
- Investigations. Soil, material, traffic and hydrological surveys in the same manual are separate work; the drone survey only gives them a better base map.
Ground control targets are fixed with DGPS before the flight; checkpoints are kept out of the processing to test the result.
## What to write into the survey scope
Most disputes over drone data in a DPR come from a vague scope. Put these in the work order:
- Corridor: the alignment as KML with chainages, and the width to cover on each side of the centre line.
- Datum: the coordinate system and UTM zone, and the GTS benchmarks the levels must be tied to.
- Control: ground control point spacing, and a separate set of checkpoints with an accuracy report against them.
- Resolution: the ground sample distance (GSD) of the imagery; work it out with the GSD calculator .
- Sensor: photogrammetry for open ground, LiDAR where the corridor runs through trees or hills (see LiDAR vs photogrammetry ).
- Deliverables and formats: orthomosaic (GeoTIFF), DTM, contours, strip plan and cross-sections in CAD, point cloud (LAS/LAZ) if LiDAR, and the benchmark register.
- Ground work included: benchmark levelling, structure details and the stretches the drone cannot see, so nothing is left between two contractors.
- Permissions: who obtains drone flight permission where the corridor crosses controlled airspace.
## Common problems that send data back
- Contours drawn from the surface model, so trees, trucks and buildings appear as humps in the ground.
- No independent checkpoints, so the accuracy claim cannot be verified.
- Levels on a local or ellipsoidal height, not tied to the project's GTS benchmarks.
- Under-canopy stretches left blank or guessed instead of filled with LiDAR or total station.
- Strip plans missing utilities and structures that were visible in the imagery but not digitised.
## How DATA PKT works on highway projects
DATA PKT is a drone service provider empanelled with NHAI in three zones, and has captured more than 3 lakh km of highway data in six years for authorities and contractors ( highway drone monitoring case study ). For DPR and ESP work we set DGPS control first, fly the corridor, build the terrain model, check it against independent checkpoints and draft the plans in CAD, with ground survey where the drone cannot see.
A DATA PKT drone team captures around 5 sq km of survey data in a day. See our roads and highways services and ESP and DPR surveys . Once construction starts, NHAI also requires a monthly video of the project: see what monthly NHAI drone videography must show .
Related reading: drone survey vs DGPS and total station , how accurate a drone survey is and what decides the cost .
Source: IRC:SP:19-2001 , clauses 8.2–8.3 and 12.2–12.4. Check the edition and terms of reference that apply to your project.
Send us the alignment KML or chainages and the DPR deliverables you need. We reply with a scope and quote.
Send an enquiry WhatsApp +91 8448559100
## Frequently asked questions
Q: Is a drone survey accepted for a highway DPR?
A drone survey tied to DGPS control and proved with checkpoints is widely used for DPR topography. IRC:SP:19 sets the outputs and accuracy, not the instrument, and accepts GPS for control. Confirm the method with the client or authority engineer and write it into the terms of reference.
Q: How wide should the survey corridor be?
IRC:SP:19-2001 says the survey should generally cover the entire right of way, with allowance for shifting the centre line. Bypasses and realignments need a wider band. State the width on each side of the centre line in the scope.
Q: Does the drone replace benchmark levelling?
No. Permanent and temporary benchmarks are still established and levelled on the ground and tied to GTS. The drone terrain model is checked against them.
Q: Drone photogrammetry or LiDAR for a highway DPR?
Photogrammetry suits open, flat corridors and gives a true-colour map. LiDAR is better where the alignment runs through trees, hills or dense roadside vegetation, because it records the ground beneath the canopy. Long corridors often use both.
Q: What cross-section interval can a drone survey give?
Any interval. Once the terrain model is built, sections can be cut every 20 m in hills, 50–100 m on plains and at every curve point, and cut again if the alignment changes.

Home / Insights / Drone vs manual solar inspection
Solar O&M
# Drone vs manual solar panel inspection: which finds more, faster?
How drone thermal inspection compares with walking the rows: coverage, speed, the faults each method finds and misses, the conditions a valid flight needs, and the workflow that uses both.
By the DATA PKT survey and inspection team · Published 23 November 2026 · Updated 24 November 2026 · 11 min read
Short answer: a drone thermal inspection covers every module of a plant in hours, maps each fault to its table and string, and in one study its findings closely matched a manual check of the same plants in a fraction of the time. Manual methods still win at measuring power loss (IV curves), finding cracks (EL imaging) and checking inside boxes. The best practice is to fly first and send the ground team only where the drone points.
600 W/m²
minimum irradiance for a valid thermal inspection [1] [2]
3 cm/pixel
coarsest resolution for a detailed inspection [3]
2 hours vs 2 days
drone vs manual check of the same plant in one study [5]
80–100 °C+
hotspots from shorted bypass diodes and heavy soiling [4]
## What each method actually checks
A manual inspection sends technicians along the rows with a handheld thermal camera, a clamp meter and an IV curve tracer. It measures well, but it measures what the team reaches: on a large plant, that usually means a sample of rows and strings. Handheld thermal imaging is slow over a large plant and some areas get missed, which is why it suits small sites best [10] .
A drone inspection flies a radiometric thermal camera and a colour camera over every table. Software stitches the images, finds modules that run warmer than their neighbours and pins each one to its table, string and module. Nothing is sampled: every module is seen in one campaign.
Ground crew, sampled rows 2 of 6 faults found. The rest stay hidden. Drone, every row 6 of 6 faults mapped to their table and module. Illustration. Dark tables = inspected. Orange = fault found. Dashed circle = fault missed.
Why sampling misses faults: a crew that walks two rows can only find the faults in those rows. A drone flight covers every row.
## Speed: hours instead of days
The clearest comparison comes from a US study that inspected four plants, 12.5 MW to 74 MW, by drone and compared the results with manual methods on the same sites. Drone inspection took about 10 minutes of flying per MW. When a manual crew was sent to check the drone's findings, its results closely matched the drone data, while the manual work took far longer on every site [5] .
Indian labour costs are lower than American ones, so the money saved per MW will be smaller here. The time saved is not: a plant that needs a week of walking for a full thermal check can be flown in a day or two, and the crew is then sent only to the modules that need them.
A thermal mosaic shows every table at once. Warmer modules stand out against their row.
## What thermal imaging can and can't see
A healthy module runs at an even temperature in the sun. When part of it stops converting light to electricity, that part turns the energy into heat, and the thermal camera sees it. Research groups describe the common patterns the same way [7] [8] :
- A single hot cell : one square clearly warmer than the cells around it, often a damaged or shaded cell.
- A bypass diode pattern : one row or column of cells, usually a third of the module, running warm because a diode has switched that substring out.
- A whole warm module or string : the module is producing nothing, often an open circuit, a blown fuse or a disconnected string.
- Soiling and shading : irregular warm areas with soft edges.
Severity varies a lot. In a 2025 field study, short-circuited bypass diodes and heavy soiling produced hotspots of 80 °C to over 100 °C, while modules with cracked cells were hard to tell apart from healthy ones [4] . That is the honest limit of thermography: it finds faults that make heat. Cracks that have not yet cut a cell off need electroluminescence (EL) imaging.
Hot cell One cell warmer than its neighbours Bypass diode One substring warm: a third of the module Module / string Whole module warm: open circuit or offline Soiling, shading Irregular warm patch, soft edges ? Cell cracks Often invisible in IR; confirm with EL Simplified patterns, after the infrared pattern descriptions used in PV research. Real images need a trained analyst.
The four patterns a thermal analyst looks for, and the one fault thermal imaging often misses.
## The conditions that make a thermal flight valid
A thermal flight on a cloudy morning produces colourful pictures, not evidence. The standard for outdoor thermography of PV plants, IEC TS 62446-3, sets the conditions [1] :
- Irradiance of at least 600 W/m² on the modules, so that faults heat up enough to show [2] . The 2025 study found some faults, such as disconnected interconnects, stayed visible only above that level [4] .
- Steady sky : cloud cover of at most 2/8 and wind below about 29 km/h [2] .
- Clean modules , or soiling noted, so dirt is not mistaken for a defect [2] .
- Resolution : a detailed inspection needs at most 3 cm per pixel. With cells of about 16 × 16 cm, that gives around 25 temperature readings per cell; at 5 cm per pixel it drops to about 9 [3] .
- Qualified people : the standard expects the thermographer to hold a recognised certification, such as ISO 9712 [3] .
The standard separates a quick simplified inspection, which looks for patterns, from a detailed inspection, which measures temperatures at the finer resolution [1] . Ask which one you are buying.
Valid thermal capture under IEC TS 62446-3: irradiance of at least 600 W/m² in the module plane, a viewing angle of more than 30° to the module plane (steep, but just off perpendicular to avoid reflections), and about 3 cm of module edge per pixel or finer.
3 cm per pixel about 25 readings per cell 5 cm per pixel about 9 readings per cell Both squares are one 16 × 16 cm solar cell. Each small square is one thermal pixel. IEC TS 62446-3 asks for at most 3 cm per pixel in a detailed inspection. A coarser flight is faster but has fewer readings per cell.
Resolution decides how many readings each cell gets. Fewer readings make small faults easier to miss.
## Where manual inspection still wins
- Measuring the loss. A thermal image shows where a fault is. An IV curve trace measures how much power a string is losing, which decides whether a repair or warranty claim is worth it.
- Cracks and early damage. EL imaging, usually at night, shows cracks and inactive cell areas that thermography cannot [4] [7] .
- Electrical parts in boxes. Combiner boxes, inverters and connectors inside enclosures need the door open and a handheld camera.
- Small rooftops. On a few hundred modules, one technician with a handheld camera can be quicker than planning a flight.
## Side by side
How the two approaches compare on a utility-scale plant. Figures link to their sources.
Question | Drone thermal inspection | Manual inspection | Better choice
Coverage | Every table, string and module | Usually a sample of rows or strings | Drone
Time on site | About 10 minutes of flying per MW in one study [5] | Days for a full plant; two days per site in the same study [5] | Drone
Finding hotspots, diodes, offline strings | Yes, mapped to the module | Yes, where the crew walks | Drone for the whole plant
Cell cracks | Often not visible [4] | EL imaging shows them | Manual EL
Measuring power loss | Estimated from the pattern | IV curve tracing measures it | Manual
Inside combiner boxes and inverters | No | Yes | Manual
Safety | No walking among live DC strings | Crews work among live equipment | Drone
Records | Geotagged map, repeatable every year | Notes and photos, hard to compare | Drone
Standard | IEC TS 62446-3 covers both, with conditions for drones [1] | IEC TS 62446-3 for thermography | Same standard
## The best practice: drone first, ground team second
The two methods are not rivals. The fastest way to a healthy plant is to let the drone find and map every fault, then send the ground team only where it is needed: to measure, to confirm cracks with EL, and to repair. A second flight after repairs proves they worked and gives you a clean baseline for next year.
1 Fly Thermal + colour under IEC conditions 2 Detect Every anomaly mapped to a module 3 Prioritise Rank by severity and energy loss 4 Confirm IV curve, EL or a ground check 5 Re-fly Prove the repair worked The drone finds and maps; the ground team measures and fixes only where the drone points them.
Drone-first inspection workflow for a solar plant.
## How often to inspect
Inspect at commissioning , to catch installation faults while the EPC contractor is still responsible; every year , as routine; after storms or hail ; and before warranties expire , so claims are filed in time. A survey of US plant owners found that of the plants doing routine plant-wide inspections, fewer than half did them more than once a year, largely because inspection was slow and costly [9] . A drone removes most of that cost.
## How we inspect solar plants at DATA PKT
Our thermal team includes a thermographer certified to ISO 9712 Level 2, the kind of qualification IEC TS 62446-3 expects, and our power-sector clients include NTPC and Adani. We fly radiometric thermal and colour cameras together, plan flights to the IEC TS 62446-3 conditions (irradiance, cloud, wind and resolution), and record the conditions with every flight. Each anomaly is classified, ranked and tied to its table, string and module, so your O&M team can go straight to it. The report follows the checklist in our guide on what a solar thermography report should include .
See our drone thermal survey service and power and energy work .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: Is a drone thermal inspection as accurate as a manual inspection?
For finding faults, yes, and it covers the whole plant. In one study, a manual inspection of the same plants closely matched the drone results but took far longer on every site. Manual tests such as IV curve tracing are still needed to measure how much power a faulty string is losing.
Q: What conditions does a drone thermal inspection of a solar plant need?
IEC TS 62446-3 asks for irradiance of at least 600 W/m² on the modules, little cloud (at most 2/8 of the sky), moderate wind and clean modules. A detailed inspection is flown at a resolution of 3 cm per pixel or finer.
Q: Can thermal imaging find cracked solar cells?
Not reliably. A 2025 field study found modules with cell cracks hard to tell apart from healthy ones in drone thermal images. Electroluminescence (EL) imaging is the better test for cracks, so cracks found by other means should be confirmed with EL.
Q: How long does a drone take to inspect a solar plant?
It depends on plant size, resolution and flight conditions. One US study measured about 10 minutes of flying per MW, and a 74 MW site took 24 hours of drone inspection time including both thermal and colour flights.
Q: How often should a solar plant be inspected by drone?
At commissioning, before the end of the module warranty, after storms or hail, and at least once a year as routine. Many plants inspect less often because manual inspection is slow and costly; a drone makes a yearly plant-wide inspection practical.
Q: What does a drone solar inspection report contain?
A geotagged map of every anomaly, its type and severity, the table, string and module it sits on, thermal and colour images of each, the flight conditions, and a prioritised repair list. Our guide to the solar thermography report lists each item.

# Highway drone videography for NHAI projects: what the monthly video must show
NHAI's monthly drone video rule in plain words: who has to fly, what every frame must show, how videos reach Data Lake, how to plan a long corridor, and how the footage stands up as evidence.
By the DATA PKT survey and inspection team · Published 23 November 2026 · 10 min read
Short answer: every NHAI project, in every contract mode, must record the highway by drone every month and upload last month's and this month's videos side by side to NHAI's Data Lake portal (Policy Circular 18.69, June 2021). The contractor flies during construction, witnessed by the supervision consultant; NHAI flies before construction, at completion and in O&M. A useful video shows chainage, date and the full right of way in every frame, and follows the same flight each month.
Monthly
drone video on every NHAI project, all contract modes [1]
Side by side
last month's and this month's video on Data Lake [1] [2]
3 lakh+ km
highway data captured by our teams in six years
≈50 km/day
videography planned per DATA PKT team
## What NHAI requires, and who it applies to
In June 2021 NHAI issued Policy Circular 18.69, Mandatory monthly drone video recording of project highway during the development, construction and O&M period . It applies to every NHAI project, whatever the mode: item rate, EPC, toll, annuity, HAM, OMT or TOT [1] .
- What to record: drone video covering the entire right of way, showing chainages, the proposed ROW and the median [1] .
- Who records it: the contractor or concessionaire, in the presence of the Team Leader of the Independent Engineer, Authority Engineer or Supervision Consultant [1] .
- How it is shown: last month's video and this month's running side by side [1] , uploaded to NHAI's portal, Data Lake [2] .
- Who reviews it: supervision consultants analyse the videos and comment on them in the digital monthly progress report [3] .
- Before and after construction: NHAI's project directors carry out monthly drone surveys from signing of the contract until construction starts, at completion, and on developed projects NHAI maintains [3] .
- Which agency: NHAI has fixed zone-wise agencies and rates, but contractors may engage an agency of their choice if the specifications and methodology match NHAI's [1] .
For HAM projects, reports at the time said the concessionaire must also record every six months during O&M and keep a project website with the monthly footage, and that non-compliance would attract a penalty of ₹5 lakh [4] . Check the current contract and any later circulars for the exact terms on your project.
Contract signed to start of construction NHAI PD flies monthly Construction Contractor / concessionaire flies monthly, side by side Completion and operation & maintenance NHAI; HAM concessionaire flies monthly; six-monthly (HAM) One video a month, last month beside this month Every video goes to NHAI's Data Lake portal, where the supervision consultant reviews it in the monthly progress report. Based on NHAI Policy Circular 18.69 (June 2021) and NHAI's statements on it.
Who flies, and how often, across the life of an NHAI project.
## What a good monthly video shows
A drone video that only looks good is not enough. The reviewer has to be able to stop at any frame and know where it is, when it was taken and what changed since last month. Every useful frame carries:
- Chainage and position on screen, so a frame can be matched to the design and to last month's video.
- Date and time , burnt into the video, not just in the file name.
- The full right of way in frame, edge to edge, with the proposed ROW visible, as the circular asks [1] .
- The median and carriageways , so progress on each side is visible.
- Structures : bridges, ROBs, underpasses and culverts, recorded slowly enough to judge their stage.
- The same flight every month : same direction, height and speed, so the side-by-side comparison lines up.
CH 8+109 Lat / long of the frame 04-02-2026 10:42 Chainage and GPS on every frame Median / centre line Proposed ROW boundary Structures in progress Full width of the ROW in frame Date and time stamp
What a reviewer needs to see in one frame. Positions and the date shown are illustrative.
Right of way and centre line marked on the frame, so the reviewer can see the whole corridor at a glance.
## Planning the flights on a long corridor
A national highway project can run to 50 or 100 km or more, so the monthly video is a planning job as much as a flying one:
- Flight blocks. The corridor is split into blocks that a battery set can cover, with overlap so no chainage is missing.
- Airspace. Each block is checked on the Digital Sky airspace map . Stretches near airports or other restricted areas need permission well before the flying date.
- Light and weather. Flying in the same part of the day each month keeps shadows and colours comparable; rain, haze and strong wind are avoided.
- The witness. The supervision consultant's team leader has to be present, so dates are agreed in advance [1] .
- Editing and upload. Videos are cut to chainage, overlays checked, last month's video placed beside this month's, and the files uploaded to Data Lake in the format its module asks for [5] .
Structures need slower, lower passes: the reviewer has to judge the stage of each girder and approach.
## Video, orthomosaic or vehicle survey: which record do you need?
The monthly video shows progress; it does not measure it. Three records are often confused:
Drone video Shows progress Monthly, side by side Required by NHAI Evidence for disputes Drone orthomosaic Measures progress Chainage-accurate map Lengths, areas, volumes Overlay on design Network survey vehicle Measures the road Roughness, cracks, rutting Pavement condition For built highways
Three different records. Most projects need the first, many benefit from the second, and the third is for completed roads.
Need | Drone video | Drone orthomosaic and survey | Network survey vehicle
Meets NHAI monthly video rule | Yes [1] | No, a different product | No
Shows visual progress | Yes | Yes, as a map | Along the carriageway only
Measures lengths, areas, volumes | No | Yes , at survey accuracy | No
Pavement roughness and distress | No | Visible cracks only | Yes : laser profilometer and 360° imagery [2]
Overlay on the design drawings | No | Yes | No
Best stage | Development, construction, O&M | Pre-construction, construction, as-built | Completed highways
If the project needs quantities, deviations from design or an as-built map, add a monthly drone orthomosaic or a DPR-grade survey to the video, flown on the same day.
## The video as evidence
NHAI has said the videos are stored permanently on Data Lake and can be used as evidence in dispute resolution before arbitral tribunals and courts [2] . For a contractor, that cuts both ways: the video can prove work done on time, or show that it wasn't. Three habits make it hold up:
- Keep the unedited original files, with their metadata, alongside the uploaded edit.
- Never re-use footage from a previous month, even for a stretch where nothing changed.
- Make sure chainage and date are readable in every frame, not only in the title card.
## Why some monthly videos don't help anyone
- No chainage on screen , so the reviewer can't tell where a frame is.
- A different route or height every month , so the side-by-side comparison doesn't line up.
- Only the finished stretches are filmed, and the problem areas are skipped.
- Too fast over structures , so the stage of a bridge or ROB can't be judged.
- Uploaded late , missing the monthly progress report it was meant to support.
## How DATA PKT runs monthly highway videography
Over six years our teams have captured more than 3 lakh km of highway data for authorities and private contractors, and more than 70,000 km in FY 2026-27. Each team plans about 50 km of videography or 35 km of survey imagery a day, and we have more than 20 pilots. We are empanelled with NHAI in three zones for monthly drone survey work.
Every video carries chainage, position and date on screen, follows the same flight plan each month, and is delivered ready for Data Lake, with the originals archived. Read the highway drone monitoring case study and see our highway survey services .

# Drone Transmission Line Inspection Services in India
Close-up visual and thermal inspection of energised transmission lines, tower by tower, with LiDAR clearance checks where you need them and every finding tied to a tower number.
By the DATA PKT survey and inspection team · Published 25 November 2026
In short: we inspect energised transmission lines by drone. A detailed inspection photographs every tower, insulator string and fitting from close range, radiometric thermal finds hot joints and clamps, and LiDAR measures conductor clearance where it is in scope. Every finding is tied to a tower number, with photos, severity and a recommended action, so your maintenance crews know where to go first.
10–15 towers
a day per crew in detailed close inspection
≈100 km
of linear corridor a day by drone photogrammetry
40%+ load
usually needed for a thermal reading to mean something [2]
ISO 9712 L2
certified thermographer in our thermal team
## What does a drone transmission line inspection cover?
A drone transmission line inspection photographs every tower, insulator string, fitting and span of an energised line from close range, adds radiometric thermal images of joints and clamps, and, where needed, measures conductor clearance to ground and trees. Each finding is tied to a tower number and position, so crews know exactly where to go.
The work is for whoever is answerable for the line staying in service: state and central transmission utilities, private transmission companies, EPC contractors handing a new line over, and plant owners whose solar, wind or thermal power leaves the site on a dedicated line. The common need is the same. A foot patrol sees a tower from below, and the defects that cause trippings often sit on top of the cross-arm, behind an insulator string or at a jumper loop. A drone hovering level with the hardware sees them. Our guide to drone inspection versus foot patrol and helicopters compares the three methods in detail.
A typical scope covers four things, in any combination:
- Towers : rust, bent or missing members, damaged step bolts and anti-climbing devices, foundation and chimney condition where visible, bird nests.
- Insulators and hardware : cracked, chipped or flashed discs, damaged polymer sheds, corroded or loose clamps, missing split pins, damaged spacers, vibration dampers and arcing horns.
- Conductors and earth wire : broken or bird-caged strands, damaged mid-span joints, earth wire and OPGW fittings and splice boxes.
- The corridor : vegetation growing towards the conductors, new buildings and other encroachment in the right of way, erosion near tower footings.
## Patrol or detailed inspection: which one do you need?
A patrol or corridor flight moves quickly along the line to find encroachment, vegetation, damaged towers and obvious faults over many kilometres. A detailed inspection stops at each tower and photographs every insulator, clamp and fitting from several angles, usually with thermal. Many owners patrol often and inspect in detail on a cycle or on priority stretches.
Question | Patrol or corridor flight | Detailed tower inspection
What it answers | Is anything wrong along the line as a whole? | What condition is each component on each tower in?
Flight pattern | Along the corridor, at a steady height and speed | Around each tower and along each insulator string, at several heights
Typical findings | Vegetation, encroachment, leaning or damaged towers, broken earth wire, washed-out footings | Cracked or flashed discs, missing pins, loose or hot clamps, broken strands, damaged dampers
Pace (DATA PKT) | About 100 km of linear corridor a day when mapped by photogrammetry | 10 to 15 towers a day per crew
Usual sensors | Mapping camera, LiDAR where clearance matters | Zoom camera and radiometric thermal camera
The two are often combined. A corridor flight on a long line shows where the problems cluster, and detailed inspection is then spent on those stretches, on the oldest sections, on river and highway crossings, and on towers with a history of trippings. If you are not sure which you need, send us the tower schedule and the problem you are trying to solve, and we will suggest a mix.
## What does each sensor find?
Each sensor answers a different question. A zoom visual camera shows physical damage to insulators, fittings and steel. A radiometric thermal camera shows joints and clamps running hotter than their neighbours. LiDAR measures conductor height, sag and clearance to trees in three dimensions. The scope decides which sensors fly; not every line needs all three.
Sensor | What it finds | Limits
Zoom visual (RGB) camera | Cracked, chipped or flashed insulator discs; damaged polymer sheds; missing split pins; corroded fittings; broken strands; damaged dampers and spacers; rust and missing members; bird nests | Shows the surface only. Light, angle and wind affect what can be seen, so each component is photographed from more than one side.
Radiometric thermal camera | Joints, clamps, jumpers and dead-end fittings running hotter than similar components; some insulator faults that show as abnormal warming | Needs real load on the line. Shiny new conductor reflects heat and reads low; sun, wind and rain distort readings. Radiometric means every pixel carries a temperature value, not just a colour.
LiDAR | Conductor and earth wire positions, sag, height above ground and trees, buildings in the right of way, clearance at crossings | Measures geometry, not condition. It will not show a cracked disc or a hot clamp.
Mapping camera (photogrammetry) | Orthomosaic and terrain of the corridor; encroachment and land use along the right of way | Does not reconstruct thin wires reliably, and cannot see ground under dense trees.
Two notes on choosing. First, a thermal camera that records only a coloured video is not enough for grading hotspots; the images need to be radiometric so that the temperature of the hot component and its reference can be read afterwards. Second, LiDAR earns its cost where clearance is the question, for example over orchards, forest or growing settlements, and on hilly stretches where sag over a valley is hard to judge. Our LiDAR vs photogrammetry guide explains why LiDAR is the better tool for wires.
Utilities sometimes also ask about corona or ultraviolet (UV) cameras. These detect electrical discharge on insulators and hardware that is invisible to visual and thermal cameras, and they are a specialist sensor rather than part of a standard visual and thermal inspection. If your maintenance programme calls for corona inspection, mention it in the enquiry so the scope can be discussed openly.
## How is a hotspot on a joint or clamp graded?
By comparing it with a similar component under similar load, such as the same clamp on the next phase. Under the widely used ANSI/NETA criteria, a rise of 1–3 °C means investigate, 4–15 °C means repair as time permits, and over 15 °C means repair immediately. The readings mean something only when the line carries real load.
A failing joint or loose clamp has a higher electrical resistance than a sound one, so it heats up as current flows through it. A thermal camera shows it as a bright spot, often long before it fails. The widely used ANSI/NETA table sets three bands for the temperature rise over a similar component under similar load [1] :
Temperature rise vs similar component | Meaning | Action
1–3 °C | Possible deficiency | Investigate
4–15 °C | Probable deficiency | Repair as time permits
Over 15 °C | Major discrepancy | Repair immediately
Two cautions apply. First, the readings only mean something when the line carries a real load; thermographers usually ask for at least 40 percent of normal load [2] . Second, the same rise can be ranked differently under other criteria sets, so a good report names the criteria it used [1] . Many utilities also set their own limits, and where they do, those limits apply.
In practice, getting a reading that can be trusted comes down to planning:
- Load window. Ask the line owner when the line is expected to carry its highest load, and fly then. Record the time of each image so the load can be matched later.
- Weather. Strong sun heats everything, wind cools hot joints, and rain or mist blurs the image. Steady, dry conditions give the cleanest comparison.
- Reference component. Compare like with like: the same clamp type on the next phase, or the next joint on the same conductor, under the same load.
- Distance and angle. Small components need to fill enough pixels to be measured, which is one reason close inspection matters for thermal.
Our thermal team includes a thermographer certified to ISO 9712 Level 2, and every graded hotspot in the report comes with its visual photo, so the maintenance crew can see which component it is. For solar plants and substations, see our thermal survey page.
## How are clearance and right of way checked?
A drone survey measures; it does not certify. LiDAR, or photogrammetry over open ground, gives conductor height above ground, trees and buildings span by span. Those measured distances are compared with the clearance values the line owner specifies, normally from the CEA regulations and its own standards. Whether a span complies is the line owner's decision.
India sets right-of-way widths and minimum clearances between conductors and trees by voltage. The table quoted in a National Green Tribunal document gives minimum conductor-to-tree clearances of 3.4 m at 66 kV, 4.0 m at 132 kV, 4.6 m at 220 kV and 5.5 m at 400 kV, with a 35 m right of way at 220 kV and 46 m for a 400 kV single-circuit line [3] . Ground and crossing clearances are set in the Central Electricity Authority (Measures relating to Safety and Electric Supply) Regulations, 2023, and the line owner's standards may set higher values. These figures are summarised for guidance; the current regulations and the owner's standards govern each line.
Line voltage | Minimum conductor-to-tree clearance [3]
66 kV | 3.4 m
132 kV | 4.0 m
220 kV | 4.6 m
400 kV | 5.5 m
Why the distinction between measurement and compliance matters:
- Sag changes. A conductor sags most at mid-span, on hot days and under heavy load. A survey records the clearance on the day of the flight. Projecting it to the maximum design temperature needs the conductor data and is an engineering calculation, so agree in the scope whether it is wanted.
- Trees grow. A span with enough clearance today may not have it after the monsoon. Clearance surveys are most useful repeated on a cycle, with trimming lists by span.
- Thresholds differ. Crossings over railways, highways and other lines carry the requirements of each crossing's owner. The report should state which threshold each span was compared against.
The output is a span-wise table: tower numbers, the closest measured distance to ground, trees or structures, where along the span it occurs, and whether it falls inside the threshold you gave us. Trimming crews then go only where clearance is short.
## Is a distribution line inspection the same job?
No. In Indian practice, transmission usually means 66 kV and above, on lattice towers spaced hundreds of metres apart across open country. Distribution means 33 kV, 11 kV and LT lines on poles spaced tens of metres apart, often along roads and through towns. The defects, flight plans, airspace questions and daily pace differ, so they are scoped separately.
- Structures. A transmission inspection looks at steel towers, long insulator strings and heavy hardware. A distribution inspection looks at poles, cross-arms, pin and disc insulators, GO switches, stays and transformer structures.
- Density. A kilometre of distribution line has many more structures than a kilometre of transmission line, so the count per day is not comparable.
- Surroundings. Distribution lines run close to houses, roads and people, which changes where the drone can launch, fly and hover.
We cover both. For distribution lines, see the distribution line inspection section of our power sector page.
## Is it safe to fly a drone near an energised line?
Yes, when the flight is planned for it. The drone keeps a safe distance from the conductors, set by the line owner's safety rules and the operator's procedure, and no one needs to climb the tower. Strong electromagnetic fields near high-voltage conductors can disturb a drone's compass, so the stand-off is planned with that margin in mind.
Safety planning for a line inspection usually covers:
- Stand-off distance from live conductors, agreed with the line owner, and a flight path that does not take the drone through the conductor space.
- Launch and landing points outside the conductor zone, with permission from the landowner where needed.
- Crossings over roads, railways and other lines, flown so that the drone never hangs over traffic or a second set of live conductors.
- The line owner's consent and any site permit, which a power utility may require even in open airspace.
### Airspace and drone permissions
Drone flights in India fall under the Drone Rules, 2021. The airspace map on Digital Sky divides the country into green, yellow and red zones: green needs no flight permission, yellow needs permission from the air traffic control authority for that airspace, and red needs permission from the Central Government. A long transmission line can cross several zones, especially near airports, borders and strategic sites, so each stretch is checked separately and the check is repeated on the day of the flight. Our flights are flown by DGCA Remote Pilot Certificate holders on drones with a Unique Identification Number. Read drone survey permissions in India for the full picture.
## How we work
- You send the line details. Line name and voltage, single or double circuit, the tower schedule with positions (or a KML of the route), the stretch to be inspected, and what you want found: defects, hotspots, clearance, or all three.
- We agree the scope. Patrol, detailed inspection or both; which sensors fly; the severity criteria and clearance thresholds to report against; and the deliverable formats your team needs.
- Desk planning. Each stretch is checked on the Digital Sky airspace map, access and launch points are planned, and thermal flights are timed with you for a high-load window.
- Permissions and safety. Yellow or red zone permissions are applied for, the line owner's consent and any site permit are arranged, and the stand-off distance is confirmed.
- Field work. Corridor flights and tower-by-tower inspection flights, with images recorded against tower numbers. Ground control is set out where the survey needs mapping accuracy.
- Processing and grading. Images are reviewed tower by tower, defects are logged and graded, thermal images are analysed by our thermal team, and LiDAR or photogrammetry data is processed for clearance.
- Review and delivery. The defect register and report are checked before delivery, with the priority findings listed first so the most urgent repairs are planned first.
## What you receive
The deliverables depend on the scope. The table lists what an inspection of this kind typically produces; the column on the right shows formats common in the industry, and the actual formats are agreed in the scope so the data loads into your own maintenance or GIS system.
Deliverable | What it shows | Typical format
Tower-wise defect register | Each defect by tower number and component, with photo reference, severity and recommended action | Spreadsheet (XLSX or CSV)
Inspection report | Summary of findings, priority list, method, severity criteria and limitations | PDF
Geotagged visual images | Close-up photos of each tower, insulator string and fitting | JPEG with position data
Radiometric thermal images | Hotspots with temperatures of the hot component and its reference | Radiometric JPEG or TIFF
Span-wise clearance table | Closest distance from conductor to ground, trees and structures in each span, against the agreed threshold | Spreadsheet
Corridor point cloud | Conductors, towers, ground and vegetation in 3D, where LiDAR is flown | LAS or LAZ
Corridor orthomosaic | Current image of the right of way, with encroachment and land use | GeoTIFF
GIS layers | Towers, defects and clearance problems on a map | KML or KMZ, shapefile
## What we do not do
A drone inspection tells you where the problems are. It does not fix them, and it does not replace the people and tests that keep a line running. To be clear about scope:
- No live-line or maintenance work. We do not replace live-line maintenance crews, change insulators, tighten clamps or carry out any repair. Those stay with the line owner's crews or their contractors.
- No replacement for utility line patrolling. Drone inspection supports the patrols your own staff carry out; it does not take over their statutory or routine duties.
- No electrical testing. We do not carry out insulation resistance, contact resistance or other electrical tests on the line or its equipment.
- No compliance certificate. We measure clearances and report them against the thresholds you give us; the decision on compliance stays with the line owner.
- No tree cutting. We produce the trimming list by span; the trimming is done by others.

## Frequently asked questions
Q: Can a drone inspect an energised transmission line?
Yes. Energised transmission line inspection is one of our services. The drone keeps a safe distance from the conductors, set by the line owner's safety rules and the flight procedure, so visual and thermal inspection need no outage.
Q: Does the line need a shutdown for a drone inspection?
No. Thermal inspection actually needs the line energised and carrying load, because a de-energised joint shows no hotspot. A shutdown is needed only for the repairs that follow, which the line owner's maintenance crews carry out.
Q: How many towers can you inspect in a day?
In a detailed close inspection, one crew typically covers 10 to 15 towers a day. Terrain, access, tower type, the sensors flown and the weather all change that figure. Corridor mapping by photogrammetry is faster, at about 100 km of linear corridor a day.
Q: What load does the line need for thermal inspection?
Thermographers usually ask for at least 40 percent of normal load. Below that, a faulty joint may not heat up enough to show. Thermal flights are therefore planned for high-load periods, with the expected load confirmed with the line owner beforehand.
Q: Do you measure clearances to CEA requirements?
We measure conductor clearance to ground, trees and structures, span by span, and report it against the values you specify, usually taken from the CEA regulations and your own standards. The measurement is ours; the compliance decision stays with the line owner.
Q: Do you inspect distribution lines too?
Yes, distribution line inspection is covered on our power sector page. It is a different job from transmission: 33 kV, 11 kV and LT lines on closely spaced poles, often along roads and through towns, so it is planned and scoped separately.
Q: What do we receive at the end of the inspection?
A tower-wise defect register with photos, severity and recommended action; graded thermal findings; and, where clearance is in scope, span-wise clearance tables and a corridor point cloud or map. Formats are agreed in the scope so the data loads into your maintenance system.
Q: Which states do you work in?
We work across India from our office in Gurugram. Every stretch of line is checked on the Digital Sky airspace map before the flight, and stretches in yellow or red zones are cleared with the authority concerned before the flight date.
Q: Who analyses the thermal images?
Our thermal team includes a thermographer certified to ISO 9712 Level 2. Each hotspot is graded against a similar component under similar load, and the report names the severity criteria used.

Power lines
# Transmission line drone inspection vs foot patrol: what each one catches
How drone inspection of power lines compares with foot patrols and helicopters: what each can see, how thermal hotspots are graded, the tree clearances India sets by voltage, and how to plan an inspection.
By the DATA PKT survey and inspection team · Published 23 November 2026 · 10 min read
Short answer: a foot patrol sees a tower from below and misses what sits on top of the hardware; a helicopter covers hundreds of kilometres a day but with less detail; a drone inspects every clamp, insulator and joint up close, with thermal for hotspots and LiDAR for tree clearance. Use foot patrol for short accessible lines, helicopters for very long corridors, and drones for detailed inspection of most lines in between.
Over 15 °C
rise over a similar joint means repair immediately (NETA) [4]
40%+ load
needed for a thermal reading to mean something [5]
4.6 m
minimum conductor-to-tree clearance at 220 kV [10]
≈1,000 km
corridor length where helicopters become cost-competitive [6]
## Three ways to inspect a line
Utilities inspect overhead lines in three main ways, and research reviews of the field describe the same split: ground patrol, helicopter, and small drones (with climbing robots as a niche fourth) [8] .
- Foot patrol. A lineman walks or drives the route with binoculars and sometimes a handheld thermal camera. It is the cheapest option per kilometre on short, accessible lines [6] , but it sees the tower from below.
- Helicopter. Fast, covering hundreds of kilometres a day, and good with LiDAR for vegetation clearance and sag; less good on fine detail of each fitting [7] . It stays cost-competitive on very long corridors, roughly 1,000 km or more in a single mobilisation [6] .
- Drone. Slower, covering several kilometres a day in close inspection, but close enough to see each clamp, insulator and fitting, with visual and thermal cameras [7] . Drones sit between the other two: a corridor mode for the line as a whole, and a fine mode that inspects each tower up close [6] .
In India, POWERGRID began drone-based patrolling of EHV lines with its own fleet of micro drones; in February 2023 it patrolled about 200 towers that way [1] . Its stated uses are tower inspection, clearance measurement and vegetation management [2] . Other transmission owners, such as IndiGrid, have adopted drone patrolling too [3] .
## What a drone sees that a patrol misses
The defects that cause outages often sit where a person on the ground can't see them: on top of the cross-arm, behind the insulator string, at the jumper loop. From level with the hardware, a drone camera shows:
- Insulators : cracked, chipped or flashed discs, and polluted strings [3] .
- Fittings : loose or corroded clamps, missing split pins, damaged spacers and dampers [3] .
- Conductors and earth wire : broken strands, sag, damaged OPGW splice boxes.
- The tower itself : rust, bent or missing members, and bird nests. Missing members from theft are a known problem; one state utility's inspection tender lists it alongside rugged terrain, cyclones and ageing assets [9] .
Patrol: sees from below Drone: level with the hardware Tops of clamps and jumpers Insulator strings, each disc Earth wire and OPGW fittings Bird nests, missing members Hot joints on a thermal camera
Why the viewpoint matters: the top of the hardware is out of sight from the ground, and in full view of a drone.
## Thermal: reading a hotspot
A failing joint or loose clamp has higher electrical resistance, so it heats up under load. A thermal camera on a drone shows it as a bright spot long before it fails. The severity is judged by how much hotter it runs than a similar component under similar load , for example the same clamp on the next phase. The widely used ANSI/NETA table sets three bands [4] :
Temperature rise vs similar component | Meaning | Action
1–3 °C | Possible deficiency | Investigate
4–15 °C | Probable deficiency | Repair as time permits
Over 15 °C | Major discrepancy | Repair immediately
Two cautions. First, the readings only mean something when the line carries a real load; thermographers usually ask for at least 40 percent of normal load [5] . Second, the same rise can be ranked differently under other criteria sets, so a good report names the criteria it used [4] .
Temperature rise over a similar component, similar load (°C) 1–3 °C Possible deficiency: investigate 4–15 °C Probable deficiency: repair as time permits over 15 °C Major discrepancy: repair immediately 0 3 15 Valid only with the line carrying a meaningful load: at least about 40 percent of rated load is the usual rule. After ANSI/NETA Table 100.18. Utilities often set their own limits; the report should name the criteria used.
Thermal severity bands for electrical connections, compared with a similar component under similar load.
## Vegetation and clearance
Trees growing into a line cause tripping and fires. India sets right-of-way widths and minimum clearances between conductors and trees by voltage. The table quoted in a National Green Tribunal order gives, for example, a 35 m right of way and 4.6 m tree clearance at 220 kV, and a 46 m right of way and 5.5 m clearance for a 400 kV single-circuit line [10] .
Clearance is not fixed: a conductor sags most at mid-span, on hot days and under heavy load. A drone with LiDAR, or photogrammetry on open ground, measures conductor height and tree height span by span, so trimming crews go only where clearance is short [3] [7] . See LiDAR vs photogrammetry for why LiDAR is the better tool for wires.
clearance Sag is lowest mid-span, on hot days and under load Minimum conductor-to-tree clearance (m) 66 kV 3.4 132 kV 4.0 220 kV 4.6 400 kV 5.5 Values from the RoW and clearance table quoted by the NGT.
Clearance is measured where the sag is greatest. Minimum values rise with voltage.
## Foot patrol, helicopter and drone side by side
Question | Foot patrol | Helicopter | Drone
Speed | Slow; limited by terrain and access | Hundreds of km a day [7] | Several km a day in close inspection [7]
Cost | Lowest on short, accessible lines [6] | Competitive above roughly 1,000 km in one mobilisation [6] | Between the two [6]
Detail on fittings and insulators | Seen from below | Limited [7] | Close-up, every fitting [7]
Thermal hotspots | Handheld, from the ground | Possible | Yes, at hardware level [3]
Vegetation clearance and sag | Estimated by eye | Yes, with LiDAR [7] | Yes, with LiDAR [3]
Hills, forests, rivers | Hard [9] | Easy | Easy within flight range
Risk to people | Climbing for close checks | Low-flying crewed aircraft | No one on the tower
Record | Notes and photos | Video, LiDAR | Geotagged photos, thermal, 3D, tower by tower
## Planning a drone line inspection in India
- Scope by tower numbers. Start from the tower schedule, with GPS positions, so every finding is tied to a tower and span.
- Choose the mode. A corridor flight for vegetation, encroachment and sag; a close inspection of each tower for fittings, insulators and thermal.
- Load and timing. Thermal flights are planned for periods of high load, and in steady weather.
- Airspace and safety. Each stretch is checked on the Digital Sky map, and the drone keeps a safe distance from energised conductors under the operator's safety procedure.
- Deliverable. A tower-wise defect register with photos, severity and action, plus span-wise clearance tables, in a format the maintenance team can load into its own system.

## Frequently asked questions
Q: Can drones inspect live transmission lines?
Yes. Drones inspect energised lines without an outage, keeping a safe distance from the conductors. POWERGRID and other utilities in India use drones for patrolling, tower inspection, clearance measurement and vegetation management.
Q: What can a drone find on a transmission line that a foot patrol misses?
Anything on top of or level with the cross-arms: loose or hot clamps, jumpers, cracked or flashed insulator discs, damaged earth wire and OPGW fittings, bird nests and missing tower members. A patroller looking up from the ground often cannot see these.
Q: How is a hotspot on a transmission line classified?
By how much hotter it is than a similar component under similar load. Under the widely used ANSI/NETA criteria, 1–3 °C warrants investigation, 4–15 °C is a probable deficiency to repair as time permits, and over 15 °C is a major discrepancy to repair immediately. The line should carry at least about 40 percent of its rated load.
Q: What is the minimum clearance between a power line and trees in India?
The right-of-way table quoted by the National Green Tribunal gives minimum conductor-to-tree clearances of 3.4 m at 66 kV, 4.0 m at 132 kV, 4.6 m at 220 kV and 5.5 m at 400 kV. Check the current CEA regulations and the utility's own standard for each line.
Q: Is a drone cheaper than a helicopter for line inspection?
For detailed inspection and for corridors of a few hundred kilometres, usually yes. Helicopters stay cost-competitive on very long corridors, roughly 1,000 km or more in one mobilisation, where their speed offsets the hourly cost. Foot patrol remains cheapest for short, accessible lines.
Q: What does a drone transmission line inspection report contain?
A tower-by-tower register: tower number and GPS position, each defect with photos (visual and thermal), its severity and recommended action, vegetation and clearance problems by span, and a summary for the maintenance plan.

# Railway drone inspection: track, OHE, bridges and yards
Where drones fit in railway inspection in India: overhead equipment with thermal cameras, the track surroundings a recording car can't see, bridges under RDSO guidelines, yard plans and ESPs, and how a railway drone job is planned.
By the DATA PKT survey and inspection team · Published 23 November 2026 · 9 min read
Short answer: drones do not replace track recording cars, which measure geometry and track defects. They add what those systems can't see: overhead equipment up close and in thermal (piloted by Indian Railways in the Raipur division), drains, cuttings and embankments, bridge undersides (RDSO guideline BS-129 R1), and full yard and station plans for ESPs. Most of the effort is in permissions and blocks, not in flying.
OHE thermal
drone monitoring piloted in Raipur division [1]
BS-129 (R1)
RDSO guidelines for drone-based bridge inspection, 2021 [2]
98 km in 3 days
drone trial on the Dedicated Freight Corridor [4]
3 ITMS
track monitoring systems deployed for track inspection [1]
## What drones are used for on Indian Railways
Indian Railways first told its zones to procure drone cameras, starting with West Central Railway, for project monitoring, the condition of track, inspections, and relief and rescue work [3] [5] . West Central Railway planned them for third-line work on Bina–Katni, doubling on Katni–Singrouli, important bridge inspections and monsoon checks of deep cuttings on ghat sections [3] . A trial on the Dedicated Freight Corridor covered 98 km in three days [4] .
The newer work goes further. The Ministry of Railways has reported drone-based thermal monitoring of overhead equipment piloted in the Raipur division, AI-enabled aerial inspection under development with IIT Madras, and three Integrated Track Monitoring Systems (ITMS) deployed for track inspection [1] . For bridges, RDSO issued guidelines in May 2021 for inspection using a 3D bridge model and drones (Report BS-129 R1) [2] .
A drone can follow the track at mast height and see the OHE, track and drains in one pass.
## Overhead equipment: visual and thermal
OHE faults stop trains. A drone flown alongside the line, level with the cantilevers, shows what a ground inspection struggles to see from below or from a tower wagon at speed:
- Contact wire and catenary : wear, kinks, broken droppers, displaced registration arms.
- Insulators : cracks, chips and flashover marks.
- Joints and connections : with a thermal camera, overheating clamps and jumpers stand out under load, the same principle used on power lines (see our guide to transmission line drone inspection for how hotspots are graded).
- Masts and foundations : tilt, corrosion and damage after floods.
The Raipur pilot is exactly this use: drone thermal imaging to detect faults in OHE [1] . Flights must keep a safe distance from the 25 kV wires and run under the division's permission, with the electrical department aware of the plan.
OHE: contact wire, droppers, insulators, hot joints Cutting slopes: cracks, slips, loose boulders Side drains: blocked or silted Track and ballast: visual condition, obstructions
What a drone inspects on an electrified line in a cutting.
## Track, formation and drainage
Track recording cars and ITMS measure track geometry and detect defects in rails, sleepers and fastenings with machine learning and image processing [1] [6] . A drone does not replace them. It adds the view around the track that a recording car cannot give:
- Drains : blocked, silted or broken side and catch-water drains, the usual cause of formation failure in the monsoon.
- Cuttings and embankments : cracks, slips, rock falls and erosion, especially on ghat sections [3] .
- Encroachment on railway land, and obstructions near the track.
- Before and after : repeat flights show how a slope or drain has changed since the last monsoon. For unstable slopes, see our guide to landslide surveys .
Track recording (ITMS) Foot / trolley patrol Drone camera + thermal Drone LiDAR Track geometry Rails, sleepers, fastenings OHE condition and hot joints Bridges: piers, girders, bearings Cuttings, slopes, drainage Yards and stations: as-built plans main tool partly, or at close range not suited
Which method suits which railway inspection task. Drones complement track recording; they do not replace it.
## Bridges
RDSO's BS-129 (R1) guidelines describe inspection of Indian Railway bridges using a 3D bridge information model built from drone data, and the Railway Board has asked zonal railways to integrate this "4D BrIM" approach with the Bridge Management System [2] . A drone reaches places that otherwise need scaffolding, a boat or a bridge inspection unit: the underside of girders, bearings, pier caps and the river bed around the piers . Photogrammetry turns the flight into a measurable 3D model, so cracks and spalling can be located and compared at the next inspection.
## Yards, stations and project monitoring
For yards and stations, a drone survey produces the base plans that remodelling and new works start from: track centre lines, points and crossings, platforms, buildings, drains and utilities, tied to kilometre posts. That is how Engineering Scale Plans (ESPs) are prepared today; see what an ESP is . On projects such as doubling, third lines and new lines , monthly flights record progress the same way highway projects do [3] .
A station yard mapped by drone: platforms, lines and surroundings in one orthomosaic, the base for an ESP or yard plan.
## Drone inspection compared with the usual methods
Task | Usual method | What a drone adds | Limit of the drone
Track geometry | Track recording car, ITMS [1] | Nothing; leave it to the recording car | Cannot measure geometry
OHE condition | Foot patrol, tower wagon | Close views and thermal of every mast [1] | Safe distance from 25 kV; permission
Bridges | Inspection from below, boats, BIU | 3D model, underside views [2] | Under-deck flying needs care; GNSS shadow
Cuttings and drains | Foot patrol before the monsoon | Whole section in a day, repeatable [3] | Dense vegetation hides the ground (use LiDAR)
Yards and stations | Total station survey | Full yard plan from one survey | Ground control needed for accuracy
Project progress | Site visits, photos | Monthly comparable record [4] | Not a measurement unless surveyed
## Planning drone work on a railway
The flight is the easy part. Railway work needs permission from the division or zone that owns the section, an airspace check on Digital Sky , and coordination with the traffic and electrical departments for a block or a safe flying window. Every output is then tied to kilometre posts and chainage, so the engineering teams can use it straight away.
1 Permission Zonal railway and Digital Sky airspace 2 Block or slot Agreed with traffic and electrical depts. 3 Fly Clear of OHE, with a railway escort 4 Process Tied to km posts and chainage 5 Deliver Defect list, plans, models, GIS layers Most of the time on a railway job goes into steps 1 and 2. The flying itself is usually the shortest part.
The five steps of a railway drone job.
## How DATA PKT works with railways
Our railway work includes corridor surveys, Engineering Scale Plans, yard plans and drainage plans. ## Frequently asked questions
Q: Does Indian Railways use drones for inspection?
Yes. Indian Railways uses drones for project monitoring, track and infrastructure inspection, bridge inspection and relief and rescue work, and has piloted drone-based thermal monitoring of overhead equipment (OHE) in the Raipur division.
Q: Can a drone inspect railway OHE?
Yes. A drone with a visual and a thermal camera can check the contact wire, droppers, insulators and fittings from close range and show hot joints. It must keep a safe distance from the 25 kV wires and fly under the railway's permission and safety arrangements.
Q: Can drones replace track recording cars?
No. Track recording systems such as ITMS measure track geometry and detect defects in rails, sleepers and fastenings from the track itself. A drone complements them with a view of everything around the track: OHE, drains, cuttings, embankments, bridges and encroachments.
Q: Is there an RDSO guideline for drone inspection of railway bridges?
Yes. RDSO Report BS-129 (R1), issued in May 2021, gives guidelines for 4D BrIM-based inspection of Indian Railway bridges using a 3D bridge information model and drones, and the Railway Board has asked zonal railways to integrate it with the Bridge Management System.
Q: How long does a drone take to cover a railway section?
It depends on the output. For project monitoring, a drone trial on the Dedicated Freight Corridor covered 98 km in three days. Detailed OHE or bridge inspection is slower because each mast or span is flown close up.
Q: What permissions are needed to fly a drone over a railway in India?
Permission from the zonal railway or division that owns the section, a check of the airspace on the Digital Sky platform with any permission it requires, and coordination with the traffic and electrical departments for a block or flying slot.

Service · Power
# Transmission line and substation survey and design
From choosing the route to drawing the switchyard: DATA PKT surveys alternate routes with drones, resolves land questions on khasra maps, spots towers, and designs substations.
In short: we deliver the survey and design inputs a new transmission line and substation need, for utilities, railways and EPC contractors: alternate routes and a feasibility report, a detailed route survey with tower spotting, substation site investigations, and substation drawings.
## Route selection
- Desk study on toposheets, satellite imagery, revenue and forest maps
- Three alternate routes flown with drone photogrammetry, so they are compared on current ground conditions
- Comparative feasibility report: length, angle points, crossings, forest, settlements and right-of-way sensitivity, with a techno-economic recommendation
## Drone maps on khasra maps
Revenue maps show plot boundaries and numbers but are often outdated. Our drone orthomosaic shows what is on the land today. Superimposed, they show which plots each route and tower would use and whether the land is residential, commercial, agricultural or forest. Land acquisition and right-of-way planning starts from facts, and the best route is easy to see.
Khasra maps in GIS, ready to be overlaid with current drone maps of the corridor.
## Detailed route survey
- DGPS and total station survey of the approved route, with levels and coordinates of every angle point
- Longitudinal profiles and tower spotting to IS 5613 and IS 802
- Tower schedules, crossing schedules and the route alignment plan
- Tree and crop enumeration; LiDAR where clearances under vegetation matter
- LILO and tap-off surveys on existing lines
Clearances on an overhead line. Sag, ground clearance and vegetation clearance are measured along the span. Right-of-way width and horizontal clearance are measured across it. A LiDAR or photogrammetric model measures all of them from one survey.
## Substation investigations
- Contour and topographic survey of the substation plot
- Geotechnical investigation: boreholes, SPT, laboratory tests, bearing capacity and foundation recommendations
- Soil resistivity by the Wenner method to IS 3043 for earthing design
- HFL data and the recommended finished ground level
## Substation design
- General arrangement drawing (GAD) of the switchyard: bus-bars, transformers, breakers, isolators, CTs, CVTs, lightning arresters, gantries, roads, drains and fire fighting
- GAD of the control and substation building
- Power-supply diagrams and single line diagrams (SLD)
- LT wiring plans, LT SLD and distribution board schedules
- Vetting by IIT, NIT or CPRI where the client requires it
## For railway traction
For 2x25 kV railway electrification we also survey and prepare location plans for traction substations (TSS), sectioning posts (SP) and sub-sectioning posts (SSP), and the power-supply diagram that links the grid to the traction network.
## Why drones are faster
A ground survey with DGPS and total station measures one point at a time, so a long corridor takes weeks. A DATA PKT drone team captures around 5 sq km of survey data in a day , which is then mapped and analysed in the office.
On a linear corridor such as a highway, one team captures about 35 km of drone imagery for photogrammetry, or about 50 km of aerial video, in a day , and DATA PKT has more than 20 drone pilots (a team of about 22) to put in the field. Ground instruments are still used, but only where they matter most: for the control points that fix the map to real coordinates, for checkpoints that prove the accuracy, and for detail the drone cannot see.
## Project example
In Uttar Pradesh we are delivering the survey and design for a 220/132 kV grid substation, its 220 kV and 132 kV lines with three alternate routes each, and location plans for 19 sites. Read the case study .
Once a line is built, we inspect it too: see drone surveys for the power sector and thermal inspection .
Inspecting an existing line? See drone transmission line inspection .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What does a transmission line route survey include?
Reconnaissance of alternate routes, a comparative feasibility report, then a detailed survey of the approved route with longitudinal profiles, tower spotting, tower and crossing schedules, and tree and crop enumeration.
Q: How does drone data help land acquisition for a transmission line?
Drone maps of the corridor are laid over khasra (revenue) maps. The khasra gives plot numbers; the drone map shows what is on each plot today, residential, commercial, agricultural or forest. That shows the land and right-of-way impact of each route before it is approved.
Q: Which substation drawings does DATA PKT prepare?
Switchyard general arrangement drawings (GAD), substation building GAD, power-supply and single line diagrams, LT wiring plans and distribution board schedules, with vetting by an IIT, NIT or CPRI where required.
Q: Which standards do you follow?
Tower spotting to IS 5613 and IS 802, earthing studies to IS 3043, geotechnical work to the relevant IS codes, and substation layouts to CEA, CBIP and, for railway traction, RDSO guidelines.
