Glossary
# Drone survey and geomatics glossary
Plain-English definitions of the terms that appear in drone survey scopes, tenders and reports, from GSD and ground control to LiDAR returns, solar thermography, power line design, railway ESPs and seismic refraction.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 25 November 2026
Short answer: a drone survey turns overlapping photos or laser scans into measured maps and 3D models. The terms below explain how those surveys are controlled (GCPs, RTK, datums), what they deliver (orthomosaic, DSM, DTM, point cloud), how accuracy is proved (checkpoints and RMSE), and the sector terms used for solar plants, power lines, railways, highways and slopes.
Terms are grouped by subject. Where a topic has its own guide on this site, a link follows the definition.
- Survey and control
- Photogrammetry
- LiDAR
- Accuracy
- Thermal and solar
- Power lines
- Railways
- Highways
- Geophysics and slopes
## Survey and control
GCP (ground control point)
A clearly marked target on the ground whose coordinates are measured with DGPS or a total station. During processing, GCPs tie the drone map to the project coordinate system and correct errors in the drone’s own position data. Ground control explained
Checkpoint
A surveyed point measured exactly like a GCP but left out of processing. Comparing its known coordinates with the finished map gives an independent measure of accuracy, usually reported as RMSE. Without checkpoints, a survey’s accuracy is unproven. How checkpoints prove accuracy
DGPS (differential GPS)
A method that improves satellite positioning by using a second receiver on a known point to correct errors. In surveying, the term usually means dual-frequency GNSS receivers used to fix control points and benchmarks to centimetre level. Drone survey vs DGPS and total station
RTK (real-time kinematic)
GNSS positioning corrected during the survey with live data from a base station or a correction network. On a drone, RTK gives each photo an accurate position, which reduces the number of ground control points needed. RTK and PPK explained
PPK (post-processed kinematic)
Applies the same base-station corrections as RTK, but after the flight rather than live. It is not affected by loss of the radio or network link in the air, so it suits long corridors and remote sites. RTK and PPK explained
CORS (continuously operating reference station)
A permanent GNSS receiver on a known point that records satellite data around the clock. Surveyors use CORS data or live corrections in place of, or alongside, their own base station. Survey of India runs a national CORS network.
Datum
The reference that coordinates and heights are measured from. A horizontal datum such as WGS 84 defines latitude and longitude; a vertical datum defines zero height, often mean sea level. Mixing datums is a common cause of misaligned survey data.
Geoid
The surface of equal gravity that best matches mean sea level, extended under the land. GNSS measures heights above a smooth mathematical ellipsoid, so a geoid model such as EGM2008 is used to convert them into heights above mean sea level.
Orthometric height
Height above the geoid, which in practice means height above mean sea level, and the height engineers design to. It equals the GNSS ellipsoidal height minus the geoid separation at that point, so the geoid model used should always be stated.
UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator)
A map projection that divides the world into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, with coordinates in metres as eastings and northings. India spans zones 42 to 47, so survey data should always state the zone used.
Chainage
Distance measured along the centre line of a road, railway, canal or pipeline from a fixed starting point, usually written as kilometres plus metres, for example 12+450. On linear projects, features, cross-sections and defects are located by chainage. Drone survey for highway DPRs
## Photogrammetry
GSD (ground sample distance)
The size of one image pixel on the ground. A 2 cm GSD means each pixel covers 2 cm by 2 cm. It depends on the camera sensor, the lens and the flying height, and it sets the finest detail a survey can map. GSD calculator
Overlap (forward and side)
The share of each photo that also appears in the next photo along the flight line (forward overlap) and in the neighbouring line (side overlap). Survey flights usually plan around 75–80% forward and 65–70% side overlap so that points match reliably. Drone photogrammetry
Aerial triangulation
The processing step that works out the exact position and orientation of every photo by matching common points across overlapping images and tying them to ground control. Its quality report is the first check that a photogrammetric survey has worked. Drone photogrammetry
Bundle adjustment
The least-squares calculation at the heart of aerial triangulation. It adjusts all camera positions, orientations and lens parameters together, so that the rays from matching points in different photos meet as closely as possible on the ground.
Orthomosaic
A single map image stitched from many aerial photos and corrected for terrain relief and camera tilt, so that it has a uniform scale and distances can be measured on it. It is the usual base map from a drone survey, delivered as GeoTIFF. Drone survey deliverables explained
DSM (digital surface model)
A height model of the top of everything the sensor sees: ground, buildings, trees, vehicles and structures. A DSM is used for obstacle, height and line-of-sight studies, but not for ground-level design. DSM or DTM?
DTM (digital terrain model)
A bare-earth height model with buildings and vegetation removed. Designers use it for levels, drainage, earthwork quantities and contours. Under dense vegetation a reliable DTM needs LiDAR or ground survey, because cameras only see the canopy. DSM or DTM?
DEM (digital elevation model)
A general term for any gridded height model. Some people use it for a bare-earth model and others for any surface, so a survey specification should say DTM or DSM, together with the grid size and the height datum.
Contour
A line joining points of equal height, drawn from the terrain model at a fixed interval such as 0.5 m or 1 m. Contours show the shape of the ground on CAD drawings and are a standard deliverable for design work. Drone survey deliverables explained
Point cloud
A set of millions of 3D points, each with X, Y and Z coordinates and often colour or intensity. It comes from LiDAR or from matching photos, and can be classified into ground, vegetation, buildings and wires . Drone survey deliverables explained
Mesh (3D model)
A 3D surface made by joining the points of a point cloud into triangles, usually draped with photo texture. A mesh gives a realistic model of structures, quarries and sites for viewing and measurement, but is not normally used as a design surface. Drone photogrammetry
## LiDAR
LiDAR (light detection and ranging)
A sensor that fires laser pulses and times their return to measure distance. Combined with GNSS and an IMU, a drone LiDAR builds a dense 3D point cloud, and some pulses reach the ground through gaps in vegetation. LiDAR survey
Pulse
A single short burst of laser light fired by a LiDAR sensor. The time it takes to travel to a surface and back gives the distance to that surface. Survey LiDAR sensors fire hundreds of thousands of pulses every second.
Returns (first, last and multiple)
The echoes recorded from one laser pulse. A pulse hitting a tree may give a first return from the canopy, intermediate returns from branches and a last return from the ground. Multiple returns are why LiDAR can map terrain under vegetation. LiDAR vs photogrammetry
Point density
The number of LiDAR points per square metre on the ground. It depends on the sensor, flying height, speed and overlap between flight lines. Higher density shows finer detail such as wires and kerbs, but produces larger files.
Classification
Sorting the points in a cloud into classes such as ground, low, medium and high vegetation, buildings, water and wires. The LAS specification sets standard class codes, for example class 2 for ground. Ground points are used to build the DTM. LiDAR survey
LAS and LAZ files
LAS is the standard open file format for point clouds, maintained by ASPRS. Each point stores its coordinates, intensity, return number and class. LAZ is a losslessly compressed version of LAS, much smaller, that opens in most GIS and CAD software. Deliverables and file formats
Boresight calibration
Measuring the small angular misalignment between a LiDAR sensor or camera and the IMU it is mounted with. Left uncorrected, even a fraction of a degree shifts points sideways, so it is checked with calibration flights over known features. LiDAR survey
Strip adjustment
A correction that aligns overlapping LiDAR flight strips with each other, so that the same surface, such as a roof or a road, matches in every strip. It removes small systematic errors left after trajectory processing and boresight calibration. LiDAR survey
IMU (inertial measurement unit)
A unit of accelerometers and gyroscopes that measures a sensor’s roll, pitch and heading many times a second. Combined with GNSS, it gives the trajectory that a LiDAR system needs to place each laser point correctly.
## Accuracy
RMSE (root mean square error)
The square root of the average of the squared differences between map coordinates and surveyed checkpoint coordinates. It is reported separately for X, Y and Z and is the usual single figure for a survey’s accuracy. How drone survey accuracy is reported RMSE calculator
ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards
The ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data, published by the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, set out how to test and report the horizontal and vertical accuracy of maps, elevation models and point clouds using independent checkpoints.
Relative and absolute accuracy
Absolute accuracy is how closely map positions match true positions in the project coordinate system. Relative accuracy is how correctly distances and height differences within the map are shown. A survey without ground control can be relatively accurate but absolutely wrong. How accurate is a drone survey?
## Thermal and solar
Radiometric thermal camera
A thermal camera that stores a calibrated temperature value for every pixel, not just a coloured picture. Temperatures can be measured and corrected afterwards for emissivity and conditions, which solar thermography reports under IEC TS 62446-3 rely on. Thermal survey
Emissivity
How efficiently a surface gives off infrared energy compared with a perfect emitter, on a scale from 0 to 1. The glass on solar modules has a high emissivity, while bare metal has a low one and can mislead a thermal camera with reflections.
Irradiance
The solar power reaching a surface, measured in watts per square metre. IEC TS 62446-3 sets a minimum of 600 W/m² in the plane of the modules for thermography, because faults only show clearly when the modules carry enough current. Solar thermography reports
IEC TS 62446-3
The International Electrotechnical Commission technical specification for outdoor infrared thermography of photovoltaic modules and plants. It covers the equipment, flight and weather conditions, personnel qualification, and how faults are classified and reported. What the report should include
Hotspot
An area of a solar module or electrical joint noticeably warmer than its surroundings in a thermal image. On modules, causes include cracked or shaded cells, soiling, faulty bypass diodes and poor connections. Severity is graded by the temperature difference. Drone vs manual solar inspection
Delta T (temperature difference)
The temperature difference between a suspected fault and a healthy reference area under the same conditions. Thermography reports use delta T, rather than absolute temperature, to grade the severity of hotspots on solar modules and electrical joints.
Bypass diode
A diode in a solar module’s junction box that lets current flow around a group of cells, called a substring, when they are shaded or faulty. An active or failed bypass diode shows as a warm substring stripe in thermal images. Solar thermography reports
PID (potential induced degradation)
Power loss caused by a high voltage difference between a module’s cells and its earthed frame, which drives leakage current. In thermal images it typically shows as a patchwork of warmer modules, often towards the negative end of a string.
ISO 9712
The international standard for qualifying and certifying personnel in non-destructive testing, including infrared thermography. Levels 1, 2 and 3 set what a person may do; a Level 2 thermographer can set up inspections and interpret and report results. Thermal survey
## Power lines
Sag
The vertical distance between a conductor and the straight line joining its two support points. Sag increases with conductor temperature and load, so line design checks it at the maximum design temperature to make sure ground clearance is kept. Transmission line design
Ground clearance
The minimum vertical distance allowed between a live conductor and the ground, roads, railways, buildings or other lines below it. In India, minimum clearances by voltage are set by the Central Electricity Authority safety regulations. Transmission line drone inspection
ROW (right of way)
The strip of land along a transmission line, road or railway that is kept clear and over which the owner has rights to build and maintain the asset. Its width depends on the voltage or road class, and encroachments are checked by survey.
Tower spotting
Placing transmission towers on a surveyed route profile to choose their positions, types and heights, so that clearances are met at the lowest overall cost. It uses the ground profile from the route survey with sag templates or line-design software. Transmission line route survey and design
PLS-CADD
Power Line Systems – Computer Aided Design and Drafting, a widely used software package for overhead line design. It models the terrain, towers and conductors in 3D for sag-tension calculations, clearance checks and tower spotting, often from LiDAR survey data.
Corona and UV inspection
Corona is a small electrical discharge at the surface of a high-voltage conductor or fitting where the electric field is strong, often at damaged or dirty parts. It gives off ultraviolet light that a UV camera can detect, revealing faults on lines and insulators.
## Railways
ESP (Engineering Scale Plan)
A railway drawing of a station yard or section made to scale, showing tracks, points and crossings, platforms, structures and chainages in their true positions. Railways use the approved ESP as the base for yard remodelling, new lines and signalling plans. What is an Engineering Scale Plan?
Yard plan
A drawing of a railway yard showing its lines, sidings, points, platforms, buildings and drainage. It may be a simplified layout or a detailed survey drawing, and it is used to plan remodelling, maintenance and drainage works. Railway yard and drainage plans
OHE (overhead equipment)
The system of contact wire, catenary, masts, cantilevers and fittings that carries 25 kV AC traction power to electric trains on Indian Railways main lines. Drone surveys record OHE masts, and thermal checks look for hotspots at joints and clamps. Railway drone inspection
## Highways
DPR (Detailed Project Report)
The report that sets out a project’s design, quantities, cost estimate and approvals before it is sanctioned and tendered. For roads, survey and investigation for DPRs follows IRC:SP:19, and a drone survey supplies much of the topography. Drone survey for highway DPRs
Strip plan
A drawing of the strip of land along a road or railway alignment, showing the existing carriageway, land boundaries, structures, utilities and trees within the corridor. Highway DPRs use it to plan widening and land acquisition. Drone survey for highway DPRs
NHAI Data Lake
NHAI’s online platform for storing and managing project documents and records. Monthly drone videos of highway projects are uploaded to it, so that the authority and supervision consultants can review progress and keep a dated record. NHAI highway drone videography
## Geophysics and slopes
Seismic refraction
A geophysical method that sends sound waves into the ground from a hammer blow or small source and times their arrival at a line of geophones. Waves bend at boundaries between layers, revealing soil and rock depths along the profile. Seismic refraction survey
P-wave velocity
The speed of compressional seismic waves through soil or rock, in metres per second. Loose soil gives low values and fresh rock high ones, so velocity layers from seismic refraction help judge depth to bedrock and how hard the ground is to excavate. Seismic refraction survey
Factor of safety
In slope stability, the ratio of the forces resisting sliding to the forces driving it. A value of 1.0 means the slope is on the point of failure, so design guidance sets higher minimum values depending on the conditions and consequences. Landslide survey in India
Writing a survey scope or tender? Tell us the site and the outputs you need.

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is the difference between DTM and DSM?
A DSM (digital surface model) records the height of the top of everything the sensor sees, including buildings and trees. A DTM (digital terrain model) removes them to show the bare ground. Designers and quantity surveyors almost always need the DTM; the DSM suits obstacle and height studies.
Q: What does GSD mean in a drone survey?
GSD stands for ground sample distance: the size of one image pixel on the ground. A 2 cm GSD means each pixel covers 2 cm by 2 cm. It depends on the camera sensor, lens and flying height, and sets the finest detail the survey can map.
Q: What is ESP in railways?
ESP stands for Engineering Scale Plan. It is a railway drawing of a station yard or section made to scale, showing tracks, points and crossings, platforms, structures and chainages in their true positions, and it is the base for yard remodelling, new lines and signalling plans.
Q: What is a GCP in a drone survey?
A GCP, or ground control point, is a marked target on the ground whose coordinates are measured with DGPS. GCPs tie the drone map to the project coordinate system. Checkpoints are measured the same way but left out of processing, to prove the final accuracy.
Q: What is RMSE in survey accuracy?
RMSE, or root mean square error, is the square root of the average of the squared differences between map coordinates and surveyed checkpoint coordinates. It is reported separately for X, Y and Z, and in general practice can be stated against a standard such as the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards.

Regulation
# Drone survey permissions in India: Digital Sky, airspace zones and what a client should check
Before a drone survey can start, the drone, the pilot and the airspace over your site all have to be in order. This guide explains the Drone Rules, the airspace map on Digital Sky, and the questions a client should ask a survey vendor.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 25 November 2026
Short answer: a commercial drone survey in India needs a drone registered with a Unique Identification Number (UIN), a pilot holding a Remote Pilot Certificate (RPC), third-party insurance, and a check of the site on the Digital Sky airspace map. In a green zone no flight permission is needed up to 400 ft. Yellow zones need air traffic control permission and red zones need Central Government permission. [1] [2]
Rules change. Check before every flight. Zone boundaries are updated and temporary red zones can be declared at short notice. The Ministry of Civil Aviation says anyone planning to fly should check the latest airspace map for changes before operating. [2] This guide is general information as of November 2026, not legal advice.
25 August 2021
Drone Rules, 2021 notified, G.S.R. 589(E) [1] [5]
400 ft
green-zone ceiling for flights without permission [2]
5, 8, 12 km
airport perimeter bands that set yellow and green limits [2]
15 February 2021
geospatial guidelines: no prior approval for Indian entities [10]
## 1. Which rules apply in 2026
Civil drone operations in India are governed by the Drone Rules, 2021 , notified by the Ministry of Civil Aviation on 25 August 2021. They replaced the earlier UAS Rules with a much shorter set of approvals, made most permissions self-generated on the Digital Sky platform, and cover drones up to 500 kg. [1] The rules have been amended since:
- Drone (Amendment) Rules, 2022 (G.S.R. 108(E), 11 February 2022) replaced the remote pilot licence with a Remote Pilot Certificate issued by an authorised remote pilot training organisation. [4]
- Drone (Amendment) Rules, 2023 (G.S.R. 715(E), 27 September 2023) let applicants for a Remote Pilot Certificate use any government-issued identity and address proof instead of a passport. [5]
- A further amendment dated 21 August 2024 is listed by the Ministry in Parliament; [6] it extended the same identity relaxation to drone registration and transfer forms. [15]
Two newer changes matter in practice. First, regulatory services such as drone registration, pilot certification and type certification have moved from Digital Sky to DGCA's eGCA portal, while operational services such as the airspace map and flight permissions remain on Digital Sky. [7] Second, in September 2025 the Ministry published a draft Civil Drone (Promotion and Regulation) Bill, 2025 for consultation, which would replace the Drone Rules with a law. [13] Until a new law is passed and notified, the Drone Rules, 2021 as amended apply. Check the current position before you sign a contract.
## 2. The drone: registration, UIN and type certificate
No one may operate a drone without first registering it and getting a Unique Identification Number (UIN) . [3] The UIN is marked on the drone and links it to its owner, so a client can ask for it and check it against the aircraft on site. Drones are grouped by maximum all-up weight including payload: [3]
Category | All-up weight | Typical survey use
Nano | Up to 250 g | Not used for survey work
Micro | More than 250 g, up to 2 kg | Small mapping drones and inspection quadcopters
Small | More than 2 kg, up to 25 kg | Most RTK mapping drones, LiDAR and fixed-wing survey drones
Medium | More than 25 kg, up to 150 kg | Specialist heavy payloads
Large | More than 150 kg | Not used for survey work
A type certificate is needed for a drone model to be operated in India; nano drones are exempt. [1] Type certificates are issued under the Certification Scheme for Unmanned Aircraft Systems, notified on 26 January 2022 and developed by the Quality Council of India, with testing by approved certification bodies. [8] For a client, the practical point is simple: the survey drone should be a certified model with a valid UIN, not an unregistered import.
## 3. The pilot: Remote Pilot Certificate
The person flying must hold a Remote Pilot Certificate (RPC) . Since 2022 it is issued by a DGCA-authorised remote pilot training organisation (RPTO) after training and a test, and it is generated through the online platform. [4] Only nano drones and micro drones flown for non-commercial use are exempt, [3] so a commercial survey always needs a certified pilot. Applicants must be between 18 and 65 years old and have passed class 10. [9] The certificate states the category and class of drone it covers, so check that it matches the drone being flown on your site.
## 4. The airspace map: green, yellow and red zones
The Ministry of Civil Aviation published India's airspace map for drones on 24 September 2021. It is free to view on Digital Sky without a login, and it divides the country into three zones. [2]
Zone | Where it applies | What is needed
Green zone | Up to 400 ft (about 120 m) above ground where the area is not yellow or red; up to 200 ft (about 60 m) in the band 8 to 12 km from an operational airport perimeter | No flight permission needed. Registration, pilot certificate and the airspace check still apply
Yellow zone | Above 400 ft in a green zone; above 200 ft in the 8 to 12 km band; all heights in the band 5 to 8 km from an operational airport perimeter | Permission from the air traffic control authority for that airspace: AAI, IAF, Navy or HAL
Red zone | No-drone zones marked on the map. Close to operational airports, inside the 5 km band, the map typically shows red | Permission from the Central Government
The yellow zone around airports was cut from 45 km to 12 km from the airport perimeter when the 2021 rules came in. [1] [2] In plain terms, around an operational airport:
- 12 km and beyond: normal green-zone rules, up to 400 ft, unless the map shows otherwise.
- 8 to 12 km: green up to 200 ft, yellow above 200 ft. Many mapping flights can be planned below 200 ft, but the GSD and overlap must still meet the specification.
- 5 to 8 km: yellow at every height, so every flight needs ATC permission.
- Inside 5 km: check the map. This area is typically shown as red.
These distances are measured from the airport perimeter , not the terminal, and military airfields count too. The map, not a rule of thumb, decides. Long corridors such as highways and railway lines often cross several zones, so each stretch has to be checked separately.
## 5. Getting permission in yellow and red zones
For a yellow zone , permission comes from the air traffic control authority for that airspace: the Airports Authority of India, the Indian Air Force, the Navy or HAL, depending on the airport. [2] For a red zone , the Central Government must give permission. [2] Requests are made online through Digital Sky, with the flight area, height, timing and drone details.
Two things often surprise clients. First, approval is not instant: a request for a yellow or red zone needs lead time, so fix the survey dates only after the zone check. Second, state governments, union territory administrations and police can declare temporary red zones for events, VIP visits or security reasons. These can appear on the map at short notice and override an approval planned earlier. [16] This is why the airspace check is repeated on the day of the flight.
## 6. Critical infrastructure, borders and site access
Airspace permission is only one layer. Sites near defence installations, international borders, nuclear and strategic facilities, ports and some government complexes are likely to sit in yellow or red zones, and may need further security clearances from the agency concerned. Even in a green zone, the asset owner usually has its own rules:
- Railways, metros and highway authorities may require a block, a work permit or an escort for flights over live lines and carriageways.
- Power utilities set safe distances from energised conductors and may need the line owner's consent.
- Refineries, plants and private campuses control entry and may restrict cameras.
Put these site permissions in the scope and the schedule. A clear airspace map does not mean the flight can go ahead on the day.
## 7. Insurance
Under the Drone Rules, third-party insurance of drones other than nano drones is governed by the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, under which third-party cover is compulsory. [14] Ask the vendor for the policy, its validity and whether it covers the drone and the location being flown. Some contracts also ask for cover for the client's assets.
## 8. Geospatial data: who may collect it, and where it is stored
The Department of Science and Technology's guidelines of 15 February 2021 removed the need for prior approval, security clearance or a licence to acquire and produce geospatial data inside India, subject to a negative list of sensitive attributes. [10] [11] The key points for a drone survey are:
- Indian entities may collect and produce geospatial data at any accuracy, with self-certification used to show compliance. [10]
- The threshold is one metre horizontal and three metres vertical. Data finer than this may be created and owned only by Indian entities, and must be stored and processed on servers in India. [10]
- Foreign companies, and foreign-owned or controlled Indian companies, may license finer data from Indian entities only to serve customers in India. [10]
Survey-grade drone data is far finer than the threshold, so it should be held and processed in India. The National Geospatial Policy, 2022 builds on the same approach. [12] Data rules are separate from airspace rules: being free to map does not mean being free to fly.
## 9. What a client should ask a survey vendor
- The UIN of each drone that will fly, and its type certificate or certified model.
- The Remote Pilot Certificate of each pilot, valid for that drone category.
- A zone check for your site from the Digital Sky map, stretch by stretch for corridors, with the permission plan for any yellow or red section.
- Who applies, and the lead time before dates are fixed.
- Third-party insurance in force for the survey period.
- Site permissions : whose consent, blocks or escorts are needed, and who arranges them.
- Data handling : is the company an Indian entity, where are raw and processed data stored and processed, who owns them, and how are sensitive features treated?
- A plan for no-fly days : what happens to the schedule if a temporary red zone or bad weather stops the flight?
These sit alongside the technical checks in our guide on how to choose a drone survey company . Permission lead times and site access are also part of what decides the cost of a drone survey . Terms such as UIN, RPC and GSD are explained in our drone survey glossary .
## How DATA PKT handles permissions
Flights are planned on the Digital Sky platform under the Drone Rules, 2021, and flown by DGCA Remote Pilot Certificate holders on drones with a Unique Identification Number. Each site, and each stretch of a corridor, is checked on the airspace map and any permission is planned before dates are agreed. Our network of 20+ pilots works with an in-house GIS team, and every survey is tied to DGPS ground control. See how this works on highway projects and in our highway drone monitoring case study . Pilots who want to fly survey projects can join our drone pilot network .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: Do I need permission for a drone survey in India?
It depends on where the site is. In a green zone on the Digital Sky airspace map, a registered drone flown by a certified pilot needs no flight permission up to 400 ft (about 120 m) above ground. In a yellow zone, permission is needed from the air traffic control authority for that airspace, and in a red zone from the Central Government. The drone must still carry a UIN and the pilot a Remote Pilot Certificate.
Q: What are the green, yellow and red zones for drones?
They are the zones of the airspace map published on Digital Sky in September 2021. Green zones allow flights up to 400 ft without permission, and up to 200 ft in the band 8 to 12 km from an operational airport perimeter. Yellow zones, including all airspace 5 to 8 km from an airport perimeter, need air traffic control permission. Red zones are no-drone zones that need Central Government permission.
Q: Who gives permission to fly a drone in a yellow zone?
The air traffic control authority that controls that airspace, such as the Airports Authority of India, the Indian Air Force, the Navy or HAL, depending on the airport. The request is made online through the Digital Sky platform, so plan for it before fixing survey dates.
Q: Does a survey drone pilot need a licence in India?
The pilot needs a Remote Pilot Certificate. Since the Drone (Amendment) Rules, 2022 it is issued by a DGCA-authorised remote pilot training organisation through the online platform, and it replaced the earlier remote pilot licence. Only nano drones and micro drones flown for non-commercial use are exempt, so a commercial survey needs a certified pilot.
Q: Do Indian companies need permission to collect drone mapping data?
Under the Department of Science and Technology guidelines of 15 February 2021, Indian entities need no prior approval, security clearance or licence to acquire and produce geospatial data inside India, subject to a negative list of sensitive attributes. Data finer than the threshold accuracy must be stored and processed in India. Airspace permission is a separate requirement.

=== https://datapkt.com/insights/solar-plant-topographic-survey.html ===
Home / Insights / Solar plant topographic survey
Solar site survey
# Drone topographic survey for solar power plants: what developers need before design
The layout, the earthwork quantities, the drainage design and the access roads of a solar plant are all drawn on a terrain model. Here is what that survey should capture, how accurate it needs to be, and what to ask for before the design team starts.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 25 November 2026
Short answer: before a solar plant is designed, the site needs a bare-earth DTM with contours, an orthomosaic, the surveyed boundary, every obstruction that could cast a shadow, and the existing drainage lines inside and around the site. A drone survey on DGPS ground control can supply all of these over a large site in one campaign, provided the accuracy is proved with checkpoints and the data is delivered in the designers' coordinate system and height datum.
## Why a solar plant needs a topographic survey
A solar site can look flat on a satellite basemap and still have enough fall, ridges and gullies to change the design. Public elevation data and web maps give a first impression of a site, but they are too coarse to grade a plant or size a drain [7] . The World Bank Group's developer guide lists a detailed site plan, "including site surveys, topographic contours", among the outputs of the feasibility stage [1] . The survey feeds five design decisions.
- Table and tracker layout. Fixed-tilt tables and single-axis trackers each have a limit on the slope and the ground undulation they can follow. The DTM shows which blocks fit as they are, which need longer posts or terrain-following structures, and which need grading. The same guide notes that topography together with the geotechnical survey shapes the choice of foundation [1] .
- Grading and earthwork. Cut and fill volumes come straight from the surface model. Uneven ground can need grading that adds cost and time [7] , and a coarse survey can leave a surprise in the earthwork bill. The 2,000 MW Pavagada solar park DPR in Karnataka, for example, proposed levelling only where undulation was high and otherwise following "the contour of the land" [2] , a decision that can only be made from a contour plan.
- Drainage design. Runoff paths, catchment areas and the positions of culverts and drains are read from the DTM. The Pavagada DPR states plainly that "a detailed terrain map is required towards designing of the drainage system" [2] .
- Roads and cable routes. Internal roads, inverter and transformer pads, cable trenches and the route to the pooling substation should run on stable ground, clear of natural drainage lines. An engineer writing in PV Tech describes a site where the access route was set "without regard to existing site drainage and soil conditions", and the problems that followed [3] .
- Shading. Ridges, trees, buildings, transmission towers and poles cast shadows that cost energy every day of the plant's life. The developer guide calls avoiding shading critical, because even small areas of shade can significantly impair output [1] , and separates far shading from the horizon from near shading by poles, control rooms and switchyard equipment [1] . The survey should record the position and height of each object, not just its outline.
## What the survey should capture
Agree the list before the flight. Adding items later usually means a second site visit.
Item | What it is for | Notes
Bare-earth DTM | Grading, layout fit, earthwork volumes, drainage | Ground only: vegetation, structures and stockpiles removed. The DSM (top surface) is kept separately for shading.
Contours | Layout drawings, grading plans, drainage | Interval set by terrain and design stage. Flat sites usually need a closer interval than rolling ground; agree it in the scope.
Spot levels and grid levels | Checking flat ground where contours are sparse | Useful on very flat land, where contours alone say little about direction of fall.
Orthomosaic | Base map for layout and land records | True-colour, georeferenced, at a stated GSD.
Boundary and land features | Fixing the usable area | Surveyed boundary pillars, fences, roads, tracks and rights of way, overlaid on revenue (khasra) maps where needed.
Obstructions | Shading study and setbacks | Trees, buildings, poles, overhead lines and towers, with heights.
Existing drainage | Drainage design and flood risk | Nallahs, gullies, ponds, culverts and bunds, inside and upstream of the boundary.
Soil and geotechnical pointers | Planning the ground investigation | Rock outcrops, erosion, waterlogged or saline patches, visible fill. These guide where boreholes and pile tests go; they do not replace them.
On the last item: a drone sees the surface, not the subsoil. The developer guide recommends a geotechnical survey before final site selection [1] , and a mixture of soil and rock below ground often does not show up on any map [7] . The topographic survey makes the ground investigation better targeted; it is not a substitute for one.
## Accuracy and ground control
Vertical accuracy matters more than horizontal on a solar site, because grading, drainage falls and post lengths all depend on levels. Three things decide it.
- Ground control. Ground control points measured with DGPS tie the model to the project coordinates. On a large block, spread them around the edge and through the middle; on a long access road or transmission route, place them along the full length. RTK or PPK positioning on the drone reduces the number of control points needed but does not remove the need for checkpoints.
- Checkpoints. Independent points left out of processing, compared with the finished model and reported as RMSE in X, Y and Z. This is the only proof of the accuracy that was achieved. Positional accuracy can be stated against a published standard such as the ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards [8] .
- Datum. The survey, the design and the construction stake-out must use the same coordinate system and the same height datum. A mismatch here shifts every level on the drawings.
Our guide to drone survey accuracy, GSD, GCPs and RTK covers these in detail, and the drone survey glossary explains terms such as DTM , GCP and RMSE .
How a drone photogrammetry survey becomes design data. The DTM used for grading and drainage, and the contours drawn from it, sit near the end of the chain, so any weakness in ground control carries through to them. The checkpoint QA step tests the whole chain against points the adjustment never saw.
## Drone photogrammetry or LiDAR for a solar site?
Many solar sites in India are open land: barren ground, fallow farmland or sparse scrub. On ground like this, drone photogrammetry on DGPS control gives a DTM, contours and a true-colour orthomosaic in one flight, and is usually the economical choice.
Two conditions change that.
- Vegetation. Photogrammetry maps the top of whatever it sees. Where dense scrub or tree cover hides the ground, a photo-derived surface sits on the canopy and the DTM is wrong by the height of the bushes. LiDAR can record ground returns through gaps in the vegetation and is the better tool there; the other options are clearing before the survey or ground survey of the covered patches.
- Very uniform terrain. Bare sand, salt flats and freshly graded earth give photogrammetry few features to match. Lower flights, more overlap and more ground control help. LiDAR does not rely on image texture, so it is less affected.
On a mixed site, one option is photogrammetry for the open blocks and LiDAR for the covered strips and drainage lines. Our comparison of LiDAR vs photogrammetry sets out the trade-offs with published accuracy figures.
## Hydrology and drainage basics for solar plants
Improperly planned drainage and erosion control at large solar plants is an area under close scrutiny. It leads to drainage and erosion problems after construction and to reduced profits over the life of a facility [3] . The same author advises a detailed hydrology assessment for large sites of 50 MW and above, and warns not to assume that large, sudden storms can pass over a plant without damage from water depth and velocity [3] . Flooding can damage electrical equipment mounted near ground level and increase the risk of erosion around foundations [1] .
The DTM is the starting point for that assessment. In GIS, the steps are standard:
- Fill sinks. Small false depressions in the model trap simulated flow and are filled first to give a conditioned DTM [5] .
- Flow direction. Water leaves each cell in the steepest downslope direction [5] , so the model gives the direction of flow everywhere on the site.
- Flow accumulation and flow paths. Counting how many upstream cells drain into each cell shows where flow concentrates; cells with enough accumulated flow form the drainage network [5] .
- Catchments. From chosen outlet points, such as a proposed culvert or the site boundary, the catchment draining to each point is delineated [5] .
Catchment area, flow length and fall then go into the design discharge. For small catchments, Indian road practice uses a form of the rational formula, in which peak runoff depends on the catchment area, a runoff coefficient and the critical rainfall intensity, set by the time of concentration [4] . IRC:SP:13 asks for catchment area, length and fall from survey maps, and recommends a traverse along the watershed for catchments smaller than 1.25 sq km [4] . It also cautions that empirical formulae should be used with due caution and in consultation with an expert [4] . Other manuals limit the rational method to small basins; the Iowa DOT design manual, for one, restricts it to drainage basins of 160 acres or less [6] . The hydrologist chooses the method; the survey has to supply the inputs.
Two points follow for the survey scope.
- Survey beyond the boundary. Water that reaches the plant often comes from land upstream of the fence. If the survey stops at the boundary, the external catchment has to be estimated from coarser data. Agree a buffer, or a separate lower-resolution flight of the upstream area.
- Keep the natural drainage where possible. The Pavagada DPR noted that "essentially the natural slope and drain is maintained for drainage in the solar field", with drains run parallel to the roads [2] . Mapping the existing nallahs and their sections accurately is what makes that approach possible.
## Deliverables checklist
Ask for these in the scope, with formats the design team can open directly:
- Orthomosaic as GeoTIFF, with the GSD stated.
- DTM and DSM as GeoTIFF rasters, with cell size stated.
- Point cloud as LAS or LAZ, classified at least into ground and non-ground.
- Contours, spot levels, boundary, obstructions and existing drainage as DWG for CAD and SHP for GIS, on agreed layers.
- Drainage layers: flow paths, catchment boundaries and outlet points as SHP, if the hydrology work is in scope.
- Ground control and checkpoint list with coordinates, descriptions and photographs of each point.
- Accuracy report with RMSE in X, Y and Z from independent checkpoints.
- Survey report stating the coordinate system, height datum, equipment, flight dates and any areas of reduced confidence, such as vegetated patches.
Our guide to drone survey deliverables explains what each output is for, and our GIS mapping and data processing page covers layer preparation and GIS to CAD work.
## Common mistakes
- Designing on satellite or public elevation data. Fine for screening sites, too coarse for grading or drainage.
- Treating the DSM as the ground. On a site with scrub, a surface model from photos is a canopy model. Ask how the DTM was filtered and where confidence is low.
- No checkpoints. Ground control without independent checkpoints gives a model whose accuracy has not been proved.
- Mismatched height datum. Survey levels on one datum and design levels on another shift every grading and drainage level.
- Stopping at the fence. Upstream catchments decide how much water arrives at the plant.
- Missing obstruction heights. A tree or pole mapped only as a point cannot be used in a shading study.
- Survey too early or too late. If the site is cleared or partly graded after the survey, the model no longer matches the ground. Plan a check flight before design freeze.
## What decides the cost
For a solar site, the main cost factors are the area and whether it is one block or several, the accuracy and GSD required, the amount of ground control, vegetation cover (which decides whether LiDAR is needed), the deliverables and the location. Our page on what decides drone survey cost explains each one.

We fly drone photogrammetry and LiDAR on DGPS ground control and process the data with our in-house GIS team into the DTM, contours, CAD and GIS layers listed above. Once the plant is built and running, the next survey it needs is usually an O&M one: see our solar plant drone thermography service, where our thermal team includes a thermographer certified to ISO 9712 Level 2. ## Frequently asked questions
Q: Why does a solar plant need a topographic survey?
The layout of tables or trackers, the grading and earthwork quantities, the drainage design, the internal roads and cable routes, and the shading study are all drawn on the terrain model. Public elevation data and satellite maps are too coarse for these, so a site-specific survey with a bare-earth DTM and contours is needed before design.
Q: What should a solar site survey include?
A bare-earth DTM, contours at an agreed interval, spot levels on very flat ground, a georeferenced orthomosaic, the surveyed boundary, obstructions with their heights, and existing drainage lines inside and upstream of the site. It should also record surface signs such as rock outcrops, erosion and waterlogging to guide the geotechnical investigation.
Q: Is a drone survey accurate enough for solar plant design?
Yes, when it is flown on DGPS ground control, at a GSD suited to the accuracy target, and proved with independent checkpoints reported as RMSE in X, Y and Z. The survey must also use the same coordinate system and height datum as the design team.
Q: Should I use LiDAR or photogrammetry for a solar site?
On open, sparsely vegetated land, drone photogrammetry usually gives the DTM, contours and orthomosaic economically. Where dense scrub or trees hide the ground, LiDAR is the better tool because it can record ground returns through gaps in the vegetation. Mixed sites can combine the two.
Q: How is a drainage study for a solar plant done from the survey?
The DTM is conditioned by filling false sinks, then flow direction, flow accumulation and catchment boundaries are computed in GIS. Catchment area, flow length and fall then feed a design discharge method, such as the rational formula in IRC:SP:13 for small catchments, chosen by the hydrologist. The survey should extend beyond the boundary to cover upstream catchments.
Once a plant is running, the next survey is usually thermal. See our solar thermography data QC case study .

Home / Insights / Railway final location survey
Railway surveys
# Railway final location survey (FLS) by drone and LiDAR: what it covers
The final location survey fixes a new railway line on the ground and produces the plans, sections and estimates the project is sanctioned on. Here is what it must deliver under the Indian Railways Engineering Code, and where drone photogrammetry and LiDAR with DGPS control fit.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 25 November 2026 · 10 min read
Short answer: a final location survey (FLS) is the last and most detailed survey before a railway project is sanctioned. It fixes the centre line, curves and gradients, and produces detailed plans, longitudinal and cross-sections, bridge and yard plans and the data for the detailed estimate [1] [2] . A drone or aerial LiDAR survey, tied to DGPS control and bench marks, supplies most of the topography; centre-line pegging, pillars, soil investigation and river studies remain ground work.
## Where the FLS sits in railway project planning
The Indian Railways Code for the Engineering Department links each survey stage to a report. A reconnaissance survey supports a feasibility study, a Preliminary Engineering-cum-Traffic Survey (PETS) leads to a Techno-Economic Survey Report, and a final location survey leads to the Project Report, which carries the detailed estimate and the abstract cost of the project [2] .
Stage | Purpose | Typical survey work | Report
Reconnaissance | Is the project worth investigating further? | Maps, imagery, site visits, waterway at major crossings [1] | Feasibility report [2]
PETS / traffic study | Compare routes, test viability, estimate cost closely | Route traverses; photogrammetry where suitable photographs exist [1] ; traffic study | Techno-Economic Survey Report [2]
Final location survey | Fix the alignment and prepare plans for construction and sanction | Centre line, levels, cross-sections, bridges, yards, land, soil | Project Report with detailed estimate [2]
Detailed estimate and DPR | Sanction of the project and award of works | Quantities and costs worked out from the FLS drawings | DPR in the Railway Board format [3]
The order matters. In 2025 the Railway Board told zonal railways to get the traffic study done before going ahead with a final location survey, so that money is not spent surveying a line that is not viable [5] . Its revised FLS rates now include the traffic study within the FLS cost [4] . Under the Railway Board's arrangements for empanelled consultants, the consultant first does the traffic study to test viability, then goes on to the FLS and the DPR [3] .
FLS and DPR work covers new lines, doubling and multi-tracking, gauge conversion and yard remodelling [3] . Yard remodelling overlaps with the Engineering Scale Plan (ESP) , which shows an existing yard to scale before changes are designed.
## What the Engineering Code asks an FLS to deliver
Chapter IV of the Engineering Code sets out the final location survey in detail. The survey should be comprehensive enough to give the information needed for the detailed plans and sections and for an accurate estimate of cost, and it should secure the most economical alignment [1] . The main requirements are below.
### Alignment, curves and gradients
- Centre line: measured in chains of 20 metres, with pegs at every chain and larger pegs at every 100 metres [1] .
- Permanent marks: masonry pillars at tangent points and at intervals along the line, so the alignment can be set out again at construction [1] .
- Curves: defined by degree and radius, with transition curves where the curvature changes; gradients are expressed per 100 metres and compensated for curvature [1] .
- Levels: bench marks at intervals of not more than one kilometre and at the sites of important bridges, referred to mean sea level [1] .
### Plans and sections
The Code lists the set of plans and sections a project should have: a general map, an index map, an index plan and section, detailed plans and sections, plans and cross-sections, station yard plans, drawings of structures and plans of junction arrangements [1] . Some of the scales it gives:
Drawing | Scale in the Code | What it shows
Index plan and section | 0.5 km to 1 cm horizontal, 10 m to 1 cm vertical | The whole line, with important bridges, rivers and spans
Detailed plans and sections (L-section) | 50 m to 1 cm horizontal, 5 m to 1 cm vertical | All features within 100 m each side of the centre line, including village boundaries; ground and formation levels
River plans and cross-sections | Plan at 50 m to 1 cm; sections at 5 m to 1 cm | Rivers needing a waterway of 110 sq. metres or more
Station yard and junction plans | 10 m to 1 cm | Stations needing special design and junction layouts
All scales above are from Chapter IV of the Engineering Code [1] . The longitudinal section carries two sets of levels, the ground and the formation, and cross-sections are referenced on it [1] . Larger scales may be used in difficult country.
### Bridges, culverts, soil and land
Every waterway crossing needs a site study: catchment, flood levels, scour and the size of opening. Large bridges need skeleton drawings for the estimate, and the Code asks for bunds and irrigation works on the route to be investigated, along with any diversion they need [1] . In hilly country a geological investigation is needed, and soil samples are taken systematically along the route and at borrow areas [1] . Land plans, drawn over village and revenue maps, show the land to be acquired and the boundaries it crosses; the detailed plan already shows village land boundaries within 100 metres of the centre line [1] .
## How drone photogrammetry and LiDAR fit an FLS
The Code was written for theodolite traverses and levelling, but it already allowed photogrammetric techniques for the preliminary survey where suitable aerial photographs were available [1] . Current Railway Board instructions for FLS and DPR consultants go further: they say technological tools such as LiDAR survey and satellite imagery on the BISAG portal should be used for survey work, that the alignment should be planned on the BISAG platform, and that a drone project video should be made where required [3] .
High-speed rail shows the method at scale. NHSRCL used helicopter-mounted aerial LiDAR, combining laser data, GPS data, flight parameters and photographs, to map the Delhi–Varanasi corridor as a 3D topographic map 50 metres either side of the proposed alignment [6] . On the Mumbai–Ahmedabad corridor the aerial LiDAR ground survey took 12 weeks, against 10 to 12 months by traditional methods, and fed the design of the vertical and horizontal alignment, structures, stations, land requirement and affected plots [7] . Drones and helicopters were also reported in use for the FLS of the Sambalpur–Gopalpur line in Odisha in 2020 [8] .
For a conventional line, a drone does the same job over a narrower strip, with lighter logistics than a helicopter. The workflow is:
- Control first. A DGPS control network along the corridor, tied to the project datum and to bench marks levelled from mean sea level.
- Flight. Photogrammetry for open country and built-up areas; drone LiDAR where vegetation, cuttings or hill slopes hide the ground. Many corridors use both.
- Processing. Orthomosaic, digital terrain model and contours, plus a classified point cloud from LiDAR.
- Engineering extraction. Longitudinal section along the chosen centre line, cross-sections at the required interval, feature mapping within the corridor and land plans over revenue maps.
- Ground work that stays on the ground. Pegging and pillars, river and bridge site studies, soil and geological investigation, and checks of features the aerial data cannot see.
The main gain is that the alignment can be moved on the terrain model without resurveying. Several options can be tested, curves and gradients adjusted, and the sections regenerated before anything is pegged. The comparison with ground methods is covered in drone survey vs DGPS and total station .
## Accuracy and ground control
An FLS is only as good as its control. On a linear corridor, ground control points are spread along the full length and alternate on both sides of the alignment, with a pair at each end, so the model does not bend or tilt along its length. Checkpoints are measured the same way but held out of processing, so the accuracy can be proved.
Ground control for a railway corridor. GCPs alternate on both sides of the alignment and are paired at the ends; checkpoints are held out of the adjustment. Chainage along the centre line ties every drawing to the FLS pegs.
- Datum: plan coordinates in the project system, and heights as orthometric heights tied to bench marks, not raw GNSS ellipsoidal heights.
- Chainage: every section, plan and point in the data should carry chainage , so the drawings, the pegs on the ground and the estimate agree.
- Accuracy report: residuals at independent checkpoints reported as RMSE in X, Y and Z.
- Vertical accuracy matters most. Earthwork quantities come from the difference between ground and formation levels, so a small bias in the terrain model becomes a large error in the estimate.
How GSD, GCP spacing and RTK or PPK positioning set the achievable accuracy is explained in how accurate is a drone survey .
## Deliverables and file formats
The output of a drone or LiDAR survey for an FLS should be ready for the alignment designer and the estimator, not only a map. A typical set:
Deliverable | Format | Used for
Orthomosaic of the corridor | GeoTIFF | Base for plans, land plans and route review
Terrain model and contours | GeoTIFF, DWG | Alignment design, earthwork, drainage
Point cloud | LAS / LAZ | Ground under vegetation, cuttings, structures
Detailed plan, L-section and cross-sections | DWG | FLS drawings at the Code scales, quantities
Bridge and culvert site plans | DWG | Waterway design, skeleton drawings
Land plans and GIS layers | SHP, DWG | Land acquisition, utilities, encroachments
Control and accuracy report | PDF, CSV | Proof of accuracy; setting out at construction
What each of these products is, and how it differs from the others, is covered in drone survey deliverables explained .
## Common pitfalls
- Too narrow a corridor. If the strip only covers the first alignment, every shift needs a new flight. Fly wide enough for realignments and for the 100 metres each side the Code's detailed plan needs [1] , more where yards or junctions will be built.
- Photogrammetry under trees. A photogrammetric model maps the canopy, not the ground. Use LiDAR or ground survey in forests, orchards and overgrown cuttings, or the L-section will be wrong; see LiDAR vs photogrammetry .
- Mixed height systems. Ellipsoidal GNSS heights mixed with levelled bench marks give formation levels that do not match the ground at construction.
- Water and river beds. Neither LiDAR nor photographs see through water. River cross-sections, bed levels and flood levels need ground survey, bathymetry and local records.
- No independent checkpoints. Without them the accuracy of the terrain model is unproven, and the earthwork estimate inherits the doubt.
- Hidden services. Buried cables, pipelines and drains do not appear in aerial data. Utility records and ground checks are still needed for the shifting estimate [3] .
- Land plans on the wrong base. Revenue maps must be fitted carefully to the orthomosaic; a poor fit puts the land boundary in the wrong field.
## How DATA PKT works on railway surveys
DATA PKT has prepared more than 60 yard plans, Engineering Scale Plans and drainage plans for railway divisions from drone survey with DGPS ground control; read the railway yard and drainage plans case study . Our in-house GIS team turns the survey data into CAD drawings and GIS layers. See railway and metro surveys , ESP and DPR surveys and railway drone inspection .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is a final location survey in railways?
A final location survey (FLS) is the last and most detailed survey before a railway project is sanctioned. It fixes the centre line, curves and gradients on the ground and produces the detailed plans, longitudinal and cross-sections, bridge and yard plans and data for the detailed estimate in the Project Report, as set out in Chapter IV of the Indian Railways Engineering Code.
Q: What is the difference between PETS and FLS?
A Preliminary Engineering-cum-Traffic Survey (PETS) compares routes and tests whether the project is viable, and leads to a Techno-Economic Survey Report. The final location survey follows on the chosen route, fixes the alignment in detail and leads to the Project Report with the detailed estimate. The Railway Board has asked zones to complete the traffic study before going ahead with an FLS.
Q: Can a drone or LiDAR survey be used for a railway FLS?
Yes. Railway Board instructions for FLS and DPR consultants say tools such as LiDAR survey and satellite imagery should be used, and aerial LiDAR has been used for high-speed rail corridors. A drone or LiDAR survey tied to DGPS control and bench marks supplies the topography; pegging, pillars, soil investigation and river studies are still done on the ground.
Q: What accuracy and control does a drone FLS need?
Ground control points measured with DGPS along the full corridor, alternating on both sides of the alignment, heights tied to bench marks referred to mean sea level, and independent checkpoints reported as RMSE in X, Y and Z. Vertical accuracy matters most because earthwork quantities come from ground and formation levels.
Q: What deliverables come out of a railway FLS survey?
An orthomosaic in GeoTIFF, a terrain model and contours, a LAS or LAZ point cloud where LiDAR is flown, the detailed plan, longitudinal section and cross-sections in DWG, bridge and culvert site plans, land plans and GIS layers in SHP, and a control and accuracy report.

=== https://datapkt.com/insights/topographic-survey-by-drone.html ===
Home / Insights / Topographic survey by drone
Topographic survey
# Topographic and contour survey by drone: method, accuracy and deliverables
How a drone topographic survey is planned, tied to ground control and checked, how to choose a contour interval the data can support, and what you should receive at the end.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 25 November 2026 · 10 min read
Short answer: a drone topographic survey flies overlapping photos or LiDAR over the site, ties them to DGPS ground control, and processes them into a bare-ground terrain model (DTM), contours, spot levels and an orthomosaic. Choose the contour interval from the proven vertical accuracy, not the other way round: a common legacy rule sets the interval at about three times the vertical RMSE [2] [3] . Accept the survey only with an independent checkpoint report.
## What a topographic survey records
A topographic survey describes the shape of the ground and the features on it, in a stated coordinate system and height datum. For design work the core outputs are the same whatever the instrument: ground levels, contours, breaklines along kerbs, drains, embankment toes and tops, and the position of built features such as roads, buildings, poles, culverts and boundary walls.
A drone changes how those levels are collected. Instead of a surveyor walking to each point, the drone captures the whole surface, and software extracts the ground from it. That gives dense, continuous coverage, but it also means the ground has to be visible to the sensor, and the result has to be proved against independent ground measurements.
## When a drone survey fits, and when it doesn't
A drone suits open land, long corridors, unsafe ground and repeat surveys. A total station or DGPS is still needed for ground control and checkpoints, detail the drone cannot see, millimetre work and small sites.
A drone is usually the efficient choice for:
- Open or lightly vegetated land: agricultural plots, industrial and township layouts, solar plant sites, quarries and mine leases, landfill and stockpile yards.
- Long corridors: highways, canals, railway alignments and transmission routes, where walking a total station along the full length is slow.
- Unsafe or hard-to-reach ground: steep slopes, active earthworks, riverbanks and landslide scars.
- Repeat surveys: monthly progress or volume checks, where the same flight plan is flown again.
A total station or DGPS is still needed for:
- Ground control and checkpoints for the drone survey itself.
- Hard detail the drone cannot see: invert levels of drains and culverts, ground under bridges and dense tree cover, inside buildings.
- Millimetre work: structural setting-out, rail levels, benchmark levelling and as-built checks to tight tolerances.
- Small sites where a day of ground survey is quicker than mobilising a flight.
Most infrastructure topography ends up as a combination of the two. Our guide to drone survey vs DGPS and total station sets out which method does which part.
## Planning the flight: GSD, overlap and terrain following
Ground sample distance (GSD) is the size of one image pixel on the ground, and it limits how much detail can be measured. It is set by the camera and the height above ground. Decide the GSD from the accuracy and contour interval you need, then work back to the flying height with our GSD calculator . For example, the Indian Bureau of Mines SOP for drone surveys of mine leases asks for imagery at 5 cm GSD or better [4] .
Overlap is how much each photo shares with the next one along the strip (forward) and with the neighbouring strip (side). Generous overlap is what lets the software match the same ground in many photos. The same IBM SOP sets a minimum of 80% forward and 70% side overlap [4] , and software makers advise raising overlap further over forests, crops, sand and other uniform surfaces [5] .
Terrain following matters on hilly or stepped sites. If the drone flies at one fixed altitude over a valley and a ridge, the GSD and overlap change across the site, and the high ground gets less overlap. Pix4D's acquisition guidance is that the camera should be kept as far as possible at a constant height over the terrain to hold the planned GSD [5] . In practice that means flying with a terrain model loaded into the flight planner, or splitting the site into blocks at different heights.
Two further checks belong in the plan: flight permissions for the site's airspace zone, and the light. Low sun casts long shadows that hide detail, while wind and haze blur images. Plan the flight window, not only the flight lines.
## Ground control and checkpoints
Ground control points (GCPs) are marked targets measured with DGPS. They fix the drone model to the project coordinate system and correct its scale and height. Checkpoints are measured the same way but kept out of processing, so they can test the finished surface independently. RTK or PPK positioning on the drone reduces the number of GCPs needed; it does not remove the need for checkpoints.
- Spread the control: around the boundary and through the middle of area sites, and in a zigzag on both sides of corridors. Clustered control leaves the far parts of the model unconstrained.
- Tie to the project datum: GNSS gives ellipsoidal heights. Design levels in India are normally referred to mean sea level through a benchmark, so the survey must state how heights were reduced, using a geoid model or a local benchmark tie, and must agree with the levels the designers will use.
- Use national references: the Survey of India operates a nationwide Continuously Operating Reference Stations (CORS) network of more than 1,000 stations, which the government describes as capable of centimetre-level positioning in real time [6] . It is a convenient way to bring control onto a common national framework.
How many GCPs, how far apart and how accuracy is proved are covered in detail in how accurate is a drone survey? This guide only summarises them.
## Photogrammetry or LiDAR for vegetated sites
Photogrammetry builds the surface from what the camera sees. On bare ground that is the ground. Over crops, scrub and trees it is the top of the vegetation, and no amount of processing can recover ground that never appeared in any photo. Ground filtering can remove isolated trees and vehicles, but under continuous cover the "terrain" is really canopy.
LiDAR fires laser pulses that can return several echoes, the last often from the ground through gaps in the leaves. That is why LiDAR is the usual choice for terrain under vegetation, forest corridors, hill roads and landslide slopes. Many projects fly both: LiDAR for the terrain, and a camera for the orthomosaic and feature mapping.
The ASPRS standard reflects this difference by reporting accuracy separately for open ground (non-vegetated vertical accuracy, NVA) and for vegetated ground (VVA). NVA must meet the specification; VVA is reported as found [1] . Ask for both on any site with vegetation. Our LiDAR vs photogrammetry guide compares the two in field studies.
## From images to a terrain model and contours
Processing follows a fixed chain. Images, camera positions and GCPs go into aerial triangulation, which solves where every photo was taken. Dense matching then builds a point cloud, from which a surface model (DSM) is made. Ground points are classified to give the terrain model (DTM). Contours, spot levels and CAD layers are drawn from the DTM, and the checkpoints test the result at the end.
The photogrammetry processing chain behind a topographic survey. Contours are drawn from the ground-only DTM, and checkpoints held out of the adjustment decide whether the result is accepted or the control is re-checked.
Two steps decide whether the contours are usable. The first is ground classification: contours drawn from the DSM put trees, trucks and buildings in as humps. The second is breaklines: digitising kerbs, drain edges, bund tops and embankment toes so that contours bend sharply where the ground does, instead of being smoothed across a hard edge.
## Choosing the contour interval
The contour interval should follow from the vertical accuracy the survey can prove. The current ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards, Edition 2 (2023), state plainly that they do not endorse contour interval, map scale or GSD as a way of expressing accuracy; accuracy is specified as a vertical RMSE [1] . The legacy rules still give a useful rule of thumb for picking an interval from that RMSE:
- ASPRS 1990, Class 1: the limiting RMSE of contours is one-third of the contour interval, and spot heights one-sixth [2] . In other words, the interval is about three times the vertical RMSE, and spot levels should be twice as good as the contours.
- NMAS (1947): no more than one tested point in ten may be in error by more than half the contour interval. Edition 2's comparison table puts the equivalent interval for its 10 cm vertical class at 30 cm under ASPRS 1990 Class 1 and about 33 cm under NMAS [3] .
Proved vertical RMSE (open ground) | Contour interval, ASPRS 1990 Class 1 (3 × RMSE) | Spot level RMSE needed (interval ÷ 6)
5 cm | 15 cm | 2.5 cm
10 cm | 30 cm | 5 cm
17 cm | 50 cm | 8 cm
33 cm | 1 m | 17 cm
Read the table from left to right. If the checkpoint report proves 10 cm, a 30 cm interval is defensible; a 10 cm interval drawn from the same data looks detailed but claims precision the survey does not have. Where a project specification already fixes an interval, such as the highway DPR requirements covered in our highway DPR guide , work backwards to the RMSE needed and plan GSD and control to reach it.
## Deliverables and file formats
A complete drone topographic survey usually includes the following. The deliverables guide explains each one in more depth.
Deliverable | What it is for | Usual formats
DTM (terrain model) | Bare-ground levels for design, earthwork and drainage | GeoTIFF; ground-classified points as LAS or LAZ
Contours | Ground shape at the agreed interval, with index contours labelled | DWG or DXF for CAD; SHP for GIS
Spot levels and breaklines | Levels on a grid and at key features; hard edges for design surfaces | DWG or DXF; SHP
Orthomosaic | Measurable true-colour base map for planning and feature mapping | GeoTIFF; KMZ for quick viewing
Topographic plan | Features such as roads, buildings, poles, drains and boundaries on the contour base | DWG or DXF; SHP or GeoPackage layers
Point cloud | Full 3D record for sections, volumes and later checks | LAS or LAZ
Survey and accuracy report | Method, control, datum, checkpoint residuals and RMSE | PDF with GCP and checkpoint tables
Agree the coordinate system, height datum, CAD layer names and sheet layout before the flight, not after. Our GIS mapping and data processing team can deliver to a client's CAD template.
## QC and the accuracy report
The accuracy report is the evidence that the contours can be trusted. Under ASPRS Edition 2 it should be based on at least 30 checkpoints, surveyed at least twice as accurately as the product being tested, and the single headline figure is the RMSE; the old 95% confidence figure has been dropped [1] . A useful report includes:
- the coordinate system, height datum and geoid or benchmark used;
- a plan showing GCPs and checkpoints;
- a table of checkpoint residuals in X, Y and Z, with horizontal and vertical RMSE;
- vertical accuracy on open ground and, where relevant, under vegetation;
- areas of low confidence, such as water, dense canopy or deep shadow, marked on the plan.
The detail of how residuals and RMSE are calculated is in the accuracy guide . Terms such as NVA, VVA and RMSE are defined in the drone survey glossary .
## Common mistakes
- Contours from the DSM. Trees and structures appear as hills. Contours must come from a classified DTM.
- Ellipsoidal heights delivered as levels. GNSS heights not reduced to the project datum can differ from benchmark levels by tens of metres, and the error is not always obvious on a contour plan.
- An interval finer than the accuracy. Tight contours from loosely controlled data give a false sense of precision.
- No independent checkpoints. Residuals on the GCPs themselves only show how well the software fitted the control, not how accurate the map is.
- Clustered or one-sided control. Errors grow towards the parts of the site with no control, especially on long corridors.
- Photogrammetry under canopy. The terrain is the treetops. Use LiDAR or ground survey for those areas.
- Missing breaklines. Drains, kerbs and embankments get smoothed away, and designers have to redraw them.
- Water treated as ground. Ponds and rivers give poor or false surfaces; mark them and survey the bed separately if needed.
## Checklist for clients
Put these items in the scope or the enquiry so that every quote covers the same survey.
Item | What to specify | Why it matters
Site boundary | KML or chainage, with any buffer | Sets the flight area and the control layout
Coordinate system and datum | Projection, zone and height datum; benchmark to tie to | Avoids levels that do not match the design
Vertical accuracy | Required RMSE on open ground | Drives GSD, control and the contour interval
Contour interval | Interval and index contour spacing | Must be supported by the accuracy above
Vegetated areas | Whether terrain under cover is needed | Decides photogrammetry, LiDAR or ground survey
Features to map | List of features and breaklines | Defines the topographic plan content
Deliverable formats | DWG or DXF, SHP, GeoTIFF, LAS; CAD template | Saves conversion and rework
Accuracy report | Checkpoint count, residual table, RMSE | The only proof of accuracy
Access and permissions | Site access, airspace zone, any restrictions | Avoids lost flight days
For what drives the price of a survey, see what a drone survey costs in India .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is a topographic survey by drone?
A drone topographic survey captures overlapping photos or LiDAR over a site, ties them to DGPS ground control, and processes them into a bare-ground terrain model, contours, spot levels, an orthomosaic and a topographic plan in the project coordinate system and height datum. Its accuracy is proved with independent checkpoints.
Q: How do I choose the contour interval for a drone survey?
Choose it from the vertical accuracy the survey can prove. Under the legacy ASPRS 1990 Class 1 rule the contour interval is about three times the vertical RMSE, so a survey proved to 10 cm supports a 30 cm interval. The current ASPRS Edition 2 standard specifies accuracy as RMSE, not as a contour interval.
Q: Can a drone contour survey map ground under trees?
Photogrammetry cannot: it maps the top of the vegetation where the ground is hidden. LiDAR pulses can reach the ground through gaps in the canopy, so LiDAR is the usual choice for vegetated sites, with ground survey for any areas neither sensor can see.
Q: Does a drone topographic survey replace a total station or DGPS?
No. DGPS is needed for ground control and checkpoints, and a total station is still used for invert levels, ground under bridges and dense cover, and millimetre-level work. Most infrastructure surveys combine a drone for coverage with ground survey for control and hidden detail.
Q: What deliverables should a drone topographic survey include?
Usually a DTM as GeoTIFF, contours and spot levels as DWG or DXF and SHP, an orthomosaic as GeoTIFF, a topographic plan of features, a point cloud as LAS or LAZ, and a survey report with the datum, GCP and checkpoint tables and RMSE in X, Y and Z.
