Bridges
# Bridge inspection by drone in India: what it can and cannot replace
A drone gives the bridge engineer close, repeatable views of piers, bearings, girders and the deck underside without an inspection unit or scaffolding. It does not replace hammer sounding, testing or the engineer's judgement. Here is where it fits under IRC guidelines and the Indian Railway Bridge Manual.
By the DATA PKT survey and inspection team · Published 25 November 2026 · 9 min read
Short answer: a drone replaces much of the access in a bridge inspection, not the inspection. It photographs the parts that otherwise need a bridge inspection unit, a boat or scaffolding, and turns them into a measurable 3D model and a located defect register. Hammer sounding, non-destructive testing, load tests, underwater and confined-space checks, and the condition assessment itself still need people on the structure and a qualified bridge engineer.
IRC:SP:35
IRC guidelines on inspection and maintenance of bridges, 1990 [1]
Once a year
inspection of every highway bridge by a qualified engineer, IRC:SP:18 [2]
1.7 lakh
national highway structures in MoRTH's IBMS survey, 2026 [3]
BS-129 (R1)
RDSO guidelines for drone-based railway bridge inspection [9]
## How bridges are inspected in India
### Highway bridges: IRC guidelines and IBMS
The Indian Roads Congress guidance comes in layers. IRC:SP:35, published in 1990, contains the guidelines on inspection and maintenance of bridges and is written for the engineers who inspect them; IRC:SP:52, the Bridge Inspector's Reference Manual, is the companion for inspectors in the field [1] . The Manual for Highway Bridge Maintenance Inspection (IRC:SP:18) asks for every bridge to be inspected by a competent qualified engineer once a year, bridges in hilly terrain prone to slips twice (before and after the monsoon), and special inspections after unusual events such as an earthquake or the passage of an abnormal load. Major and special-type bridges should also be seen by a senior engineer [2] .
MoRTH is now building a central record. Under the Indian Bridge Management System (IBMS), field engineers record inventory and condition on a mobile app, and a web dashboard gives agencies such as NHAI, NHIDCL, BRO and state PWDs access to the data. The 2026 drive covers about 1.7 lakh structures longer than six metres, including bridges, flyovers and culverts, and the ministry has said drones may be used for the hard-to-reach parts of bridges [3] . IBMS uses condition ratings and importance to prioritise repair, rehabilitation and maintenance [4] . The Indian Academy of Highway Engineers (IAHE) runs a course on bridge inspection, repair, maintenance management and health monitoring of structures for highway engineers [5] .
### Railway bridges: IRBM, BMS and RDSO BS-129
On Indian Railways, Chapter II of the Indian Railway Bridge Manual (IRBM) sets the schedule of bridge inspection by each grade of engineering official, and para 1107 lists the aspects an inspection must cover [6] . Pre-monsoon inspection is done by the SSE (P.Way) or SSE (Works) and post-monsoon inspection by the ADEN, and their paper bridge registers have been replaced by the online Bridge Management System (BMS) [7] . Underwater inspection of substructures follows IRBM para 1107(d): a routine or swim-by inspection once a year, a detailed inspection once in five years, and special inspections when needed [8] . Steel bridges also get periodic technical inspection by Bridge Inspectors, and in 2023 the Railway Board ordered intensive inspection of all open web and under-slung girder bridges by senior officers [6] .
Drones already have a written place in this system. RDSO Report BS-129 (R1), May 2021, gave guidelines for drone-based bridge inspection. The Railway Board later noted that drone photography alone allows only an inference about condition, an incomplete inspection, and the guidelines were revised for complete inspection using photogrammetry and LiDAR, with the data held in a 3D bridge information model (BrIM) reached through BMS [9] . For railway work in general, see our guide to railway drone inspection .
## What a drone does well on a bridge
- Close views of the parts that need access : pier caps, bearings, girder soffits, diaphragms, expansion joints, drainage spouts and the deck underside. A camera on a gimbal that tilts upwards photographs the soffit without a bridge inspection unit on the deck or a boat underneath.
- Defect imagery : cracks, spalling, exposed and corroded reinforcement, leaching, honeycombing, corrosion and section loss on steel, missing or visibly loose bolts and rivets, vegetation growth, and debris or erosion at the waterline. Flown a few metres from the surface with a zoom lens, the images can show fine cracks; the engineer decides what they mean.
- A measurable 3D model : overlapping photographs are processed into a point cloud and textured mesh, tied to DGPS ground control, so each defect can be located on the structure, measured and compared at the next inspection. See photogrammetry for how the model is built.
- Orthomosaics of the deck and elevations : a scaled, distortion-free image of the deck surface or a pier face that can be marked up like a drawing.
- Thermal imagery, where it applies : on a concrete deck warmed by the sun, delaminated areas can show as warmer patches because the separation slows the flow of heat into the slab. Results depend on weather, time of day and surfacing, and every suspect area has to be confirmed by sounding. Our thermal survey page explains the camera and conditions.
- Approaches and surroundings : embankments, guide bunds, river training works, the channel upstream and downstream, and encroachments, all in one flight.
- Less disruption : fewer lane closures or traffic blocks for access, and fewer people working at height or over water.
An overview flight shows the deck, piers, approaches and channel together; the close-range passes on each span come after.
## What a drone cannot replace
- Hands-on testing. IRC:SP:52 relies on touch and sound: tapping concrete and masonry with a hammer, checking rivets by striking one side and feeling the other, and tests for carbonation depth and chemical attack [1] . Non-destructive tests such as rebound hammer, ultrasonic pulse velocity, half-cell potential and cover measurement need contact with the surface.
- Bearings in detail. A drone shows the bearing and its seat. It cannot by itself confirm whether a bearing is working as fixed or free, which SP:52 asks the inspector to establish first [1] , or measure gaps and movement to the precision of a gauge.
- Load tests and deflection. Load-carrying capacity comes from testing, instrumentation and analysis, not imagery.
- Underwater substructure and scour. Below the waterline the work needs divers, special equipment or soundings [8] [2] .
- Confined and GNSS-denied spaces. Inside box girders and closed cells there is no satellite signal, little light and no room to recover a drone safely. Under a wide deck, satellite positioning weakens or drops out. A person with a torch is usually the safer choice inside a box girder.
- The assessment. Condition rating, cause of distress, load capacity and repair decisions belong to a qualified bridge engineer. Parts that could not be seen should be recorded as "not inspected", as SP:52 advises [1] , rather than assumed sound.
Inspection task | What a drone gives | What is still needed
Deck underside, girders, pier caps | Close imagery without an inspection unit | Engineer's review; sounding of suspect areas
Cracks and spalling | Located, measured, comparable images | Crack width gauge, cause of cracking
Bearings | Visual condition of bearing and seat | Movement measurement, fixed or free check
Concrete quality | Surface signs only | Hammer sounding, NDT, cores [1]
Delamination | Thermal indications, conditions permitting | Confirmation by sounding
Substructure under water | Waterline only | Divers, soundings [8]
Load capacity | Nothing | Load test and analysis
## How a drone bridge inspection is done
### 1. Plan
Start from the drawings, the last inspection report and the span arrangement, and fix the component numbering (spans, piers, bearings, faces) before anyone flies, so every photograph has an address. Check the airspace on Digital Sky and get the owner's permission: for a railway bridge, the division and a block or safe flying window; for a highway bridge, the authority and any traffic management. Note the river level, overhead lines and nearby buildings.
### 2. Safety
Each site gets a risk assessment, an exclusion zone, a spotter and an agreed abort plan. Hazards specific to bridges include gusting wind under the deck, birds and bee hives under girders, overhead power lines, and railway OHE, which a drone must keep well clear of.
### 3. Flying under and near the deck
Under the deck and beside tall piers the drone may lose satellite positioning and fall back on its vision sensors, which need light and surface texture. The pilot flies slowly and manually, keeps the aircraft in sight or works with an observer, and uses a compact drone with obstacle sensing and an upward-tilting camera. Image positions are taken from control on the structure, not from the drone's GNSS.
### 4. Image overlap for the 3D model
Each face is photographed in parallel strips at a constant distance, with enough forward and side overlap that every point appears in several photographs, plus oblique shots around corners and edges. Even light matters: shadow lines under a deck confuse both the software and the reviewer. DGPS ground control on the approaches and measured targets on the structure fix the scale and position. The drone survey glossary explains GSD, GCPs and related terms.
### 5. Defect logging
Every defect is logged with its component, its position on that component (span, face, distance from a bearing or joint), type, approximate size, photo reference and a note on change since the last inspection. The register is a tool for the inspecting engineer, not a substitute for the engineer's rating.
## Deliverables
- Inspection imagery : full-resolution photographs and video, organised by span and component, each with its location.
- Defect register : a spreadsheet and GIS layer listing each defect with component, position, type, size, photo reference and priority for the engineer's review.
- 3D model : point cloud and textured mesh of the bridge, checked against DGPS checkpoints.
- Orthomosaics of the deck and of each elevation, scaled for mark-up.
- Thermal images , where used, with the time, weather and surface conditions recorded.
- Coverage note : what was flown, what was not inspected and why.
## Checklist for bridge owners and consultants
- State the format the results must feed: IBMS, an IRC inspection proforma, the railway BMS, or RDSO's BrIM guidelines.
- Share the drawings, span arrangement and last inspection report.
- Agree the component numbering before the flight.
- Name the inspecting engineer; the drone team supports that engineer.
- Plan hammer sounding, NDT and underwater inspection separately.
- Confirm permissions, blocks or traffic arrangements and the flying window.
- Ask for a coverage map and a "not inspected" list.
- Ask for every defect to be located on a component and linked to a photograph.
- Ask how the 3D model was checked against ground control.
- Agree file formats and that the data belongs to you.
## How DATA PKT works on bridges
Our 20+ pilots fly the overview and close-range passes, our in-house GIS team builds the 3D models, orthomosaics and defect registers, and DGPS ground control ties every output to the site. We work alongside the client's bridge engineer, who makes the assessment. See highway and road surveys and railway and metro surveys .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: Can a drone replace a bridge inspection in India?
No. A drone replaces much of the access: it photographs piers, bearings, girders and the deck underside without an inspection unit, boat or scaffolding, and builds a measurable 3D model. Hammer sounding, non-destructive tests, load tests, underwater checks and the condition assessment still need people on the structure and a qualified bridge engineer.
Q: How often must highway bridges be inspected under IRC guidelines?
IRC:SP:18 asks for every bridge to be inspected by a competent qualified engineer once a year, bridges in hilly terrain prone to slips twice (before and after the monsoon), and special inspections after events such as an earthquake or an abnormal load. IRC:SP:35 (1990) sets out the guidelines for inspection and maintenance of bridges.
Q: Does Indian Railways allow drone inspection of bridges?
Yes. RDSO Report BS-129 (R1), issued in May 2021, gives guidelines for drone-based bridge inspection. The Railway Board noted that photography alone is an incomplete inspection, and the guidelines were revised to use photogrammetry and LiDAR, with the data held in a 3D bridge model reached through the Bridge Management System.
Q: Can a drone fly under a bridge deck?
Yes, with care. Under the deck satellite positioning weakens or drops out, so the pilot flies slowly and manually with vision sensors, an upward-tilting camera and an observer. Image positions come from control points on the structure. Inside box girders and other confined spaces a person is usually the safer choice.
Q: What should a drone bridge inspection deliver?
Full-resolution imagery organised by span and component, a defect register giving each defect's component, position, type, size and photo reference, a 3D model checked against DGPS checkpoints, orthomosaics of the deck and elevations, thermal images where used, and a note of what was not inspected.

Home / Insights / Point cloud classification
GIS and data processing
# Point cloud classification explained: LAS classes, ground filtering and QC
What classifying a LiDAR or photogrammetric point cloud means, the standard ASPRS LAS class codes, how ground filters work and where they fail, how to check the result, and what to put in the scope when you outsource it.
By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team · Published 25 November 2026 · 10 min read
Short answer: point cloud classification gives every point a code that says what it hit: ground, vegetation, building, water, wire, noise and so on. The codes come from the ASPRS LAS 1.4 specification. The step that matters most is ground classification, because the terrain model, contours and every earthwork quantity are built from it. Ask for the class list, density, accuracy, tiling and coordinate system in writing, and for a QC report that proves them.
Class 2
ground: the class the terrain model is built from [1] [2]
9 classes
in the USGS minimum classification scheme [6]
≥30
checkpoints for an accuracy test under ASPRS Edition 2 [7]
64–255
class codes left free for project-defined classes [2]
## What point cloud classification is
A drone LiDAR flight, or a photogrammetry job, produces millions of 3D points. On their own they are just coordinates. Classification sorts them into the things they represent, by writing a number into the classification field of each point in the LAS file. Software can then show only ground for a bare-earth DTM, or pull out conductors to check clearances.
Classification is usually done in two passes. Automatic routines label most points by geometry (height above a local surface, slope, number of returns) and, for photogrammetric clouds, colour. An operator then checks profiles and 3D views and fixes what the routines got wrong. That second pass decides the quality of everything built afterwards.
Figure 1. Where classification sits in the LiDAR chain. Strips must fit together before points are classified, and the DTM, DSM and contours are only as good as the classes they are built from.
## The standard ASPRS LAS classes
The LAS format is published by ASPRS; the current edition is LAS 1.4, revision R15 (July 2019) [1] . It fixes what each class number means. The standard codes for the LAS 1.4 point formats used for new work are [1] [2] .
Code | Class | Typical use
0 | Created, never classified | Raw points straight from processing; none should remain in a delivered file
1 | Unassigned (processed, but unclassified) | Points checked but not in any class the project needs
2 | Ground | Bare-earth DTM, contours, cross-sections, earthwork volumes
3 | Low vegetation | Grass and crops; often merged with medium vegetation
4 | Medium vegetation | Shrubs and scrub
5 | High vegetation | Trees: canopy height, tree felling counts, clearance studies
6 | Building | Roof outlines, encroachment and property mapping
7 | Low point (low noise) | Points below the ground surface, such as multipath echoes
8 | Reserved (model key-point in earlier versions) | Use the key-point flag instead
9 | Water | Rivers, ponds and canals; hydro-flattening of the DTM
10 | Rail | Railway track and rail-head levels
11 | Road surface | Carriageway models for highway design and resurfacing
12 | Reserved (overlap in earlier versions) | Use the overlap flag instead
13 | Wire, guard (shield) | Earth wire on transmission lines
14 | Wire, conductor (phase) | Conductor sag and clearance checks
15 | Transmission tower | Tower positions and heights
16 | Wire-structure connector (insulator) | Attachment points for line modelling
17 | Bridge deck | Keeps decks out of the ground surface
18 | High noise | Birds, dust and other points far above the surface
19 | Overhead structure | Conveyors and similar overhead machinery, for example on mine sites; added in revision R14 [3] [4]
20 | Ignored ground | Ground points set aside, typically close to breaklines
21 | Snow | Snow cover, where present and identifiable
22 | Temporal exclusion | Data superseded by a later capture, for example in tidal zones
23–63 | Reserved | Kept by ASPRS for future classes
64–255 | User-definable | Project classes such as poles, signboards, OHE masts or kerbs
Alongside the class number, LAS 1.4 carries four flags that can be set on any point: synthetic (not from the laser, for example digitised from a stereo model), key-point (keep when thinning), withheld (keep in the file but leave out of processing) and overlap (lies in the overlap between flight strips) [2] . That is why codes 8 and 12 are no longer used. Some software still lists 19 as reserved, so check your tools before agreeing a class list.
## How ground filtering works
Ground filtering decides which points are the bare earth. Three families of methods are in common use:
- Progressive TIN densification. The method described by Axelsson and used in TerraScan: the area is divided into a grid, the lowest point in each cell is taken as ground, and those points are triangulated into a first surface. Further points are added if they are close enough to the surface and do not change its angle too much, and the TIN is rebuilt after each pass [11] . In the ISPRS comparison of filters, Axelsson's filter did well on steep slopes [10] .
- Morphological filters. The Simple Morphological Filter (SMRF) of Pingel, Clarke and McBride takes the lowest point in each grid cell, then applies a morphological opening with a window that grows each pass. Cells that drop by more than a height threshold are marked as objects. A slope term relaxes the threshold on steep ground [13] .
- Cloth simulation (CSF). Zhang and colleagues turn the point cloud upside down and let a simulated cloth settle onto it. Where the cloth rests is taken as the ground surface, and points within a set distance of it are classed as ground. The user sets only a few values: cloth resolution, rigidness and an option for steep slopes [12] .
No single setting suits a whole project: flat farmland, a hill road and a dense town need different parameters, so large jobs are filtered zone by zone.
## Where ground filters go wrong
The ISPRS filter test found the same problem areas across the algorithms it compared [10] . Look there first:
- Low vegetation. Grass, crops and scrub are hard to separate from the ground, especially on slopes. Left in class 2, they lift the DTM.
- Steep slopes and sharp breaks. Embankment shoulders, cutting crests, river banks and retaining walls look like objects to a filter, so the edges get shaved off [10] . The cloth filter can also give larger errors on steep slopes, which its optional slope post-processing is meant to reduce [12] . On a slope stability study, a shaved crest changes the geometry the analysis depends on.
- Bridges and ramps. Filters remove bridges completely, partly or not at all, and in the ISPRS test every filter removed ramps [10] . The cloth filter cannot tell objects joined to the ground, such as bridges, from the ground itself [12] . Decks belong in class 17, with the ground surface running beneath them.
- Water. Water surfaces return few, scattered points, and some of them are noise. Water is usually classified using breaklines drawn along the banks, and ground points too close to them can go to class 20 [5] [6] .
- Low noise. One point far below the surface can pull the surface down and cause nearby real ground to be rejected [10] . Noise filtering into classes 7 and 18 comes before ground filtering.
- Complex built-up areas. Courtyards, stepped buildings and multi-level structures remain difficult for every filter [10] .
## Photogrammetric vs LiDAR point clouds
The LAS classes are the same for both, but the clouds differ. A LiDAR pulse can return several echoes, so points under trees often reach the ground, and return number and intensity help classification. A photogrammetric cloud has one surface only: what the camera saw. Under canopy there is no ground to classify, and no filter can recover it. Its true colour does help separate grass from bare soil or roads from verges.
Image matching also adds noise on water and plain surfaces and blurs sharp edges. A photogrammetric DTM is reliable on open ground and doubtful under vegetation. Our guide to LiDAR vs photogrammetry gives the field-test figures.
## Quality control: how to check a classified cloud
A classified cloud should come with evidence that it is right. Four checks cover most of it:
- Visual checks. View the cloud coloured by class, and a hillshade of the ground-only DTM. Pits, spikes and buildings left as bumps show up at once.
- Profiles. Cut cross-sections at intervals and wherever the terrain changes: embankments, drains, bridge approaches, cuttings. They show vegetation left in ground, or ground lost at a slope edge.
- Checkpoints. Compare the DTM with independent surveyed points that were not used in processing. Under ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards, Edition 2, an accuracy test needs at least 30 checkpoints, up to 120 on large projects. Accuracy is reported as RMSE; the non-vegetated vertical accuracy must meet the specification, and the vegetated accuracy is reported [7] .
- Class accuracy. The USGS Lidar Base Specification requires every point in its minimum scheme to be properly classified, no points left in class 0 unless they are withheld, and classification that is consistent across the project. Noticeable variation between tiles, swaths or lifts can be cause to reject the whole delivery [5] .
First, the flight strips must fit. The same specification checks overlap between swaths: differences up to 8 cm in localised areas are acceptable, while differences over 16 cm that follow the flight lines are not [5] .
## Deliverables
- Classified point cloud in LAS 1.4. The USGS specification asks for LAS 1.4-R15 using point data record formats 6 to 10 [5] .
- LAZ. A lossless compressed version of LAS that keeps the LAS structure, now an OGC community standard [9] . USGS has moved its own point cloud deliveries to LAZ 1.4 [8] .
- DTM and DSM as GeoTIFF rasters: the DTM from ground, the DSM from the highest surface.
- Contours in DWG, DXF or SHP at the interval the drawings need.
- A QC report: class list, checkpoint RMSE, swath overlap checks and known problem areas.
See drone survey deliverables explained for what each output is for, and the drone survey glossary for terms such as DTM, DSM, RMSE and LAS.
## What to specify when you outsource classification
A scope that only says "classified point cloud" invites disputes. Put these six items in writing: the classes needed, density, accuracy, tiles, CRS and datum, and formats and QC.
Item | What to state
Classes needed | The exact codes, for example 1, 2, 3–5, 6, 7, 9, 17 and 18, plus any project classes from 64 upwards (poles, kerbs, OHE masts). Say which classes are checked for accuracy. USGS lists nine classes as its minimum [6] .
Density | Minimum pulse or point density. For reference, USGS QL1 needs at least 8 pulses/m² and QL2 at least 2 [6] ; drone LiDAR is usually much denser.
Accuracy | The vertical RMSE target on open ground, how vegetated areas are reported, and who surveys the checkpoints [7] .
Tiles | One non-overlapping tile scheme agreed before work starts, in the same CRS as the data, with tiles that edge-match without gaps [5] . Give tile size and naming.
CRS and datum | Horizontal coordinate system and zone, vertical datum or geoid model, and units. In India this is often WGS 84 / UTM with heights tied to the project benchmarks.
Formats and QC | LAS or LAZ version and point format, raster cell size, contour interval, CAD layer names, and the QC report contents listed above.
## How we handle classification at DATA PKT
Point cloud classification is done by our in-house GIS team in Gurugram, on our own LiDAR and photogrammetry surveys and on data that survey and engineering firms send us. When we fly the site ourselves, our surveyors measure the ground control and checkpoints with DGPS, and the classified cloud is checked against them. We also offer remote processing to firms outside India; all our projects so far have been in India. See our GIS mapping and data processing and LiDAR survey services, or send us a sample tile with your class list for a scope.

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What are the ASPRS LAS classes?
They are the standard class codes in the ASPRS LAS 1.4 specification: 0 created, never classified; 1 unassigned; 2 ground; 3, 4 and 5 low, medium and high vegetation; 6 building; 7 low noise; 9 water; 10 rail; 11 road surface; 13 to 16 wires, towers and insulators; 17 bridge deck; 18 high noise; 19 overhead structure; 20 ignored ground; 21 snow; and 22 temporal exclusion. Codes 64 to 255 are free for project-defined classes.
Q: What is ground classification in LiDAR?
It is the step that decides which points are the bare earth and puts them in class 2. Automatic filters such as progressive TIN densification, morphological filters and cloth simulation do most of it, and an operator then corrects the errors in profiles. The DTM, contours and earthwork quantities are all built from the ground class.
Q: Can a photogrammetric point cloud be classified like LiDAR?
Yes, with the same LAS classes, and its true colour helps. But a photogrammetric cloud only has the surface the camera saw, so under trees and dense scrub there are no ground points to classify. Its terrain model is reliable on open ground and doubtful under vegetation.
Q: How do you check the quality of a classified point cloud?
View it coloured by class and as a hillshade of the ground surface, cut profiles across embankments, drains, bridges and cuttings, and test the terrain model against independent checkpoints. ASPRS Edition 2 calls for at least 30 checkpoints and reports accuracy as RMSE. Classification should be consistent across all tiles.
Q: What should I specify when outsourcing point cloud classification?
The exact class codes you need and which are checked for accuracy, the minimum point density, the vertical accuracy target and checkpoints, a non-overlapping tile scheme, the coordinate system and vertical datum, the output formats such as LAS 1.4 or LAZ, DTM, DSM and contours, and the contents of the QC report.

## Using the calculator
Enter one checkpoint per row, either as surveyed and map coordinates or as residuals you have already worked out. Use projected coordinates in metres or feet, such as UTM, not latitude and longitude, and make sure both sets are in the same coordinate system and height datum. The unit setting only labels the results; it does not convert your numbers. Nothing you type leaves your browser.
## What RMSE measures
RMSE (root mean square error) is the usual single figure for the accuracy of a map, a digital terrain model or a point cloud. For each checkpoint the residual is the value read from the map minus the surveyed value. Square the residuals, take their mean and then the square root:
RMSEx = √( Σ dX² ÷ n ) · RMSEy = √( Σ dY² ÷ n ) · RMSEz = √( Σ dZ² ÷ n )
Squaring stops positive and negative errors cancelling out, and it gives large errors more weight than small ones, so one bad point shows up clearly. See RMSE in the glossary .
## Horizontal and vertical accuracy
Horizontal accuracy combines the X and Y errors into one radial figure:
RMSEr = √( RMSEx² + RMSEy² )
Vertical accuracy, RMSEz, is reported on its own because heights behave differently. On a drone photogrammetry survey the vertical error is usually larger than the horizontal error, and it also depends on the ground cover: bare, hard surfaces test better than grass or crops. The GSD calculator gives a rule-of-thumb link between pixel size and the accuracy you can expect.
## Why checkpoints must be held out
Checkpoints are surveyed exactly like ground control points (GCPs) but are not used to process the map. If a point helped to fix the model, the model will fit it closely whatever the real error is, so testing against GCPs makes a survey look better than it is. Use independent checkpoints, spread them over the whole site or along the whole corridor, place them on firm, clearly visible ground, and measure them in the same coordinate system and height datum as the deliverable. Our guide on how accurate a drone survey is explains how ground control and checkpoints are laid out.
## How to read the result
- Compare RMSE with the specification. The contract or the standard you work to sets the target, for example a horizontal and a vertical RMSE in centimetres. Check that both figures meet it.
- Look at the mean error. If the mean error on an axis is close to the RMSE, most of the error is a shift in one direction. That usually points to a datum, geoid or control problem rather than random noise, and it can often be corrected.
- Check the largest residual. One point far worse than the rest may be a mis-identified target, a disturbed marker or a typing error. Investigate it before you remove it, and report any point you leave out.
- Count the points. The 2023 ASPRS standard asks for at least 30 checkpoints for a product accuracy assessment. With fewer, the RMSE is still a useful check but a less reliable estimate.
For contour and terrain work, the checkpoint test is what proves the DTM. Read more in topographic and contour survey by drone .

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What is RMSE in a drone survey?
RMSE, or root mean square error, is the square root of the average of the squared differences between map coordinates and surveyed checkpoint coordinates. It is calculated separately for X, Y and Z and is the usual single figure for a survey's accuracy.
Q: How is horizontal RMSE calculated?
Horizontal RMSE, often written RMSEr, combines the two horizontal axes: RMSEr = √(RMSEx² + RMSEy²). Vertical accuracy is reported separately as RMSEz.
Q: How many checkpoints do I need?
The 2023 ASPRS standard asks for at least 30 checkpoints for a product accuracy assessment, spread across the whole area. With fewer checkpoints the RMSE is still a useful check, but it is a less reliable estimate of the true accuracy.
Q: What does the mean error tell me?
The mean error, or bias, shows whether the errors lean in one direction. If it is close to the RMSE on an axis, most of the error is a systematic shift, which usually points to a datum, geoid or ground control problem rather than random noise.

About DATA PKT
# Editorial standards: how we write our guides
How the guides, case studies and service pages on datapkt.com are written, sourced, dated and corrected.
By the DATA PKT team · Published 25 November 2026
In short: our guides are written by the DATA PKT team from our survey, GIS and inspection work. Facts and figures from outside sources link to the source, standards are named by number, and company figures are only those the company has approved for publication. Clients are named only where they have allowed it. Each guide shows its published date, and an updated date when its content changes. Nothing on the site is paid for by a third party. To report an error, email consult@datapkt.com .
## Who writes the guides
The guides in Insights are written by the DATA PKT team: the pilots, surveyors, GIS analysts and engineers who run our projects. Each guide carries a team byline, such as "By the DATA PKT survey and GIS engineering team". We do not publish the names of individual staff on the website.
The guides answer questions clients ask us before a survey starts: which method to use, how accurate the result will be, what the deliverables are and what to put in the scope. Where a guide explains how we do something, it describes how our own projects run.
## How we cite sources
Facts and figures that come from outside DATA PKT, such as a rule from the drone regulations, a value from a standard, a research result or a manufacturer's specification, are linked to where they come from. Most guides end with a numbered Sources list, and the figure in the text points to its entry, for example [1]. Shorter guides that rely on one or two sources link them in the text.
We prefer primary sources: the Gazette or ministry release, the standard itself, the published study or the manufacturer's own page.
## How we name standards
Standards are named by their number, with the edition or year where it matters, so readers can find the exact document. For example: ASPRS Positional Accuracy Standards for Digital Geospatial Data, Edition 2 (2023), and IEC TS 62446-3:2017 for thermographic inspection of PV plants. Indian standards and circulars are named by their IS number or circular number and date.
## Company figures and client names
Figures about DATA PKT itself, such as kilometres of highway data captured, team size or plans delivered, are limited to figures the company has approved for publication.
Client names appear on the site only where we are permitted to name them. Our case studies describe the work, the method and the outputs; they do not name the client, division or site unless we are permitted to, and their text does not give contract values or site coordinates. Project images have project names and GPS coordinates blurred or removed before they are published. Where a client cannot be named, the case study says so; one, for example, lists its client as "Private client (name withheld)".
## Dates and updates
Each guide shows the date it was first published. When we change the content of a guide, for example to add a section, correct a figure or reflect a new rule, we update it and show the "Updated" date beside the published date. The same dates are recorded in the page's structured data.
## No paid placements or sponsored content
We do not accept payment to feature, link to or recommend a product, manufacturer or company in our guides. There is no sponsored content on datapkt.com. Where a guide names equipment, it is to explain a specification.
## Why we do not publish prices
We do not publish prices or price bands. A survey's cost depends on its location, the area or corridor length, the accuracy needed and the deliverables, so we quote per project. Our survey cost page explains what sets the cost; to get a quote, send us the site and the outputs you need .
## How to report an error
If you find a mistake on any page, or a source that has changed, email consult@datapkt.com with the page address and what needs correcting. We check the point against the source and, where the page is wrong, correct it and change its "Updated" date.

Case study · Solar PV thermography
# Solar PV thermography in Tamil Nadu: what data QC catches before the report
At a utility-scale solar plant of about 340 MWp in Tamil Nadu, DATA PKT set the scope of the drone thermal and RGB acquisition and checked every block of data before analysis. This is what that check found, and what we now put in every solar flight brief.
Published 25 November 2026
Location
Tamil Nadu
Plant
About 340 MWp; 19 blocks; about 1.03 million modules
Scope
Drone thermal (radiometric IR) and RGB acquisition, processing and QC
Status
Re-flight of affected areas agreed; report follows on data that passes QC
In short: a partner flight crew flew a solar PV plant of about 340 MWp in Tamil Nadu in mid-October 2026, working to DATA PKT's scope. Before any thermal analysis, DATA PKT's processing QC checked the data against the IEC TS 62446-3 capture conditions, overlap and positioning. It found blocks split across several days, image positions off by several metres because there was no RTK or ground control, and edge tables not covered by two flight lines. DATA PKT identified the areas to be recaptured, and the partner agreed to re-fly them. The thermography report is prepared only from data that passes these checks.
## Scope and plant
The work was drone-based thermal (radiometric IR) and RGB data acquisition, with processing and quality control by DATA PKT. The flights were made by a partner flight crew working to DATA PKT's scope and to the plant layout (KML) that DATA PKT supplied.
Item | Quantity
Plant capacity | About 340 MWp, utility-scale solar PV
Blocks | 19
Module structures | 16,548
Strings | 33,096
Modules | 1,025,976 (about 1.03 million), rated 330–340 Wp
Flights | 12–18 October 2026
## How the plant was flown
The partner crew flew the plant between 12 and 18 October 2026 to DATA PKT's scope, using the plant layout KML to define each block. Intermittent rain forced pauses, so some blocks were flown over several days instead of in one session.
### The thermal capture rule
Thermal images only show module faults reliably when the modules are working under enough sunlight and conditions are stable. IEC TS 62446-3, the technical specification for aerial thermography of PV plants, sets a minimum irradiance of 600 W/m² in the plane of the modules. On this plant the rule was:
- IR imagery captured only before 16:00, and only with plane-of-array irradiance at or above 600 W/m².
- Flights after 16:00 captured RGB only.
Capture geometry for drone thermography of a PV plant (illustrative). On this plant, IR imagery was captured only before 16:00 and only with plane-of-array irradiance at or above 600 W/m².
For what each capture condition means in practice, see our guide to drone versus manual solar panel inspection .
## What processing QC found
DATA PKT checks every acquisition against the IEC TS 62446-3 conditions, overlap and positioning before analysis starts. On this plant the checks found three problems.
Check | What QC found | Why it matters for the report
One session per block | Several blocks split across days: one block over four days, nine blocks over three days | Irradiance, temperature and wind change from day to day, so modules in the same block can be imaged under different conditions, which makes temperature differences within the block harder to compare
Positioning | No RTK and no ground control, so image positions were off by several metres | The report locates each anomaly by block, string and module. A position error of several metres can place an anomaly on the wrong table or string
Overlap and coverage | Side overlap of about 65 % (flight lines 13.5 m apart), with lines stopping at the last table row, so some edge tables were not covered by two lines | Modules at block edges are seen in fewer images, so they are harder to map and check than modules in the middle of a block
### What DATA PKT did
- Requested the flight records and mission files from the partner: the DJI Pilot 2 FlightRecords and the KMZ mission files.
- Identified the areas to be recaptured.
- Passed the recapture areas to the partner, who agreed to re-fly them.
## Why QC comes before analysis
A solar thermography report is a list of anomalies, each with its type, location (block, string, module), temperature difference and severity. Every one of those fields depends on the acquisition. If images were captured outside valid conditions, if a block mixes days, if positions are off, or if edge tables are missing from the overlap, the report inherits the problem.
Checking the data first means the problem is fixed in the data, by recapture, rather than explained in the report. It also means the O&M team can trust that an anomaly marked on a table is on that table.
### What DATA PKT checks on every acquisition
- Capture conditions: that thermal images fall inside the IEC TS 62446-3 conditions, with plane-of-array irradiance at or above 600 W/m², and inside the capture window set for the site.
- Sessions: which days each block was flown on.
- Overlap and coverage: line spacing, side overlap, and whether edge tables are covered by two lines.
- Positioning: whether the images are tied to RTK, PPK or ground control, and how well they fit the plant layout.
## What we now specify in every solar flight brief
These are DATA PKT's requirements going forward, for our own crews and for partner crews flying to our survey plan:
- Positioning: RTK or PPK on the drone, or ground control points, so that anomalies land on the right table, string and module. See how GSD, GCPs and RTK set drone survey accuracy .
- Higher side overlap than was flown on this plant.
- One session per block: each block completed in one session where weather allows.
- Flight lines extended past the last table row, so edge tables are covered by two lines.
- Thermal capture only in valid conditions: IEC TS 62446-3 conditions, with plane-of-array irradiance at or above 600 W/m², and RGB only outside the thermal window.
- Flight logs and mission files delivered with the data, so that every block can be traced to how it was flown.
## Where the project stands
The partner has agreed to re-fly the areas DATA PKT identified. The thermography analysis and report are prepared only from data that passes the same checks.
See the service: solar plant drone thermography and thermal surveys .
Send us the plant layout KML and the outputs you need. We reply with a survey plan and quote.

## Frequently asked questions
Q: What did this project cover?
Drone-based thermal (radiometric IR) and RGB data acquisition at a utility-scale solar PV plant of about 340 MWp in Tamil Nadu, with processing and quality control by DATA PKT. The plant has 19 blocks, 16,548 module structures, 33,096 strings and about 1.03 million modules rated 330–340 Wp.
Q: What conditions must thermal images of a solar plant meet?
IEC TS 62446-3 sets a minimum irradiance of 600 W/m² in the plane of the modules, with stable conditions. On this plant, IR imagery was captured only before 16:00 and only with plane-of-array irradiance at or above 600 W/m². Flights after 16:00 were RGB only.
Q: Why do RTK or ground control matter for a thermography report?
The report locates each anomaly by block, string and module. Without RTK or ground control, image positions on this plant were off by several metres, which can place an anomaly on the wrong table or string. DATA PKT now specifies RTK or PPK, or ground control points, in every solar flight brief.
Q: Is the thermography report complete?
No. DATA PKT's QC identified the areas to be recaptured, and the partner flight crew agreed to re-fly them. The analysis and report are prepared only from data that passes the same checks.
